column5: Landmark on Judah's northern border
column7: Strength; confidence, a place on the border of Judah, on the side of Mount Jearim ([[@6015010|Josh. 15:10]]); probably identified with the modern village of Kesla, on the western mountains of Judah.

column5: Son of Nahor, Abraham's nephew
column6: as a devil, or a destroyer
column7: Chesed was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and Milcah.

column5: Town in Judah's southern region
column7: Ungodly, a town in the south of Judah ([[@6015030|Josh. 15:30]]); probably the same as Bethul (19:4) and Bethuel ([[@13004030|1 Chr. 4:30]]); now Khelasa.

column5: Border town of Issachar and Zebulun
column7: Fertile places; the loins, a town of Issachar, on the slopes of some mountain between Jezreel and Shunem ([[@6019018|Josh. 19:18]]).

column5: Son of David and Abigail the Carmelitess
column6: judgment of God; God my judge
column7: Protected by the father, David’s second son by Abigail ([[@10003003|2 Sam. 3:3]]); called also Daniel ([[@13003001|1 Chr. 3:1]]).

column5: Son of Elimelech and Naomi; husband of Orpah
column7: The pining one, the younger son of Elimelech and Naomi, and husband of Orpah, Ruth’s sister ([[@8001002|Ruth 1:2]]; [[@8004009|Ruth 4:9]]).

column5: Trading partner of Tyre
column7: A place or country unknown which, along with Sheba and Asshur, traded with Tyre ([[@26027023|Ezek. 27:23]]).

column5: Barzillai's son, accompanied David to Jerusalem
column7: Pining, probably the youngest son of Barzillai the Gileadite ([[@10019037-10019040|2 Sam. 19:37-40]]). The “habitation of Chimham” ([[@24041017|Jer. 41:17]]) was probably an inn or khan, which is the proper meaning of the Hebrew geruth , rendered “habitation”, established in later times in his possession at Bethlehem, which David gave to him as a reward for his loyalty in accompanying him to Jerusalem after the defeat of Absalom ([[@11002007|1 Kings 2:7]]).

column5: Lake in northern Israel; and the plain on its north west
column7: Lyre, the singular form of the word ([[@5003017|Deut. 3:17]]; [[@6019035|Josh. 19:35]]), which is also used in the plural form, Chinneroth, the name of a fenced city which stood near the shore of the lake of Galilee, a little to the south of Tiberias. The town seems to have given its name to a district, as appears from [[@11015020|1 Kings 15:20]], where the plural form of the word is used.

column5: Island visited by Paul on his journey
column7: Mentioned in [[@44020015|Acts 20:15]], an island in the Aegean Sea, about 5 miles distant from the mainland, having a roadstead, in the shelter of which Paul and his companions anchored for a night when on his third missionary return journey.

column5: Father of Elidad, a leader from Benjamin
column7: Chislon was the father of Elidad, a leader from the tribe of Benjamin.

column5: Town in Judah's Shephelah region
column6: it is a wall; the company of a lioness
column7: A man’s wall, a town in the plain of Judah ([[@6015040|Josh. 15:40]]).

column5: Believer whose household reported divisions in Corinthian church
column7: Verdure, a female Christian ([[@46001011|1 Cor. 1:11]]), some of whose household had informed Paul of the divided state of the Corinthian church.

column5: Town in Galilee; rebuked by Jesus for unbelief
column6: the secret; here is a mystery
column7: Named along with Bethsaida and Capernaum as one of the cities in which our Lord’s “mighty works” were done, and which was doomed to woe because of signal privileges neglected ([[@40011021|Matt. 11:21]]; [[@42010013|Luke 10:13]]).

column5: Herod's steward, whose wife Joanna supported Jesus
column7: Chuza, Herod's steward, was the husband of Joanna, who supported Jesus' ministry.

column5: Province in Asia Minor; Paul's birthplace and ministry area
column7: A maritime province in the south-east of Asia Minor. Tarsus, the birth-place of Paul, was one of its chief towns, and the seat of a celebrated school of philosophy. Its luxurious climate attracted to it many Greek residents after its incorporation with the Macedonian empire. It was formed into a Roman province, B.C. 67.

But the promises made to Abraham included the promise of redemption ([[@48003014|Gal. 3:14]]), a promise which has come upon us. The covenant with Abraham was a dispensation or a specific form of the covenant of grace, and circumcision was a sign and seal of that covenant. It had a spiritual meaning. It signified purification of the heart, inward circumcision effected by the Spirit ([[@5010016|Deut. 10:16]]; [[@5030006|Deut 30:6]]; [[@26044007|Ezek. 44:7]]; [[@44007051|Acts 7:51]]; [[@45002028|Rom. 2:28]]; [[@51002011|Col. 2:11]]).

The rendering of a Hebrew word bor , which means a receptacle for water conveyed to it; distinguished from beer , which denotes a place where water rises on the spot ([[@24002013|Jer. 2:13]]; [[@20005015|Prov. 5:15]]; [[@23036016|Isa. 36:16]]), a fountain. Cisterns are frequently mentioned in Scripture. The scarcity of springs in Palestine made it necessary to collect rain-water in reservoirs and cisterns ([[@4021022|Num. 21:22]]). (See WELL.) Empty cisterns were sometimes used as prisons ([[@24038006|Jer. 38:6]]; [[@25003053|Lam. 3:53]]; [[@19040002|Ps. 40:2]]; [[@19069015|Ps 69:15]]).

column5: Town in the wilderness of Judah
column7: The City of Salt was a town located in the wilderness of Judah, near the Dead Sea.

column5: Believer in Rome who sent greetings to Timothy
column7: A female Christian mentioned in [[@55004021|2 Tim. 4:21]].

column5: Roman emperor during Paul's ministry
column6: a name applied to those who are cut out of the womb
column7: The fourth Roman emperor. He succeeded Caligula (A.D. 41). Though in general he treated the Jews, especially those in Asia and Egypt, with great indulgence, yet about the middle of his reign (A.D. 49) he banished them all from Rome ([[@44018002|Acts 18:2]]). In this edict the Christians were included, as being, as was supposed, a sect of Jews.

column5: Fellow laborer with Paul in the gospel
column7: Mild, a Christian of Philippi, Paul’s “fellow-labourer,” whose name he mentions as “in the book of life” ([[@50004003|Phil. 4:3]]). It was an opinion of ancient writers that he was the Clement of Rome whose name is well known in church history, and that he was the author of an Epistle to the Corinthians, the only known manuscript of which is appended to the Alexandrian Codex, now in the British Museum. It is of some historical interest, and has given rise to much discussion among critics.

column5: City on the coast of Asia Minor
column7: A town and harbour on the extreme south-west of the peninsula of Doris in Asia Minor.

column5: Father of Shallum, who repaired the Fountain Gate
column7: Col-hozeh was the father of Shallum (or 'Shallun'), who repaired the Fountain Gate.

column5: Ancestor of Maaseiah, who settled in Jerusalem
column7: Col-hozeh was an ancestor of Maaseiah, who settled in Jerusalem after the exile.

column5: City in Phrygia; recipient of Paul's epistle
column7: Or Colosse, a city of Phrygia, on the Lycus, which is a tributary of the Maeander. It was about 12 miles above Laodicea, and near the great road from Ephesus to the Euphrates, and was consequently of some mercantile importance. It does not appear that Paul had visited this city when he wrote his letter to the church there ([[@51001002|Col. 1:2]]). He expresses in his letter to Philemon (ver. 1:22) his hope to visit it on being delivered from his imprisonment.

column5: Levite in charge of offerings during Hezekiah's reign
column7: Whom Jehovah hath set, a Levite placed over the tithes brought into the temple ([[@14035009|2 Chr. 35:9]]).

column5: Offering dedicated to God; temple treasury
column7: A Hebrew word adopted into the Greek of the New Testament and left untranslated. It occurs only once ([[@41007011|Mark 7:11]]). It means a gift or offering consecrated to God. Anything over which this word was once pronounced was irrevocably dedicated to the temple.

A Hebrew word adopted into the Greek of the New Testament and left untranslated. It occurs only once ([[@41007011|Mark 7:11]]). It means a gift or offering consecrated to God. Anything over which this word was once pronounced was irrevocably dedicated to the temple.

column5: Ancient Greek city; recipient of Paul's epistles
column7: A Grecian city, on the isthmus which joins the Peloponnesus to the mainland of Greece. It is about 48 miles west of Athens. The ancient city was destroyed by the Romans (B.C. 146), and that mentioned in the New Testament was quite a new city, having been rebuilt about a century afterwards and peopled by a colony of freedmen from Rome. It became under the Romans the seat of government for Southern Greece or Achaia ([[@44018012-44018016|Acts 18:12-16]]).

column5: Centurion, first Gentile convert to Christianity
column7: A centurion whose history is narrated in Acts 10. He was a “devout man,” and like the centurion of Capernaum, believed in the God of Israel. His residence at Caesrea probably brought him into contact with Jews who communicated to him their expectations regarding the Messiah; and thus he was prepared to welcome the message Peter brought him. He became the first fruit of the Gentile world to Christ. He and his family were baptized and admitted into the Christian church ([[@44010001|Acts 10:1]], [[@44010044|Acts 10:44]]-48).

column5: Fortified gate in Jerusalem's wall
column7: The Corner Gate was a fortified gate in Jerusalem's wall, mentioned in connection with repairs and measurements of the city.

column5: Island visited by Paul on his journey
column7: (written Cos in the R.V.), a small island, one of the Sporades in the Aegean Sea, in the north-west of Rhodes, off the coast of Caria. Paul on his return from his third missionary journey, passed the night here after sailing from Miletus ([[@44021001|Acts 21:1]]).

column5: Ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy
column7: Cosam is listed as an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy.

The word is used with reference to God’s revelation of himself in the way of promise or of favour to men. Thus God’s promise to Noah after the Flood is called a covenant (Gen. 9; [[@24033020|Jer. 33:20]], “my covenant”).

column5: Midianite woman killed for immorality with an Israelite
column7: Cozbi, a Midianite woman, was killed along with an Israelite man for their immorality.

column5: Companion of Paul who went to Galatia
column7: Increasing, probably one of the seventy disciples of Christ.

column5: Synagogue leader in Corinth who believed in Jesus
column7: Curled, the chief of the synagogue at Corinth ([[@44018008|Acts 18:8]]).

In the New Testament the instrument of crucifixion, and hence used for the crucifixion of Christ itself ([[@49002016|Eph. 2:16]]; [[@58012002|Heb. 12:2]]; [[@46001017|1 Cor. 1:17]], [[@46001018|1 Cor. 1:18]]; [[@48005011|Gal. 5:11]]; [[@48006012|Gal 6:12]], [[@48006014|Gal 6:14]]; [[@50003018|Phil. 3:18]]). The word is also used to denote any severe affliction or trial ([[@40010038|Matt. 10:38]]; [[@40016024|Matt 16:24]]; [[@41008034|Mark 8:34]]; [[@41010021|Mark 10:21]]). The forms in which the cross is represented are these: 1. The crux simplex (I), a “single piece without transom.” 2.

A common mode of punishment among heathen nations in early times. It is not certain whether it was known among the ancient Jews; probably it was not. The modes of capital punishment according to the Mosaic law were, by the sword (Ex. 21), strangling, fire (Lev. 20), and stoning (Deut. 21). This was regarded as the most horrible form of death, and to a Jew it would acquire greater horror from the curse in [[@5021023|Deut. 21:23]]. This punishment began by subjecting the sufferer to scourging.

Heb. ‘ammah; i.e., “mother of the arm,” the fore-arm, is a word derived from the Latin cubitus, the lower arm. It is difficult to determine the exact length of this measure, from the uncertainty whether it included the entire length from the elbow to the tip of the longest finger, or only from the elbow to the root of the hand at the wrist. The probability is that the longer was the original cubit. The common computation as to the length of the cubit makes it 20.24 inches for the ordinary cubit, and 21.888 inches for the sacred one. This is the same as the Egyptian measurements.

column5: Ancient region in Africa; associated with Egypt and Babylon
column7: A son, probably the eldest, of Ham, and the father of Nimrod ([[@1010008|Gen. 10:8]]; [[@13001010|1 Chr. 1:10]]). From him the land of Cush seems to have derived its name. The question of the precise locality of the land of Cush has given rise to not a little controversy. The second river of Paradise surrounded the whole land of Cush ([[@1002013|Gen. 2:13]], R.V.).

column5: Son of Ham; father of Nimrod and other descendants
column7: A son, probably the eldest, of Ham, and the father of Nimrod ([[@1010008|Gen. 10:8]]; [[@13001010|1 Chr. 1:10]]). From him the land of Cush seems to have derived its name. The question of the precise locality of the land of Cush has given rise to not a little controversy. The second river of Paradise surrounded the whole land of Cush ([[@1002013|Gen. 2:13]], R.V.).

column5: Benjamite mentioned in the title of Psalm 7
column7: Cush, a Benjamite, is mentioned in the title of Psalm 7, which David sang to the Lord.

column5: Unknown location, possibly related to Cush
column7: Probably a poetic or prolonged name of the land of Cush, the Arabian Cush ([[@35003007|Hab. 3:7]]). Some have, however, supposed this to be the same as Chushan-rishathaim ([[@7003008|Judg. 3:8]], [[@7003010|Judg. 3:10]]), i.e., taking the latter part of the name as a title or local appellation, Chushan “of the two iniquities” (= oppressing Israel, and provoking them to idolatry), a Mesopotamian king, identified by Rawlinson with Asshur-ris-ilim (the father of Tiglathpileser I.); but incorrectly, for the empire of Assyria was not yet founded.

column5: Ancestor of Jehudi, who read Jeremiah's scroll
column7: Cushi was the great grandfather of Jehudi, who was sent to fetch Baruch to read Jeremiah's scroll.

column5: Ancestor of Zephaniah the prophet
column7: Cushi was an ancestor of Zephaniah the prophet, mentioned in his genealogy.

column5: Babylonian city; origin of Samaritan settlers
column7: One of the Babylonian cities or districts from which Shalmaneser transplanted certain colonists to Samaria ([[@12017024|2 Kings 17:24]]). Some have conjectured that the “Cutheans” were identical with the “Cossaeans” who inhabited the hill-country to the north of the river Choaspes.

column5: Island in the Mediterranean Sea; early Christian community
column7: One of the largest islands of the Mediterranean, about 148 miles long and 40 broad. It is distant about 60 miles from the Syrian coast. It was the “Chittim” of the Old Testament ([[@4024024|Num. 24:24]]). The Greek colonists gave it the name of Kypros, from the cyprus, i.e., the henna (see CAMPHIRE), which grew on this island.

column5: City in North Africa; home of early Christians
column7: A city (now Tripoli) in Upper Libya, North Africa, founded by a colony of Greeks (B.C. 630). It contained latterly a large number of Jews, who were introduced into the city by Ptolemy, the son of Lagus, because he thought they would contribute to the security of the place. They increased in number and influence; and we are thus prepared for the frequent references to them in connection with the early history of Christianity. Simon, who bore our Lord’s cross, was a native of this place ([[@40027032|Matt. 27:32]]; [[@41015021|Mark 15:21]]).

column5: Persian Emperor who decreed the rebuilding of the Temple
column7: (Heb. Ko’resh), the celebrated “King of Persia” (Elam) who was conqueror of Babylon, and issued the decree of liberation to the Jews ([[@15001001|Ezra 1:1]], [[@15001002|Ezra 1:2]]). He was the son of Cambyses, the prince of Persia, and was born about B.C. 599. In the year B.C. 559 he became king of Persia, the kingdom of Media being added to it partly by conquest. Cyrus was a great military leader, bent on universal conquest.

column5: Border town of Zebulun
column7: Dabbesheth was a town on the border of the territory allocated to the tribe of Zebulun.

column5: Levitical city in Issachar's territory
column6: the word; the thing; a bee; obedient
column7: Pasture, a Levitical town of Issachar ([[@6019012|Josh. 19:12]]; [[@6021028|Josh 21:28]]), near the border of Zebulum. It is the modern small village of Deburich, at the base of Mount Tabor.

column5: Region on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea.
column7: A mountainous country on the eastern shore of the Adriatic, a part of the Roman province of Illyricum. It still bears its ancient name. During Paul’s second imprisonment at Rome, Titus left him to visit Dalmatia ([[@55004010|2 Tim. 4:10]]) for some unknown purpose. Paul had himself formerly preached in that region ([[@45015019|Rom. 15:19]]).

column5: Son of Haman, enemy of the Jews
column7: Dalphon was one of the ten sons of Haman who were killed and hanged.

column5: Woman who believed Paul's message in Athens
column7: A heifer, an Athenian woman converted to Christianity under the preaching of Paul ([[@44017034|Acts 17:34]]).

column5: Ancient city, capital of Syria, important in biblical history.
column6: a sack full of blood; the similitude of burning
column7: Activity, the most ancient of Oriental cities; the capital of Syria ([[@23007008|Isa. 7:8]]; [[@23017003|Isa 17:3]]); situated about 133 miles to the north of Jerusalem. Its modern name is Esh-Sham; i.e., “the East.” The situation of this city is said to be the most beautiful of all Western Asia. It is mentioned among the conquests of the Egyptian king Thothmes III.

column5: Israelite tribe; city in northern Israel; originally called Laish/Leshem.
column7: The fifth son of Jacob. His mother was Bilhah, Rachel’s maid ([[@1030006|Gen. 30:6]], “God hath judged me”, Heb. dananni). The blessing pronounced on him by his father was, “Dan shall judge his people” (49:16), probably in allusion to the judgeship of Samson, who was of the tribe of Dan. The tribe of Dan had their place in the march through the wilderness on the north side of the tabernacle ([[@4002025|Num. 2:25]], [[@4002031|Num. 2:31]]; 10:25).

column5: Fifth son of Jacob, founder of Israelite tribe
column7: The fifth son of Jacob. His mother was Bilhah, Rachel’s maid ([[@1030006|Gen. 30:6]], “God hath judged me”, Heb. dananni). The blessing pronounced on him by his father was, “Dan shall judge his people” (49:16), probably in allusion to the judgeship of Samson, who was of the tribe of Dan. The tribe of Dan had their place in the march through the wilderness on the north side of the tabernacle ([[@4002025|Num. 2:25]], [[@4002031|Num. 2:31]]; 10:25).

column5: Priest who returned from Babylonian exile
column6: judgment of God; God my judge
column7: Daniel, a priest, was among those who returned to Jerusalem from the Babylonian exile.

column5: Prophet in Babylon, known for wisdom and visions
column6: judgment of God; God my judge
column7: Daniel, also called Belteshazzar, was a prophet in Babylon known for his wisdom, integrity, and interpretation of dreams and visions.

column5: A city in the hill country of Judah.
column7: Murmuring, a city ([[@6015049|Josh. 15:49]]) in the mountains of Judah about 8 miles south-west of Hebron.

column5: Son of Zerah, grandson of Judah
column7: Pearl of wisdom, one of the four who were noted for their wisdom, but whom Solomon excelled ([[@11004031|1 Kings 4:31]]).

column5: Wise man surpassed by Solomon's wisdom
column7: Pearl of wisdom, one of the four who were noted for their wisdom, but whom Solomon excelled ([[@11004031|1 Kings 4:31]]).

column5: Persian king who decreed the rebuilding of the Temple
column7: Darius, king of Persia, issued a decree allowing the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem.

column5: Persian Emperor during the time of the Levites
column7: Darius the Persian ([[@16012022|Neh. 12:22]]) was probably the Darius II. (Ochus or Nothus) of profane history, the son of Artaxerxes Longimanus, who was the son and successor of Ahasuerus (Xerxes). There are some, however, who think that the king here meant was Darius III.

column5: Mede who became Emperor over Babylon
column7: Darius the Mede ([[@27011001|Dan. 11:1]]), “the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes” (9:1). On the death of Belshazzar the Chaldean he “received the kingdom” of Babylon as viceroy from Cyrus. During his brief reign (B.C. 538-536) Daniel was promoted to the highest dignity ([[@27006001|Dan. 6:1]], [[@27006002|Dan 6:2]]); but on account of the malice of his enemies he was cast into the den of lions. After his miraculous escape, a decree was issued by Darius enjoining “reverence for the God of Daniel” (6:26).

column5: Ancestor of a family of temple servants
column7: Darkon was the ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned from the Babylonian exile.

column5: Reubenite who rebelled against Moses and Aaron
column7: Welled; belonging to a fountain, a son of Eliab, a Reubenite, who joined Korah (q.v.) in his conspiracy, and with his accomplices was swallowed up by an earthquake ([[@4016001|Num. 16:1]]; [[@4026009|Num 26:9]]; [[@5011006|Deut. 11:6]]; [[@19106017|Ps. 106:17]]).

column5: Elder daughter of Lot; mother of Moab
column7: Lot's unnamed elder daughter, who bore Moab after the destruction of Sodom.

column5: Younger daughter of Lot; mother of Ben-ammi
column7: Lot's unnamed younger daughter, who bore Ben-ammi after the destruction of Sodom.

column5: The wife of Caiaphas the high priest.
column7: A reference to the unnamed wife of Caiaphas, the high priest who condemned Jesus.

column5: Married Hezron, bore Segub
column7: The daughter of Machir married Hezron and gave birth to Segub.

column5: Married Jehohanan, son of Tobiah the Ammonite
column7: The daughter of Meshullam was married to Jehohanan, the son of Tobiah the Ammonite.

column5: Daughter of Pharaoh - Rescued and adopted Moses
column7: Pharaoh's daughter rescued the infant Moses from the Nile and adopted him as her son.

column5: Daughter of Pharaoh - Wife of King Solomon
column7: Solomon married the daughter of Pharaoh, forming a political alliance with Egypt.

column5: Daughter of Putiel - Wife of Eleazar the priest
column7: The daughter of Putiel was the wife of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest.

column5: Married to a grandson of the high priest Eliashib
column7: The daughter of Sanballat the Horonite was married to a grandson of the high priest Eliashib.

column5: Married to one of Tobiah's sons
column7: The daughter of Shecaniah was married to one of Tobiah the Ammonite's sons.

column5: Anointed king of Israel, ancestor of Jesus Christ
column7: Beloved, the eighth and youngest son of Jesse, a citizen of Bethlehem. His father seems to have been a man in humble life. His mother’s name is not recorded. Some think she was the Nahash of [[@10017025|2 Sam. 17:25]].

column5: Amorite king of Eglon, defeated by Joshua
column7: The king of Eglon, one of the five Canaanitish kings who were hanged by Joshua ([[@6010003|Josh. 10:3]], [[@6010023|Josh. 10:23]]) after the victory at Gibeon. These kings fled and took refuge in a cave at Makkedah.

column5: Canaanite city captured by Joshua and Caleb's family.
column7: One of the eleven cities to the west of Hebron, in the highlands of Judah ([[@6015049|Josh. 15:49]]; [[@7001011-7001015|Judg. 1:11-15]]). It was originally one of the towns of the Anakim ([[@6015015|Josh. 15:15]]), and was also called Kirjath-sepher (q.v.) and Kirjath-sannah (49). Caleb, who had conquered and taken possession of the town and district of Hebron ([[@6014006-6014015|Josh. 14:6-15]]), offered the hand of his daughter to any one who would successfully lead a party against Debir.

column5: A place on the northern border of Judah.
column7: A place near the “valley of Achor” ([[@6015007|Josh. 15:7]]), on the north boundary of Judah, between Jerusalem and Jericho.

column5: Rebekah's nurse, buried near Bethel
column7: Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died and was buried under an oak below Bethel.

column5: Prophetess and judge who led Israel to victory over Canaanites.
column7: A prophetess, “wife” (woman?) of Lapidoth. Jabin, the king of Hazor, had for twenty years held Israel in degrading subjection. The spirit of patriotism seemed crushed out of the nation. In this emergency Deborah roused the people from their lethargy.

column5: A group of ten Hellenistic cities in ancient Palestine.
column7: Ten cities=deka, ten, and polis, a city, a district on the east and south-east of the Sea of Galilee containing “ten cities,” which were chiefly inhabited by Greeks. It included a portion of Bashan and Gilead, and is mentioned three times in the New Testament ([[@40004025|Matt. 4:25]]; [[@41005020|Mark 5:20]]; [[@41007031|Mark 7:31]]).

column5: Grandson of Cush, son of Raamah
column7: A son of Raamah ([[@1010007|Gen. 10:7]]). His descendants are mentioned in [[@23021013|Isa. 21:13]], and [[@26027015|Ezek. 27:15]].

column5: Grandson of Abraham through Jokshan
column7: A son of Jokshan, Abraham’s son by Keturah ([[@13001032|1 Chr. 1:32]]). His descendants settled on the Syrian borders about the territory of Edom.

column5: An Arabian people and region, involved in trade.
column7: A son of Raamah ([[@1010007|Gen. 10:7]]). His descendants are mentioned in [[@23021013|Isa. 21:13]], and [[@26027015|Ezek. 27:15]].

column5: People group who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem
column7: The Dehavites were a people group who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem during the time of Ezra.

column5: Son of Abinadab, one of Solomon's twelve officers
column7: Ben-Deker was one of Solomon's twelve officers in charge of providing food for the king and his household.

column5: Descendant of David through Jeconiah
column7: Delaiah was a descendant of David through Jeconiah, mentioned in the genealogy of David's descendants.

column5: Priest in charge of the twenty-third division
column7: The head of the twenty-third division of the priestly order ([[@13024018|1 Chr. 24:18]]).

column5: Ancestor of a family that returned from exile
column7: The head of one of the bands of exiles that returned under Zerubbabel to Jerusalem ([[@15002060|Ezra 2:60]]; [[@16007062|Neh. 7:62]]).

column5: Father of Shemaiah, who tried to deceive Nehemiah
column7: Delaiah was the father of Shemaiah, who tried to deceive Nehemiah into hiding in the temple.

column5: Official during King Jehoiakim's reign
column7: A son of Shemaiah, and one of the courtiers to whom Jeremiah’s first roll of prophecy was read ([[@24036012|Jer. 36:12]]).

column5: Philistine woman who betrayed Samson
column7: Languishing, a Philistine woman who dwelt in the valley of Sorek ([[@7016004-7016020|Judg. 16:4-20]]). She was bribed by the “lords of the Philistines” to obtain from Samson the secret of his strength and the means of overcoming it ([[@7016004-7016018|Judg. 16:4-18]]). She tried on three occasions to obtain from him this secret in vain.

column5: Companion of Paul who later deserted him
column7: A companion and fellow-labourer of Paul during his first imprisonment at Rome ([[@57001001|Philemon 1]]:24; [[@51004014|Col. 4:14]]).

column5: Silversmith who opposed Paul in Ephesus
column6: belonging to corn, or to Ceres
column7: A silversmith at Ephesus, whose chief occupation was to make “silver shrines for Diana” (q.v.), [[@44019024|Acts 19:24]], i.e., models either of the temple of Diana or of the statue of the goddess. This trade brought to him and his fellow-craftsmen “no small gain,” for these shrines found a ready sale among the countless thousands who came to this temple from all parts of Asia Minor.

(Gr. denarion), a silver coin of the value of about 7 1/2d. or 8d. of our present money. It is thus rendered in the New Testament, and is more frequently mentioned than any other coin ([[@40018028|Matt. 18:28]]; [[@40020002|Matt 20:2]], [[@40020009|Matt 20:9]], [[@40020013|Matt 20:13]]; [[@41006037|Mark 6:37]]; [[@41014005|Mark 14:5]], etc.). It was the daily pay of a Roman soldier in the time of Christ. In the reign of Edward III. an English penny was a labourer’s day’s wages.

column5: City in Lycaonia visited by Paul on missionary journeys.
column7: A small town on the eastern part of the upland plain of Lycaonia, about 20 miles from Lystra. Paul passed through Derbe on his route from Cilicia to Iconium, on his second missionary journey ([[@44016001|Acts 16:1]]), and probably also on his third journey (18:23; 19:1). On his first journey (14:20, 21) he came to Derbe from the other side; i.e., from Iconium. It was the native place of Gaius, one of Paul’s companions (20:4).

column5: Father of Eliasaph, leader of the tribe of Gad
column7: Deuel, also called Reuel, was the father of Eliasaph, who was the leader of the tribe of Gad during the wilderness journey.

(Gr. diabolos), a slanderer, the arch-enemy of man’s spiritual interest ([[@18001006|Job 1:6]]; [[@66002010|Rev. 2:10]]; [[@38003001|Zech. 3:1]]). He is called also “the accuser of the brethen” ([[@66012010|Rev. 12:10]]). In [[@3017007|Lev. 17:7]] the word “devil” is the translation of the Hebrew sair , meaning a “goat” or “satyr” ([[@23013021|Isa. 13:21]]; [[@23034014|Isa 34:14]]), alluding to the wood-daemons, the objects of idolatrous worship among the heathen.

column5: Father of Gomer, Hosea's wife
column7: Doubled cakes, the mother of Gomer, who was Hosea’s wife ([[@28001003|Hos. 1:3]]).

column5: A place where the Israelites camped during their wilderness wanderings.
column6: hidden in a cluster of fig trees
column7: Two cakes, a city of Moab, on the east of the Dead Sea ([[@4033046|Num. 33:46]]; [[@24048022|Jer. 48:22]]).

column5: Moabite city, allotted to Gad, later possessed by Moab.
column7: A city in Moab ([[@4021030|Num. 21:30]]); called also Dibon-gad (33:45), because it was built by Gad and Dimon ([[@23015009|Isa. 15:9]]). It has been identified with the modern Diban, about 3 miles north of the Arnon and 12 miles east of the Dead Sea.

column5: A city in Judah, inhabited by the tribe of Judah.
column7: A city of the tribe of Judah, inhabited after the Captivity ([[@16011025|Neh. 11:25]]); called also Dimonah ([[@6015022|Josh. 15:22]]).

column5: Father of Shelomith, whose son blasphemed God's name
column7: Dibri, of the tribe of Dan, was the father of Shelomith, whose son blasphemed the name of God and was stoned to death.

column5: Descendant of Shem through Joktan
column7: Diklah was a descendant of Shem through Joktan, mentioned in the genealogies of Genesis and 1 Chronicles.

column5: A city in the lowlands of Judah.
column7: Dilean, a city located in the lowlands of Judah (<ref="Joshua 15:38">Joshua 15:38</ref>).

column5: A Levitical city in the territory of Zebulun.
column7: Dunghill, a city of Zebulun given to the Merarite Levites ([[@6021035|Josh. 21:35]]).

column5: A city in the Negev region of Judah.
column7: Dimonah, a city located in the Negev region of Judah (<ref="Joshua 15:22">Joshua 15:22</ref>).

column5: Daughter of Jacob and Leah
column7: Judged; vindicated, daughter of Jacob by Leah, and sister of Simeon and Levi ([[@1030021|Gen. 30:21]]). She was seduced by Shechem, the son of Hamor, the Hivite chief, when Jacob’s camp was in the neighbourhood of Shechem. This led to the terrible revenge of Simeon and Levi in putting the Shechemites to death (Gen. 34). Jacob makes frequent reference to this deed of blood with abhorrence and regret ([[@1034030|Gen. 34:30]]; [[@1049005-1049007|Gen 49:5-7]]).

column5: People group who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem
column7: The Dinaites were one of the groups who wrote to King Artaxerxes, opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem during Ezra's time.

column5: The capital city of Edom during Bela's reign.
column7: Robbers’ den, an Edomitish city, the capital of king Bela ([[@1036032|Gen. 36:32]]).

column5: Areopagite who believed Paul's message in Athens
column7: The Areopagite, one of Paul’s converts at Athens ([[@44017034|Acts 17:34]]).

column5: Church leader who opposed John
column7: Jove-nourished, rebuked by John for his pride ([[@64001001|3 John 1]]:9).

column5: Descendant of Seir the Horite
column7: Antelope, the youngest son of Seir the Horite, head of one of the tribes of Idumaea ([[@1036021|Gen. 36:21]], [[@1036028|Gen. 36:28]], [[@1036030|Gen. 36:30]]).

column5: Descendant of Seir the Horite, son of Anah
column7: Dishon was a descendant of Seir the Horite and the son of Anah, mentioned in the genealogies of Esau's family.

column5: Grandson of Seir the Horite through Anah
column7: Dishon was a grandson of Seir the Horite through Anah, mentioned in the genealogies of Esau's family.

column5: A tree near Shechem, associated with pagan divination practices.
column7: The Diviners' Oak was a tree near Shechem, likely associated with pagan divination practices (<ref="Judges 9:37">Judges 9:37</ref>).

column5: A place near where Moses delivered his final speeches.
column7: Region of gold, a place in the desert of Sinai, on the western shore of the Elanitic gulf ([[@5001001|Deut. 1:1]]).

column5: Descendants of Javan, son of Japheth
column7: Leaders, a race descended from Javan ([[@1010004|Gen. 10:4]]). They are known in profane history as the Dardani, originally inhabiting Illyricum. They were a semi-Pelasgic race, and in the ethnographical table (Gen. 10) they are grouped with the Chittim (q.v.). In [[@13001007|1 Chr. 1:7]], they are called Rodanim.

column5: Prophet who rebuked Jehoshaphat for his alliance with Ahaziah
column7: Dodavahu, son of Eliezer of Mareshah, prophesied against Jehoshaphat for his alliance with Ahaziah, king of Israel.

column5: Son of Puah, a judge of Israel
column7: Dodo, son of Puah, was a judge of Israel who led the nation for 23 years.

column5: Father of Eleazar, one of David's mighty men
column7: An Ahohite, father of Eleazar, who was one of David’s three heroes ([[@10023009|2 Sam. 23:9]]; [[@13011012|1 Chr. 11:12]]).

column5: Father of Elhanan, one of David's mighty men
column7: A Bethlehemite, and father of Elhanan, who was one of David’s thirty heroes ([[@10023024|2 Sam. 23:24]]).

column5: Edomite chief shepherd who betrayed David to Saul
column7: Fearful, an Edomite, the chief overseer of Saul’s flocks ([[@9021007|1 Sam. 21:7]]). At the command of Saul he slew the high priest Ahimelech (q.v.) at Nob, together with all the priests to the number of eighty-five persons. (Comp.

The ass’s colt (Heb. ‘air), mentioned [[@7010004|Judg. 10:4]]; [[@7012014|Judg 12:14]]. It is rendered “foal” in [[@1032015|Gen. 32:15]]; [[@1049011|Gen 49:11]]. (Comp. [[@18011012|Job 11:12]]; [[@23030006|Isa. 30:6]].) The ass is an unclean animal, because it does not chew the cud ([[@3011026|Lev. 11:26]]. Comp. [[@12006025|2 Kings 6:25]]).

column5: A place where the Israelites camped during their wilderness wanderings.
column7: Knocking, an encampment of the Israelites in the wilderness ([[@4033012|Num. 33:12]]).

column5: A Canaanite city, later allotted to Manasseh but not conquered.
column7: Dwelling, the Dora of the Romans, an ancient royal city of the Canaanites ([[@6011001|Josh. 11:1]], [[@6011002|Josh 11:2]]; [[@6012023|Josh 12:23]]). It was the most southern settlement of the Phoenicians on the coast of Syria. The original inhabitants seem never to have been expelled, although they were made tributary by David. It was one of Solomon’s commissariat districts ([[@7001027|Judg. 1:27]]; [[@11004011|1 Kings 4:11]]).

column5: A place where Joseph found his brothers and was sold.
column7: Two wells, a famous pasture-ground where Joseph found his brethren watching their flocks. Here, at the suggestion of Judah, they sold him to the Ishmaelite merchants ([[@1037017|Gen. 37:17]]). It is mentioned on monuments in B.C. 1600. It was the residence of Elisha ([[@12006013|2 Kings 6:13]]), and the scene of a remarkable vision of chariots and horses of fire surrounding the mountain on which the city stood.

column5: A water source near Jerusalem, mentioned in Nehemiah's wall inspection.
column7: The Dragon Spring was a water source near Jerusalem, mentioned during Nehemiah's inspection of the city walls (<ref="Nehemiah 2:13">Nehemiah 2:13</ref>).

Consisted of wine ([[@4015005|Num. 15:5]]; [[@28009004|Hos. 9:4]]) poured around the altar ([[@2030009|Ex. 30:9]]). Joined with meat-offerings ([[@4006015|Num. 6:15]], [[@4006017|Num. 6:17]]; [[@12016013|2 Kings 16:13]]; [[@29001009|Joel 1:9]], [[@29001013|Joel 1:13]]; 2:14), presented daily ([[@2029040|Ex. 29:40]]), on the Sabbath ([[@4028009|Num. 28:9]]), and on feast-days (28:14). One-fourth of an hin of wine was required for one lamb, one-third for a ram, and one-half for a bullock ([[@4015005|Num. 15:5]]; [[@4028007|Num 28:7]], [[@4028014|Num 28:14]]).

column5: Jewish wife of Felix, the Roman governor
column7: Third and youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I. ([[@44012001-44012004|Acts 12:1-4]], [[@44012020-44012023|Acts 12:20-23]]). Felix, the Roman procurator of Judea, induced her to leave her husband, Azizus, the king of Emesa, and become his wife. She was present with Felix when Paul reasoned of “righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come” ([[@44024024|Acts 24:24]]).

column5: Son of Ishmael and grandson of Abraham
column7: Silence, (comp. [[@19094017|Ps. 94:17]]), the fourth son of Ishmael; also the tribe descended from him; and hence also the region in Arabia which they inhabited ([[@1025014|Gen. 25:14]]; [[@13001030|1 Chr. 1:30]]). There was also a town of this name in Judah ([[@6015052|Josh. 15:52]]), which has been identified with ed-Domeh, about 10 miles southwest of Hebron.

column5: A city in the hill country of Judah.
column7: Silence, (comp. [[@19094017|Ps. 94:17]]), the fourth son of Ishmael; also the tribe descended from him; and hence also the region in Arabia which they inhabited ([[@1025014|Gen. 25:14]]; [[@13001030|1 Chr. 1:30]]). There was also a town of this name in Judah ([[@6015052|Josh. 15:52]]), which has been identified with ed-Domeh, about 10 miles southwest of Hebron.

column5: A city or region in Arabia, recipient of a prophetic oracle.
column7: Silence, (comp. [[@19094017|Ps. 94:17]]), the fourth son of Ishmael; also the tribe descended from him; and hence also the region in Arabia which they inhabited ([[@1025014|Gen. 25:14]]; [[@13001030|1 Chr. 1:30]]). There was also a town of this name in Judah ([[@6015052|Josh. 15:52]]), which has been identified with ed-Domeh, about 10 miles southwest of Hebron.

column5: A gate in Jerusalem's wall, possibly used for waste removal.
column7: The Dung Gate was one of the gates in Jerusalem's wall, possibly used for removing waste from the city (<ref="Nehemiah 2:13; 3:13-14; 12:31">Nehemiah 2:13; 3:13-14; 12:31</ref>).

column5: A plain in Babylon where Nebuchadnezzar set up a statue.
column7: The circle, the plain near Babylon in which Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image, mentioned in [[@27003001|Dan. 3:1]]. The place still retains its ancient name. On one of its many mounds the pedestal of what must have been a colossal statue has been found.

column5: A direction associated with invading armies and nomadic tribes.
column7: The orient (mizrah); the rising of the sun. Thus “the east country” is the country lying to the east of Syria, the Elymais ([[@38008007|Zech. 8:7]]). (2). Properly what is in front of one, or a country that is before or in front of another; the rendering of the word kedem . In pointing out the quarters, a Hebrew always looked with his face toward the east.

column5: A gate in Jerusalem's wall, near the house of Shemaiah.
column7: The East Gate was a gate in Jerusalem's wall, located near the house of Shemaiah (<ref="Nehemiah 3:29">Nehemiah 3:29</ref>).

column5: Son of Shobal and descendant of Seir the Horite
column7: A descendant of Seir the Horite ([[@1036023|Gen. 36:23]]).

column5: A mountain in Canaan, site of curses and blessings ceremony.
column7: Shady; or Zalmon (q.v.), a hill covered with dark forests, south of Shechem, from which Abimelech and his men gathered wood to burn that city ([[@7009048|Judg. 9:48]]). In [[@19068014|Ps. 68:14]] the change from war to peace is likened to snow on the dark mountain, as some interpret the expression. Others suppose the words here mean that the bones of the slain left unburied covered the land, so that it seemed to be white as if covered with snow. The reference, however, of the psalm is probably to Josh. 11 and 12.

column5: Father of Gaal, who opposed Abimelech's rule
column7: Slave, the father of Gaal, in whom the men of Shechem “put confidence” in their conspiracy against Abimelech ([[@7009026|Judg. 9:26]], [[@7009026|Judg 9:26]], [[@7009030|Judg 9:30]], [[@7009031|Judg 9:31]]).

column5: Descendant of Adin who returned with Ezra
column7: Slave, the father of Gaal, in whom the men of Shechem “put confidence” in their conspiracy against Abimelech ([[@7009026|Judg. 9:26]], [[@7009026|Judg 9:26]], [[@7009030|Judg 9:30]], [[@7009031|Judg 9:31]]).

column5: Ethiopian eunuch who rescued Jeremiah from a cistern
column7: A servant of the king; probably an official title, an Ethiopian, “one of the eunuchs which was in the king’s house;” i.e., in the palace of Zedekiah, king of Judah.

column5: A stone memorial set up by Samuel to commemorate victory.
column7: Stone of help, the memorial stone set up by Samuel to commemorate the divine assistance to Israel in their great battle against the Philistines, whom they totally routed ([[@9007007-9007012|1 Sam. 7:7-12]]) at Aphek, in the neighbourhood of Mizpeh, in Benjamin, near the western entrance of the pass of Beth-horon. On this very battle-field, twenty years before, the Philistines routed the Israelites, “and slew of the army in the field about four thousand men” (4:1, 2; here, and at 5:1, called “Eben-ezer” by anticipation).

column5: Ancestor of Abraham; father of Peleg and Joktan
column7: . The third post-duluvian patriach after Shem ([[@1010024|Gen. 10:24]]; [[@1011014|Gen 11:14]]). He is regarded as the founder of the Hebrew race (10:21; [[@4024024|Num. 24:24]]).

column5: A Gadite chief during the reign of Jotham
column7: One of the seven heads of the families of the Gadites ([[@13005013|1 Chr. 5:13]]).

column5: Son of Elpaal, a Benjamite
column7: Eber was a son of Elpaal and a descendant of Benjamin, mentioned in the genealogy of the Benjamites.

column5: Son of Shashak, a Benjamite
column7: Eber was a son of Shashak and a descendant of Benjamin, mentioned in the genealogy of the Benjamites.

column5: A priest during the time of Joiakim
column7: The head of the priestly family of Amok in the time of Zerubbabel ([[@16012020|Neh. 12:20]]).

column5: A town allotted to the tribe of Issachar.
column7: Tin, or white, a town in the tribe of Issachar ([[@6019020|Josh. 19:20]]), at the north of the plain of Esdraelon.

column5: Levite descendant of Korah, ancestor of temple gatekeepers
column6: a father that gathers or adds
column7: Father of gathering; the gatherer, the youngest of the three sons of Korah the Levite, head of a family of Korhites ([[@2006024|Ex. 6:24]]); called Ebisaph ([[@13006037|1 Chr. 6:37]]).

column5: A city in Media where a significant scroll was found.
column7: Ecbatana was a city in Media where a scroll was found containing a decree by King Cyrus (<ref="Ezra 6:2">Ezra 6:2</ref>).

column5: The perfect garden where God placed Adam and Eve.
column7: The garden in which our first parents dewlt ([[@1002008-1002017|Gen. 2:8-17]]). No geographical question has been so much discussed as that bearing on its site. It has been placed in Armenia, in the region west of the Caspian Sea, in Media, near Damascus, in Palestine, in Southern Arabia, and in Babylonia. The site must undoubtedly be sought for somewhere along the course of the great streams the Tigris and the Euphrates of Western Asia, in “the land of Shinar” or Babylonia.

column5: A city or region, possibly in Mesopotamia or Syria.
column7: One of the markets whence the merchants of Tyre obtained richly embroidered stuffs ([[@26027023|Ezek. 27:23]]); the same, probably, as that mentioned in [[@12019012|2 Kings 19:12]], and [[@23037012|Isa. 37:12]], as the name of a region conquered by the Assyrians.

column5: Levite who assisted in Hezekiah's temple cleansing
column7: Son of Joah, and one of the Levites who assisted in reforming the public worship of the sanctuary in the time of Hezekiah ([[@14029012|2 Chr. 29:12]]).

column5: Levite appointed by Hezekiah to distribute offerings
column7: Eden, along with other Levites, was appointed by Hezekiah to distribute the contributions, tithes, and dedicated gifts to his brethren in their cities.

column5: A town in the Negev region of Judah.
column7: A city in the south of Judah, on the border of Idumea ([[@6015021|Josh. 15:21]]).

column5: Descendant of Benjamin, son of Beriah
column7: Eder was a descendant of Benjamin, mentioned as one of the sons of Beriah in the genealogy of the Benjamites.

column5: Levite descendant of Merari during David's reign
column7: The second of the three sons of Mushi, of the family of Merari, appointed to the Levitical office ([[@13023023|1 Chr. 23:23]]; [[@13024030|1 Chr. 24:30]]).

column5: Descendants of Esau; enemy nation southeast of Israel
column7: Idumea ([[@23034005|Isa. 34:5]], [[@23034006|Isa. 34:6]]; [[@26035015|Ezek. 35:15]]). “The field of Edom” ([[@1032003|Gen. 32:3]]), “the land of Edom” ([[@1036016|Gen. 36:16]]), was mountainous (Obad. 1:8, 9, 19, 21). It was called the land, or “the mountain of Seir,” the rough hills on the east side of the Arabah. It extended from the head of the Gulf of Akabah, the Elanitic gulf, to the foot of the Dead Sea ([[@11009026|1 Kings 9:26]]), and contained, among other cities, the rock-hewn Sela (q.v.), generally known by the Greek name Petra ([[@12014007|2 Kings 14:7]]).

column5: Amorite city defeated by Moses and the Israelites
column6: a very great mass, or cloud
column7: One of the chief towns of the kingdom of Bashan ([[@6012004|Josh. 12:4]], [[@6012005|Josh. 12:5]]). Here Og was defeated by the Israelites, and the strength of the Amorites broken ([[@4021033-4021035|Num. 21:33-35]]). It subsequently belonged to Manasseh, for a short time apparently, and afterwards became the abode of banditti and outlaws ([[@6013031|Josh. 13:31]]). It has been identified with the modern Edr’a, which stands on a rocky promontory on the south-west edge of the Lejah (the Argob of the Hebrews, and Trachonitis of the Greeks).

column5: David's wife and mother of Ithream
column7: A heifer, one of David’s wives, and mother of Ithream ([[@10003005|2 Sam. 3:5]]; [[@13003003|1 Chr. 3:3]]).

column5: Moabite city; its destruction prophesied by Isaiah
column7: Two ponds, ([[@23015008|Isa. 15:8]]), probably En-eglaim of [[@26047010|Ezek. 47:10]].

column5: Moabite city; its destruction prophesied by Isaiah and Jeremiah
column7: Eglath-shelishiyah, a Moabite city whose destruction was prophesied by Isaiah and Jeremiah.

column5: Amorite king of Lachish; city in Judah
column7: A city in Judah, near Lachish ([[@6015039|Josh. 15:39]]). It was destroyed by Joshua (10:5, 6). It has been identified with Tell Nejileh, 6 miles south of Tell Hesy or Ajlan, north-west of Lachish.

column5: King of Moab who oppressed Israel
column7: Chieftain or king of one of the Moabite tribes ([[@7003012-7003014|Judg. 3:12-14]]). Having entered into an alliance with Ammon and Amalek, he overran the trans-Jordanic region, and then crossing the Jordan, seized on Jericho, the “city of palm trees,” which had been by this time rebuilt, but not as a fortress. He made this city his capital, and kept Israel in subjection for eighteen years.

column5: Descendant of Ham, ancestor of African peoples
column7: The land of the Nile and the pyramids, the oldest kingdom of which we have any record, holds a place of great significance in Scripture. The Egyptians belonged to the white race, and their original home is still a matter of dispute.

column5: Ancient nation; Israelites enslaved there; plagues and Exodus
column7: The land of the Nile and the pyramids, the oldest kingdom of which we have any record, holds a place of great significance in Scripture. The Egyptians belonged to the white race, and their original home is still a matter of dispute.

column5: Likely the Gulf of Suez, part of the Red Sea
column7: The Egypt Sea, probably referring to the Gulf of Suez, an arm of the Red Sea.

column5: Left-handed Benjamite judge who delivered Israel from Moabite oppression
column7: The son of Gera, of the tribe of Benjamin ([[@7003015|Judg. 3:15]]). After the death of Othniel the people again fell into idolatry, and Eglon, the king of Moab, uniting his bands with those of the Ammonites and the Amalekites, crossed the Jordan and took the city of Jericho, and for eighteen years held that whole district in subjection, exacting from it an annual tribute. At length Ehud, by a stratagem, put Eglon to death with a two-edged dagger a cubit long, and routed the Moabites at the fords of the Jordan, putting 10,000 of them to death.

column5: A Benjamite, son of Bilhan.
column7: A descendant of Benjamin ([[@13007010|1 Chr. 7:10]]), his great-grandson.

column5: Son of Ram, descendant of Judah
column7: Eker was a son of Ram and descendant of Judah.

column5: One of the five major Philistine city-states
column7: Firm-rooted, the most northerly of the five towns belonging to the lords of the Philistines, about 11 miles north of Gath. It was assigned to Judah ([[@6013003|Josh. 13:3]]), and afterwards to Dan (19:43), but came again into the full possession of the Philistines ([[@9005010|1 Sam. 5:10]]). It was the last place to which the Philistines carried the ark before they sent it back to Israel ([[@9005010|1 Sam. 5:10]]; [[@9006001-9006008|1 Sam. 6:1-8]]). There was here a noted sanctuary of Baal-zebub (2 Kings 1: 2, 3, 6, 16).

column5: Wilderness area where the Horites were defeated by Chedorlaomer
column7: El-paran, a wilderness region where Chedorlaomer and his allies defeated the Horites during their campaign.

column5: Son of Uzzi, an official under Solomon
column7: Ela, the son of Uzzi, served as an official under King Solomon.

column5: A chief of Edom, descendant of Esau
column7: One of the Edomite chiefs or “dukes” of Mount Seir ([[@1036041|Gen. 36:41]]).

column5: Son of Baasha, king of Israel
column7: The son and successor of Baasha, king of Israel ([[@11016008-11016010|1 Kings 16:8-10]]). He was killed while drunk by Zimri, one of the captains of his chariots, and was the last king of the line of Baasha.

column5: Father of Hoshea, the last king of Israel
column7: The father of Hoshea, the last king of Israel ([[@12015030|2 Kings 15:30]]; [[@12017001|2 Kings 17:1]]).

column5: Son of Uzzi, a Benjamite
column7: Elah was a Benjamite, the son of Uzzi.

column5: Site of David's victory over Goliath
column7: The Elah Valley, where David defeated the Philistine giant Goliath.

column5: Son of Shem, grandson of Noah
column6: a young man; a virgin; a secret
column7: Highland, the son of Shem ([[@1010022|Gen. 10:22]]), and the name of the country inhabited by his descendants (14:1, 9; [[@23011011|Isa. 11:11]]; [[@23021002|Isa 21:2]], etc.) lying to the east of Babylonia, and extending to the shore of the Mediterranean, a distance in a direct line of about 1,000 miles. The name Elam is an Assyrian word meaning “high.” “The inhabitants of Elam, or ‘the Highlands,’ to the east of Babylon, were called Elamites. They were divided into several branches, speaking different dialects of the same agglutinative language.

column5: Ancient kingdom east of Babylon; ally and enemy of Israel
column6: a young man; a virgin; a secret
column7: Highland, the son of Shem ([[@1010022|Gen. 10:22]]), and the name of the country inhabited by his descendants (14:1, 9; [[@23011011|Isa. 11:11]]; [[@23021002|Isa 21:2]], etc.) lying to the east of Babylonia, and extending to the shore of the Mediterranean, a distance in a direct line of about 1,000 miles. The name Elam is an Assyrian word meaning “high.” “The inhabitants of Elam, or ‘the Highlands,’ to the east of Babylon, were called Elamites. They were divided into several branches, speaking different dialects of the same agglutinative language.

column5: Son of Shashak, a Benjamite

column7: En-hazor, a city allotted to the tribe of Naphtali during the division of the Promised Land.

In process of time Jacob, following his natural bent, became a shepherd; while Esau, a “son of the desert,” devoted himself to the perilous and toilsome life of a huntsman.

It is identified with es-Semu’a, a village about 3 1/2 miles east of Socoh, and 7 or 8 miles south of Hebron, around which there are ancient remains of the ruined city. It is the centre of the “south country” or Negeb.
