column7: “Of the Abi-ezrites.” A city of Manasseh, 6 miles south-west of Shechem, the residence of Gideon ([[@7006011|Judg. 6:11]]; [[@7008027|Judg 8:27]], [[@7008032|Judg 8:32]]). After his great victory over the Midianites, he slew at this place the captive kings (8:18-21). He then assumed the function of high priest, and sought to make Ophrah what Shiloh should have been.

column5: Son of Meonothai
column7: Ophrah was the son of Meonothai, a descendant of Judah.

column5: Midianite prince, killed by Ephraimites
column7: Raven, a prince of Midian, who, being defeated by Gideon and put to straits, was slain along with Zeeb ([[@7007020-7007025|Judg. 7:20-25]]).

column5: Son of Jerahmeel
column7: Ash or pine, the son of Jerahmeel ([[@13002025|1 Chr. 2:25]]).

column5: Jebusite, sold threshing floor to David
column7: Ornan (Araunah) was a Jebusite who sold his threshing floor to King David, which later became the site of Solomon's temple.

column5: Naomi's daughter-in-law, stayed in Moab
column7: Forelock or fawn, a Moabitess, the wife of Chilion ([[@8001004|Ruth 1:4]]; [[@8004010|Ruth 4:10]]).

column5: Assyrian king who settled people in Samaria
column7: Osnappar (probably Ashurbanipal) was an Assyrian king who brought people from various regions and settled them in Samaria.

column5: Son of Shemaiah, gatekeeper of the ark
column7: A lion of Jehovah, a son of Shemaiah, and one of the temple porters in the time of David ([[@13026007|1 Chr. 26:7]]).

column5: First judge of Israel, Caleb's nephew
column7: Lion of God, the first of the judges. His wife Achsah was the daughter of Caleb ([[@6015016|Josh. 15:16]], [[@6015017|Josh. 15:17]]; [[@7001013|Judg. 1:13]]). He gained her hand as a reward for his bravery in leading a successful expedition against Debir (q.v.). Some thirty years after the death of Joshua, the Israelites fell under the subjection of Chushan-rishathaim (q.v.), the king of Mesopotamia.

column5: Brother of David
column7: One of David’s brothers; the sixth son of Jesse ([[@13002015|1 Chr. 2:15]]).

column5: Nephew of Caleb
column7: Ozem was a son of Jerahmeel and a nephew of Caleb.

column5: One of David's mighty men
column7: Opening of the Lord, “the Arbite,” one of David’s heroes ([[@10023035|2 Sam. 23:35]]); called also Naarai, [[@13011037|1 Chr. 11:37]].

column5: A place mentioned in some manuscripts of 1 Timothy
column7: Pacatiana is a place mentioned in some manuscripts of <ref="1Ti.6.21">1Ti.6.21</ref>, but its exact location and significance are unknown.

column5: The homeland of the patriarchs in Mesopotamia
column6: highness, magnificence, one that deceives; curse
column7: The son of Shem ([[@1010022|Gen. 10:22]]); according to [[@1022021|Gen. 22:21]], a grandson of Nahor. In [[@40001003|Matt. 1:3]], [[@40001004|Matt. 1:4]], and [[@42003033|Luke 3:33]], this word is the Greek form of Ram, the father of Amminadab ([[@13002010|1 Chr. 2:10]]). The word means high, or highlands, and as the name of a country denotes that elevated region extending from the northeast of Palestine to the Euphrates. It corresponded generally with the Syria and Mesopotamia of the Greeks and Romans.

column5: Ancestor of temple servants
column7: Padon was an ancestor of a group of temple servants who returned from the Babylonian exile.

column5: Leader of the tribe of Asher
column7: God allots, a prince of the tribe of Asher ([[@4001013|Num. 1:13]]), in the wilderness.

column5: Group of returnees from Babylonian exile
column7: Governor of Moab, a person whose descendants returned from the Captivity and assisted in rebuilding Jerusalem ([[@15002006|Ezra 2:6]]; [[@15008004|Ezra 8:4]]; [[@15010030|Ezra 10:30]]).

column5: Repairer of the wall of Jerusalem
column7: Governor of Moab, a person whose descendants returned from the Captivity and assisted in rebuilding Jerusalem ([[@15002006|Ezra 2:6]]; [[@15008004|Ezra 8:4]]; [[@15010030|Ezra 10:30]]).

column5: Signatory of the covenant
column7: Governor of Moab, a person whose descendants returned from the Captivity and assisted in rebuilding Jerusalem ([[@15002006|Ezra 2:6]]; [[@15008004|Ezra 8:4]]; [[@15010030|Ezra 10:30]]).

column5: Son of Uzai, repaired Jerusalem's wall
column7: Palal, son of Uzai, repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall near the Parbar during Nehemiah's time.

column5: Son of Reuben, ancestor of the Palluites
column7: Separated, the second son of Reuben ([[@13005003|1 Chr. 5:3]]); called Phallu, [[@1046009|Gen. 46:9]].

column5: Son of Raphu, spy from Benjamin
column7: Deliverance from the Lord, one of the spies representing the tribe of Benjamin ([[@4013009|Num. 13:9]]).

column5: Michal's husband from Gallim
column7: Deliverance from the Lord, one of the spies representing the tribe of Benjamin ([[@4013009|Num. 13:9]]).

column5: Leader from Issachar, helped divide Canaan
column7: Deliverance of God, the prince of Issachar who assisted “to divide the land by inheritance” ([[@4034026|Num. 34:26]]).

column5: A Roman province in Asia Minor
column6: a nation made up of every tribe
column7: Paul and his company, loosing from Paphos, sailed north-west and came to Perga, the capital of Pamphylia ([[@44013013|Acts 13:13]], [[@44013014|Acts 13:14]]), a province about the middle of the southern sea-board of Asia Minor. It lay between Lycia on the west and Cilicia on the east.

column5: A city on the island of Cyprus
column6: which boils, or is very hot
column7: The capital of the island of Cyprus, and therefore the residence of the Roman governor. It was visited by Paul and Barnabas on their first missionary tour ([[@44013006|Acts 13:6]]). It is new Paphos which is here meant. It lay on the west coast of the island, about 8 miles north of old Paphos.

(Gr. parabole), a placing beside; a comparison; equivalent to the Heb. mashal, a similitude. In the Old Testament this is used to denote (1) a proverb ([[@9010012|1 Sam. 10:12]]; [[@9024013|1 Sam. 24:13]]; [[@14007020|2 Chr. 7:20]]), (2) a prophetic utterance ([[@4023007|Num. 23:7]]; [[@26020049|Ezek. 20:49]]), (3) an enigmatic saying ([[@19078002|Ps. 78:2]]; [[@20001006|Prov. 1:6]]).

A Persian word (pardes), properly meaning a “pleasure-ground” or “park” or “king’s garden.” (See EDEN.) It came in course of time to be used as a name for the world of happiness and rest hereafter ([[@42023043|Luke 23:43]]; [[@47012004|2 Cor. 12:4]]; [[@66002007|Rev. 2:7]]).

column5: A city in Benjamin's territory
column7: The heifer, a town in Benjamin ([[@6018023|Josh. 18:23]]), supposed to be identical with the ruins called Far’ah, about 6 miles north-east of Jerusalem, in the Wady Far’ah, which is a branch of the Wady Kelt.

column5: A desert region in the Sinai Peninsula
column7: Abounding in foliage, or abounding in caverns, ([[@1021021|Gen. 21:21]]), a desert tract forming the north-eastern division of the peninsula of Sinai, lying between the ‘Arabah on the east and the wilderness of Shur on the west. It is intersected in a north-western direction by the Wady el-‘Arish. It bears the modern name of Badiet et-Tih, i.e., “the desert of the wanderings.” This district, through which the children of Israel wandered, lay three days’ march from Sinai ([[@4010012|Num. 10:12]], [[@4010033|Num. 10:33]]).

column5: A mountain associated with God's appearance
column7: Mount Paran is mentioned in poetic passages as a place from which God comes or shines forth.

column5: A colonnade or structure in the temple complex
column7: ([[@13026018|1 Chr. 26:18]]), a place apparently connected with the temple, probably a “suburb” (q.v.), as the word is rendered in [[@12023011|2 Kings 23:11]]; a space between the temple wall and the wall of the court; an open portico into which the chambers of the official persons opened ([[@13026018|1 Chr. 26:18]]).

column5: Son of Haman, killed by the Jews
column7: Strong-fisted, a son of Haman, slain in Shushan ([[@17009009|Esther 9:9]]).

column5: One of the seven deacons
column7: Constant, one of the seven “deacons” ([[@44006005|Acts 6:5]]).

column5: Father of Elizaphan, leader from Zebulun
column7: Parnach was the father of Elizaphan, the leader from the tribe of Zebulun who helped divide the land of Canaan.

column5: Family that returned from Babylonian exile
column6: a flea; the fruit of a moth
column7: Parosh was the head of a family that returned to Jerusalem from the Babylonian exile, some of whom married foreign women.

column5: Leader who returned with Zerubbabel
column6: a flea; the fruit of a moth
column7: Parosh was a leader who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, bringing a group of his descendants.

column5: A man involved in repairing Jerusalem's wall
column6: a flea; the fruit of a moth
column7: Parosh, a man who made repairs near the house of Pedaiah son of Parosh.

column5: A clan leader who sealed Nehemiah's covenant
column6: a flea; the fruit of a moth
column7: Parosh, a clan leader who sealed the covenant of Nehemiah.

column5: Son of Haman killed by the Jews
column7: An interpreter of the law, the eldest of Haman’s sons, slain in Shushan ([[@17009007|Esther 9:7]]).

column5: People group present at Pentecost
column7: Were present in Jerusalem at Pentecost ([[@44002009|Acts 2:9]]). Parthia lay on the east of Media and south of Hyrcania, which separated it from the Caspian Sea.

column5: Father of one of Solomon's district governors
column7: Flourishing, the father of Jehoshaphat, appointed to provide monthly supplies for Solomon from the tribe of Issachar ([[@11004017|1 Kings 4:17]]).

column5: A place from which Solomon obtained gold
column7: The name of a country from which Solomon obtained gold for the temple ([[@14003006|2 Chr. 3:6]]). Some have identified it with Ophir, but it is uncertain whether it is even the name of a place.

column5: Son of Japhlet from the tribe of Asher
column7: Clearing, one of the sons of Japhlet, of the tribe of Asher ([[@13007033|1 Chr. 7:33]]).

column5: Son of Eshton from the tribe of Judah
column7: Paseah, a son of Eshton, who was from the tribe of Judah.

column5: Ancestor of temple servants who returned from exile
column7: Paseah, whose descendants were among the temple servants that returned from Babylonian exile.

column5: Father of Joiada, who repaired the Old Gate
column7: Paseah the father of Joiada (or 'Jehoiada'), who helped repair the Old Gate of Jerusalem.

column5: Head of a priestly family that returned from exile
column6: that extends or multiplies the hole; whiteness
column7: Pashhur, the ancestor of a priestly family that returned from Babylonian exile.

column5: Priest who sealed Nehemiah's covenant
column6: that extends or multiplies the hole; whiteness
column7: The son of Immer (probably the same as Amariah, [[@16010003|Neh. 10:3]]; [[@16012002|Neh 12:2]]), the head of one of the priestly courses, was “chief governor [Heb. paqid nagid, meaning “deputy governor”] of the temple” ([[@24020001|Jer. 20:1]], [[@24020002|Jer 20:2]]). At this time the nagid , or “governor,” of the temple was Seraiah the high priest ([[@13006014|1 Chr. 6:14]]), and Pashur was his paqid , or “deputy.”

column5: Priest who opposed Jeremiah and was renamed Magor-missabib
column7: Fear on every side, ([[@24020003|Jer. 20:3]]), a symbolical name given to the priest Pashur, expressive of the fate announced by the prophet as about to come upon him. Pashur was to be carried to Babylon, and there die.

column5: Priest sent by Zedekiah to inquire of Jeremiah
column6: that extends or multiplies the hole; whiteness
column7: A priest sent by king Zedekiah to Jeremiah to inquire of the Lord ([[@13024009|1 Chr. 24:9]]; [[@24021001|Jer. 21:1]]; [[@24038001-24038006|Jer 38:1-6]]).

The name given to the chief of the three great historical annual festivals of the Jews. It was kept in remembrance of the Lord’s passing over the houses of the Israelites ([[@2012013|Ex. 12:13]]) when the first born of all the Egyptians were destroyed. It is called also the “feast of unleavened bread” ([[@2023015|Ex. 23:15]]; [[@41014001|Mark 14:1]]; [[@44012003|Acts 12:3]]), because during its celebration no leavened bread was to be eaten or even kept in the household ([[@2012015|Ex. 12:15]]).

column5: A city in Lycia visited by Paul
column7: A city on the south-west coast of Lycia at which Paul landed on his return from his third missionary journey ([[@44021001|Acts 21:1]], [[@44021002|Acts 21:2]]). Here he found a larger vessel, which was about to sail across the open sea to the coast of Phoenicia.

column5: A region in Upper Egypt
column6: Pathrusim, mouthful of dough; persuasion of ruin
column7: The name generally given to Upper Egypt (the Thebaid of the Greeks), as distinguished from Matsor, or Lower Egypt ([[@23011011|Isa. 11:11]]; [[@24044001|Jer. 44:1]], [[@24044015|Jer. 44:15]]; [[@26030014|Ezek. 30:14]]), the two forming Mizraim.

column5: Descendants of Mizraim, son of Ham
column7: Pathrusim, a People from Mizraim, son of Ham, according to <ref="Genesis 10:14">Genesis 10:14</ref>.

column5: An island where John received the Revelation
column7: A small rocky and barren island, one of the group called the “Sporades,” in the AEgean Sea. It is mentioned in Scripture only in [[@66001009|Rev. 1:9]]. It was on this island, to which John was banished by the emperor Domitian (A.D. 95), that he received from God the wondrous revelation recorded in his book. This has naturally invested it with the deepest interest for all time.

column5: Believer in Rome greeted by Paul
column6: paternal; that pursues the steps of his father
column7: A Christian at Rome to whom Paul sent salutations ([[@45016014|Rom. 16:14]]).

column5: A city in Edom
column7: ([[@1036039|Gen. 36:39]]) or Pai ([[@13001050|1 Chr. 1:50]]), bleating, an Edomitish city ruled over by Hadar.

column5: Apostle to the Gentiles, author of many NT epistles
column7: =Saul (q.v.) was born about the same time as our Lord. His circumcision-name was Saul, and probably the name Paul was also given to him in infancy “for use in the Gentile world,” as “Saul” would be his Hebrew home-name. He was a native of Tarsus, the capital of Cilicia, a Roman province in the south-east of Asia Minor. That city stood on the banks of the river Cydnus, which was navigable thus far; hence it became a centre of extensive commercial traffic with many countries along the shores of the Mediterranean, as well as with the countries of central Asia Minor.
(Heb. shelamim), detailed regulations regarding given in Lev. 3; [[@3007011-3007021|Lev 7:11-21]], [[@3007029-3007034|Lev 7:29-34]].

column5: Leader from Naphtali appointed to divide Canaan
column7: Redeemed of God, the son of Ammihud, a prince of Naphtali ([[@4034028|Num. 34:28]]).

column5: Father of Gamaliel, leader from Manasseh
column6: strong or powerful savior; stone of redemption
column7: Rock of redemption, the father of Gamaliel and prince of Manasseh at the time of the Exodus ([[@4001010|Num. 1:10]]; [[@4002020|Num 2:20]]).

column5: Father of Zebidah, mother of King Jehoiakim
column7: The father of Zebudah, who was the wife of Josiah and mother of king Jehoiakim ([[@12023036|2 Kings 23:36]]).

column5: Descendant of King Jehoiachin of Judah
column7: Pedaiah, a descendant of King Jehoiachin of Judah born during the Babylonian captivity.

column5: Officer over the half-tribe of Manasseh
column7: Pedaiah, son of Parosh, an officer over the half-tribe of Manasseh in King David's administration.

column5: Father of a man who repaired Jerusalem's wall
column7: Pedaiah, father of a man who made repairs to the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time.

column5: Levite who assisted Ezra in reading the Law
column7: Pedaiah, a Levite who stood with Ezra when he read the Law to the people.

column5: Benjamite who settled in Jerusalem after the exile
column7: Pedaiah, a Benjamite who settled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile.

column5: Levite appointed as a treasurer by Nehemiah
column7: Pedaiah, a Levite Nehemiah appointed as a treasurer over the storehouses.

column5: King of Israel who reigned for 20 years
column6: he that opens; that is at liberty
column7: Open-eyed, the son of Remaliah a captain in the army of Pekahiah, king of Israel, whom he slew, with the aid of a band of Gileadites, and succeeded (B.C. 758) on the throne ([[@12015025|2 Kings 15:25]]). Seventeen years after this he entered into an alliance with Rezin, king of Syria, and took part with him in besieging Jerusalem ([[@12015037|2 Kings 15:37]]; [[@12016005|2 Kings 16:5]]). But Tiglath-pilser, who was in alliance with Ahaz, king of Judah, came up against Pekah, and carried away captive many of the inhabitants of his kingdom ([[@12015029|2 Kings 15:29]]).

column5: King of Israel who reigned for 2 years
column6: it is the Lord that opens
column7: The Lord opened his eyes, the son and successor of Menahem on the throne of Israel. He was murdered in the royal palace of Samaria by Pekah, one of the captains of his army ([[@12015023-12015026|2 Kings 15:23-26]]), after a reign of two years (B.C. 761-759).

column5: Descendant of King David
column7: Pelaiah, a descendant of King David, mentioned in the genealogy of 1Chronicles 3.

column5: Levite who helped explain the Law and signed the covenant
column7: A Levite who expounded the law ([[@16008007|Neh. 8:7]]).

column5: Priest in Jerusalem during Nehemiah's time
column7: Pelaliah, a priest who lived in Jerusalem during Nehemiah's time.

column5: Descendant of King Solomon
column6: let the Lord deliver; deliverance of the Lord
column7: A son of Hananiah and grandson of Zerubbabel ([[@13003021|1 Chr. 3:21]]).

column5: Simeonite leader who attacked the Amalekites
column6: let the Lord deliver; deliverance of the Lord
column7: Pelatiah, a Simeonite leader who joined in an attack against the Amalekites.

column5: Priest who signed Nehemiah's covenant
column6: let the Lord deliver; deliverance of the Lord
column7: Pelatiah, a priest who signed the covenant during Nehemiah's time.

column5: Prince of Israel whom Ezekiel saw in a vision
column6: let the Lord deliver; deliverance of the Lord
column7: One of the twenty-five princes of the people against whom Ezekiel prophesied on account of their wicked counsel ([[@26011001-26011013|Ezek. 11:1-13]]).

column5: Descendant of Shem, ancestor of Abraham
column7: Division, one of the sons of Eber; so called because “in his days was the earth divided” ([[@1010025|Gen. 10:25]]). Possibly he may have lived at the time of the dispersion from Babel.

column5: Son of Jahdai, descendant of Judah
column7: Pelet, a son of Jahdai, mentioned in the genealogy of Judah in 1Chronicles 2.

column5: Benjamite warrior who joined David at Ziklag
column7: A Benjamite who joined David at Ziklag ([[@13012003|1 Chr. 12:3]]).

column5: Reubenite, father of On who rebelled against Moses
column7: A Reubenite whose son was one of the conspirators against Moses and Aaron ([[@4016001|Num. 16:1]]).

column5: Son of Jonathan, descendant of Jerahmeel
column7: Peleth, a son of Jonathan and descendant of Jerahmeel, mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.

column5: Elite military unit loyal to King David
column7: Mentioned always along with the Cherethites, and only in the time of David. The word probably means “runners” or “couriers,” and may denote that while forming part of David’s bodyguard, they were also sometimes employed as couriers ([[@10008018|2 Sam. 8:18]]; [[@10020007|2 Sam. 20:7]], [[@10020023|2 Sam. 20:23]];[[@11001038|1 Kings 1:38]], [[@11001044|1 Kings 1:44]]; [[@13018017|1 Chr. 18:17]]). Some, however, think that these are the names simply of two Philistine tribes from which David selected his body-guard.

column5: Designation for two of David's mighty warriors
column7: The designation of one of David’s heroes ([[@10023026|2 Sam. 23:26]]); called also the Pelonite ([[@13011027|1 Chr. 11:27]]).

column5: An Egyptian city, also known as Sin
column7: “Sin against the Holy Ghost” (q.v.), or a “sin unto death” ([[@40012031|Matt. 12:31]], [[@40012032|Matt 12:32]]; [[@62005016|1 John 5:16]]), which amounts to a wilful rejection of grace. Sin, a city in Egypt, called by the Greeks Pelusium, which means, as does also the Hebrew name, “clayey” or “muddy,” so called from the abundance of clay found there. It is called by Ezekel ([[@26030015|Ezek. 30:15]]) “the strength of Egypt, “thus denoting its importance as a fortified city. It has been identified with the modern Tineh, “a miry place,” where its ruins are to be found.

column5: A place where Jacob wrestled with God
column6: face or vision of God; that sees God
column7: Face of God, a place not far from Succoth, on the east of the Jordan and north of the river Jabbok. It is also called “Peniel.” Here Jacob wrestled ([[@1032024-1032032|Gen. 32:24-32]]) “with a man” (“the angel”, [[@28012004|Hos. 12:4]]. Jacob says of him, “I have seen God face to face”) “till the break of day.” A town was afterwards built there ([[@7008008|Judg. 8:8]]; [[@11012025|1 Kings 12:25]]).

column5: Elkanah's wife, rival of Hannah
column7: Peninnah, one of Elkanah's two wives and the rival of Hannah, Samuel's mother.

I.e., “fiftieth”, found only in the New Testament ([[@44002001|Acts 2:1]]; [[@44020016|Acts 20:16]]; [[@46016008|1 Cor. 16:8]]). The festival so named is first spoken of in [[@2023016|Ex. 23:16]] as “the feast of harvest,” and again in [[@2034022|Ex. 34:22]] as “the day of the firstfruits” ([[@4028026|Num. 28:26]]).

column5: Son of Hur, descendant of Judah
column6: face or vision of God; that sees God
column7: Face of God, a place not far from Succoth, on the east of the Jordan and north of the river Jabbok. It is also called “Peniel.” Here Jacob wrestled ([[@1032024-1032032|Gen. 32:24-32]]) “with a man” (“the angel”, [[@28012004|Hos. 12:4]]. Jacob says of him, “I have seen God face to face”) “till the break of day.” A town was afterwards built there ([[@7008008|Judg. 8:8]]; [[@11012025|1 Kings 12:25]]).

column5: Son of Shashak, descendant of Benjamin
column6: face or vision of God; that sees God
column7: Face of God, a place not far from Succoth, on the east of the Jordan and north of the river Jabbok. It is also called “Peniel.” Here Jacob wrestled ([[@1032024-1032032|Gen. 32:24-32]]) “with a man” (“the angel”, [[@28012004|Hos. 12:4]]. Jacob says of him, “I have seen God face to face”) “till the break of day.” A town was afterwards built there ([[@7008008|Judg. 8:8]]; [[@11012025|1 Kings 12:25]]).

column5: A gate in Jerusalem mentioned by Jeremiah
column7: The People's Gate was one of the gates of Jerusalem, where the prophet Jeremiah was instructed to proclaim God's message.

column5: A mountain in Moab associated with idolatry
column7: A mountain peak ([[@4023028|Num. 23:28]]) to which Balak led Balaam as a last effort to induce him to pronounce a curse upon Israel. When he looked on the tribes encamped in the acacia groves below him, he could not refrain from giving utterance to a remarkable benediction (24:1-9). Balak was more than ever enraged at Balaam, and bade him flee for his life.

column5: A place where David defeated the Philistines
column7: Mount Perazim was the location where David, with God's help, defeated the Philistines, and it is used by Isaiah as an example of God's judgment.

column5: Son of Machir, grandson of Manasseh
column7: Peresh, a son of Machir and grandson of Manasseh, mentioned in the genealogy of 1Chronicles 7.

column5: Son of Judah, ancestor of David and Jesus
column7: =Pharez, (q.v.), breach, the son of Judah ([[@16011004|Neh. 11:4]]). “The chief of all the captains of the host for the first month” in the reign of David was taken from his family ([[@13027003|1 Chr. 27:3]]).

column5: A place named after Uzzah's death
column6: division of Uzza, or of strength
column7: Perez-uzza was the name given to the place where Uzzah died after touching the Ark of the Covenant during its transport to Jerusalem.

column5: A city in Pamphylia visited by Paul
column7: The capital of Pamphylia, on the coast of Asia Minor. Paul and his companions landed at this place from Cyprus on their first missionary journey ([[@44013013|Acts 13:13]], [[@44013014|Acts 13:14]]), and here Mark forsook the party and returned to Jerusalem. Some time afterwards Paul and Barnabas again visited this city and “preached the word” (14:25). It stood on the banks of the river Cestrus, some 7 miles from its mouth, and was a place of some commercial importance.

column5: A city in Asia Minor with a church
column7: The chief city of Mysia, in Asia Minor. One of the “seven churches” was planted here ([[@66001011|Rev. 1:11]]; [[@66002017|Rev 2:17]]). It was noted for its wickedness, insomuch that our Lord says “Satan’s seat” was there. The church of Pergamos was rebuked for swerving from the truth and embracing the doctrines of Balaam and the Nicolaitanes.

column5: Canaanite people group living in the land of Canaan
column7: Villagers; dwellers in the open country, the Canaanitish nation inhabiting the fertile regions south and south-west of Carmel. “They were the graziers, farmers, and peasants of the time.” They were to be driven out of the land by the descendants of Abraham ([[@1015020|Gen. 15:20]]; [[@2003008|Ex. 3:8]], [[@2003017|Ex. 3:17]]; 23:23; 33:2; 34:11). They are afterwards named among the conquered tribes ([[@6024011|Josh. 24:11]]).

column5: An empire that ruled over the exiled Jews
column6: that cuts or divides; a nail; a gryphon; a horseman
column7: An ancient empire, extending from the Indus to Thrace, and from the Caspian Sea to the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. The Persians were originally a Medic tribe which settled in Persia, on the eastern side of the Persian Gulf. They were Aryans, their language belonging to the eastern division of the Indo-European group. One of their chiefs, Teispes, conquered Elam in the time of the decay of the Assyrian Empire, and established himself in the district of Anzan.

column5: Female Christian in Rome greeted by Paul
column6: that cuts or divides; a nail; a gryphon; a horseman
column7: A female Christian at Rome whom Paul salutes ([[@45016012|Rom. 16:12]]).

column5: Ancestor of a family of Solomon's servants
column7: One whose descendants returned with Zerubbabel ([[@15002055|Ezra 2:55]]); called also Perida ([[@16007057|Neh. 7:57]]).

column5: Apostle of Jesus, leader in the early church
column7: Originally called Simon (=Simeon, i.e., “hearing”), a very common Jewish name in the New Testament. He was the son of Jona ([[@40016017|Matt. 16:17]]). His mother is nowhere named in Scripture. He had a younger brother called Andrew, who first brought him to Jesus ([[@43001040-43001042|John 1:40-42]]).

column5: Head of the 19th priestly division
column6: the Lord opening; gate of the Lord
column7: The chief of one of the priestly courses (the nineteenth) in the time of David ([[@13024016|1 Chr. 24:16]]).

column5: Levite who married a foreign woman
column6: the Lord opening; gate of the Lord
column7: Pethahiah, a Levite who married a foreign woman during the time of Ezra.

column5: Levite who led the people in confession
column6: the Lord opening; gate of the Lord
column7: Pethahiah, a Levite who led the people in confession and worship during the time of Nehemiah.

column5: Levite appointed for the king's matters
column6: the Lord opening; gate of the Lord
column7: A descendant of Judah who had some office at the court of Persia ([[@16011024|Neh. 11:24]]).

column5: The hometown of Balaam in Mesopotamia
column7: Interpretation of dreams, identified with Pitru, on the west bank of the Euphrates, a few miles south of the Hittite capital of Carchemish ([[@4022005|Num. 22:5]], “which is by the river of the land of the children of [the god] Ammo”).

column5: Father of the prophet Joel
column6: mouth of God; persuasion of God
column7: Vision of God, the father of Joel the prophet ([[@29001001|Joel 1:1]]).

column5: Son of Obed-Edom, a temple gatekeeper
column7: Wages of the Lord, one of the sons of Obed-edom, a Levite porter ([[@13026005|1 Chr. 26:5]]).

column5: Father of the prophetess Anna
column7: Face of God, father of the prophetess Anna (q.v.), [[@42002036|Luke 2:36]].

column5: Egyptian ruler during Abraham's visit
column7: Pharaoh, the Egyptian ruler who took Abraham's wife Sarah into his palace during their visit to Egypt.

column5: Egyptian ruler during Joseph's time
column7: The Pharaoh of Joseph’s days (Gen. 41) was probably Apopi, or Apopis, the last of the Hyksos kings. To the old native Egyptians, who were an African race, shepherds were “an abomination;” but to the Hyksos kings these Asiatic shepherds who now appeared with Jacob at their head were congenial, and being akin to their own race, had a warm welcome ([[@1047005|Gen. 47:5]], [[@1047006|Gen. 47:6]]).

column5: Egyptian Pharaoh during Moses' birth and early life
column7: Pharaoh, the Egyptian ruler who oppressed the Israelites and decreed the killing of Hebrew male infants during the time of Moses' birth.

column5: Egyptian Pharaoh during the Exodus
column7: Pharaoh, the Egyptian ruler who refused to release the Israelites from slavery, resulting in the ten plagues and the Exodus.

column5: Egyptian Pharaoh during Solomon's reign
column7: Pharaoh, the Egyptian ruler who made an alliance with King Solomon and gave him his daughter in marriage.

column5: Egyptian Pharaoh during Hezekiah's reign
column7: Pharaoh, in whom Hezekiah put his trust in his war against Sennacherib ([[@12018021|2 Kings 18:21]]).

column5: Pharaoh and father-in-law of Mered, a descendant of Judah
column7: Pharaoh, the Egyptian ruler whose daughter Bithiah married Mered, a descendant of Judah.

column5: Egyptian Pharaoh during Jeremiah's time
column7: Pharaoh, the Egyptian ruler mentioned among those who would face God's judgment, as prophesied by Jeremiah.

Separatists (Heb. persahin, from parash, “to separate”). They were probably the successors of the Assideans (i.e., the “pious”), a party that originated in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes in revolt against his heathenizing policy. The first mention of them is in a description by Josephus of the three sects or schools into which the Jews were divided (B.C. 145). The other two sects were the Essenes and the Sadducees.

column5: A river in Damascus, Syria
column7: Swift, one of the rivers of Damascus ([[@12005012|2 Kings 5:12]]). It has been identified with the ‘Awaj, “a small lively river.” The whole of the district watered by the ‘Awaj is called the Wady el-‘Ajam, i.e., “the valley of the Persians”, so called for some unknown reason. This river empties itself into the lake or marsh Bahret Hijaneh, on the east of Damascus.

column5: Commander of Abimelech's army
column6: the mouth of all, or every tongue
column7: Great, the chief captain of the army of Abimelech, the Philistine king of Gerar.

column5: One of the seven churches in Asia Minor
column7: Brotherly love, a city of Lydia in Asia Minor, about 25 miles south-east of Sardis. It was the seat of one of the “seven churches” ([[@66003007-66003012|Rev. 3:7-12]]). It came into the possession of the Turks in A.D. 1392. It has several times been nearly destroyed by earthquakes.

column5: Recipient of Paul's letter, Colossian slave owner
column7: An inhabitant of Colosse, and apparently a person of some note among the citizens ([[@51004009|Col. 4:9]]; [[@57001001|Philemon 1]]:2). He was brought to a knowledge of the gospel through the instrumentality of Paul (19), and held a prominent place in the Christian community for his piety and beneficence (4-7).

column5: False teacher who opposed Paul
column7: Amiable, with Hymenaeus, at Ephesus, said that the “resurrection was past already” ([[@55002017|2 Tim. 2:17]], [[@55002018|2 Tim. 2:18]]). This was a Gnostic heresy held by the Nicolaitanes.

column5: One of the twelve apostles of Jesus
column7: One of the twelve apostles; a native of Bethsaida, “the city of Andrew and Peter” ([[@43001044|John 1:44]]). He readily responded to the call of Jesus when first addressed to him (43), and forthwith brought Nathanael also to Jesus (45, 46). He seems to have held a prominent place among the apostles ([[@40010003|Matt. 10:3]]; [[@41003018|Mark 3:18]]; [[@43006005-43006007|John 6:5-7]]; [[@43012021|John 12:21]], [[@43012022|John 12:22]]; [[@43014008|John 14:8]], [[@43014009|John 14:9]]; [[@44001013|Acts 1:13]]). Of his later life nothing is certainly known.

column5: Herod Antipas' brother, first husband of Herodias
column7: Mentioned only in connection with the imprisonment of John the Baptist ([[@40014003|Matt. 14:3]]; [[@41006017|Mark 6:17]]; [[@42003019|Luke 3:19]]). He was the son of Herod the Great, and the first husband of Herodias, and the father of Salome.

column5: Tetrarch of Iturea and Traconitis
column7: The “tetrarch of Ituraea” ([[@42003001|Luke 3:1]]); a son of Herod the Great, and brother of Herod Antipas. The city of Caesarea-Philippi was named partly after him ([[@40016013|Matt. 16:13]]; [[@41008027|Mark 8:27]]).

column5: One of the seven deacons, evangelized in Samaria
column7: One of the “seven” ([[@44006005|Acts 6:5]]), called also “the evangelist” (21:8, 9). He was one of those who were “scattered abroad” by the persecution that arose on the death of Stephen. He went first to Samaria, where he laboured as an evangelist with much success (8:5-13). While he was there he received a divine command to proceed toward the south, along the road leading from Jerusalem to Gaza.

column5: A city in Macedonia visited by Paul
column7: Formerly Crenides, “the fountain,” the capital of the province of Macedonia. It stood near the head of the Sea, about 8 miles north-west of Kavalla. It is now a ruined village, called Philibedjik. Philip of Macedonia fortified the old Thracian town of Crenides, and called it after his own name Philippi (B.C. 359-336).

column5: An ancient people and region in Canaan
column6: which is covered; watered; or brings and causes ruin

column5: Descendants of Mizraim, son of Ham
column7: The Philistines, a people group descended from Mizraim, the son of Ham, according to the Table of Nations in Genesis and 1 Chronicles.

column5: Believer in Rome greeted by Paul
column6: a lover of letters, or of the word
column7: Philologus, a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings in his letter to the Romans.

column5: Aaron's grandson; zealous priest who opposed idolatry
column6: bold aspect; face of trust or protection
column7: Son of Eleazar, the high priest ([[@2006025|Ex. 6:25]]). While yet a youth he distinguished himself at Shittim by his zeal against the immorality into which the Moabites had tempted the people ([[@4025001-4025009|Num. 25:1-9]]), and thus “stayed the plague” that had broken out among the people, and by which twenty-four thousand of them perished. For his faithfulness on that occasion he received the divine approbation (10-13). He afterwards commanded the army that went out against the Midianites (31:6-8).

column5: Wicked son of Eli the priest
column6: bold aspect; face of trust or protection
column7: One of the sons of Eli, the high priest ([[@9001003|1 Sam. 1:3]]; [[@9002012|1 Sam. 2:12]]). He and his brother Hophni were guilty of great crimes, for which destruction came on the house of Eli (31).

column5: Priest during Ezra's time
column6: bold aspect; face of trust or protection
column7: Phinehas, a priest who assisted in weighing and recording the gold, silver, and vessels brought to Jerusalem by Ezra.

column5: Believer in Rome greeted by Paul
column7: Burning, a Roman Christian to whom Paul sent salutations ([[@45016014|Rom. 16:14]]).

column5: Deacon of the church in Cenchreae
column7: A “deaconess of the church at Cenchrea,” the port of Corinth. She was probably the bearer of Paul’s epistle to the Romans.

column5: A region and people on the Mediterranean coast
column7: Phoenicia was a region along the Mediterranean coast, north of Israel, known for its maritime trade and mentioned in the New Testament in connection with the spread of the gospel.

column5: A harbor on the island of Crete
column7: Properly Phoenix a palm-tree (as in the R.V.), a town with a harbour on the southern side of Crete ([[@44027012|Acts 27:12]]), west of the Fair Havens.

column5: A region in Asia Minor with early Christians
column7: Dry, an irregular and ill-defined district in Asia Minor. It was divided into two parts, the Greater Phrygia on the south, and the Lesser Phrygia on the west. It is the Greater Phrygia that is spoken of in the New Testament.

column5: Believer who deserted Paul in Asia
column7: Fugitive, a Christian of Asia, who “turned away” from Paul during his second imprisonment at Rome ([[@55001015|2 Tim. 1:15]]).

column5: An Egyptian city mentioned in Ezekiel's prophecy
column6: abode of the goddess Bahest or Bast
column7: ([[@26030017|Ezek. 30:17]]), supposed to mean. “a cat,” or a deity in the form of a cat, worshipped by the Egyptians. It was called by the Greeks Bubastis. The hieroglyphic name is “Pe-bast”, i.e., the house of Bast, the Artemis of the Egyptians.

column5: A place near the Red Sea crossing
column6: the mouth; the pass of Hiroth
column7: Place where the reeds grow (LXX. and Copt. read “farmstead”), the name of a place in Egypt where the children of Israel encamped ([[@2014002|Ex. 14:2]], [[@2014009|Ex. 14:9]]), how long is uncertain. Some have identified it with Ajrud, a fortress between Etham and Suez. The condition of the Isthmus of Suez at the time of the Exodus is not exactly known, and hence this, with the other places mentioned as encampments of Israel in Egypt, cannot be definitely ascertained. The isthmus has been formed by the Nile deposits.

column5: Roman governor who presided over Jesus' trial
column7: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea who presided over the trial of Jesus and ultimately ordered his crucifixion.

column5: Nephew of Abraham
column7: Pildash, one of the sons of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and Milcah.

column5: Signatory to Nehemiah's covenant
column7: Pilha, one of the leaders of the people who signed the covenant during Nehemiah's time.

column5: Head of a priestly family
column7: Piltai, the head of the priestly family of Moadiah during the time of Joiakim, the high priest.

column5: Edomite clan chief descended from Esau
column7: Pinon, one of the chiefs of Edom, descended from Esau, mentioned in the genealogies of Genesis and 1 Chronicles.

column5: Amorite king of Jarmuth
column7: Like a wild ass, a king of Jarmuth, a royal city of the Canaanites, who was conquered and put to death by Joshua (10:3, 23, 26).

column5: A town in Ephraim, home of several notable Israelites
column6: his dissipation or deprivation; his rupture
column7: Prince, or summit, a place “in the land of Ephraim” ([[@7012015|Judg. 12:15]]), now Fer’on, some 10 miles south-west of Shechem.

column5: A mountain range in Moab, east of the Jordan
column7: A part, a mountain summit in the land of Moab, in the territory of Reuben, where Balak offered up sacrifices ([[@4021020|Num. 21:20]]; [[@4023014|Num 23:14]]), and from which Moses viewed the promised land ([[@5003027|Deut. 3:27]]). It is probably the modern Jebel Siaghah.

column5: A river flowing from Eden, encircling Havilah
column7: Babylonian, the current, broad-flowing, one of the “four heads” into which the river which watered the garden of Eden was divided ([[@1002011|Gen. 2:11]]).

column5: A region in Asia Minor visited by Paul
column7: A district in Asia Minor, to the north of Pamphylia.

column5: Descendant of Asher
column7: Pispa, a descendant of Asher, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher in 1 Chronicles.

column5: A store city built by the Israelites in Egypt
column6: their mouthful; a dilatation of the mouth
column7: Egyptian, Pa-Tum, “house of Tum,” the sun-god, one of the “treasure” cities built for Pharaoh Rameses II. by the Israelites ([[@2001011|Ex. 1:11]]). It was probably the Patumos of the Greek historian Herodotus. It has now been satisfactorily identified with Tell-el-Maskhuta, about 12 miles west of Ismailia, and 20 east of Tel-el-Kebir, on the southern bank of the present Suez Canal. Here have recently (1883) been discovered the ruins of supposed grain-chambers, and other evidences to show that this was a great “store city.”

column5: Descendant of King Saul
column7: Pithon, a descendant of King Saul, mentioned in the genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles.

column5: Family of Solomon's servants
column7: Pochereth-hazzebaim, a family listed among the descendants of Solomon's servants who returned from the Babylonian exile.

column5: A region in Asia Minor with Jewish inhabitants
column7: A province of Asia Minor, stretching along the southern coast of the Euxine Sea, corresponding nearly to the modern province of Trebizond. In the time of the apostles it was a Roman province. Strangers from this province were at Jerusalem at Pentecost ([[@44002009|Acts 2:9]]), and to “strangers scattered throughout Pontus,” among others, Peter addresses his first epistle ([[@60001001|1 Pet. 1:1]]). It was evidently the resort of many Jews of the Dispersion.

column5: Son of Haman, enemy of the Jews
column7: Poratha, one of the ten sons of Haman, who was hanged along with his brothers after their father's downfall.

column5: Egyptian official who bought Joseph as a slave
column6: bull of Africa; a fat bull
column7: Dedicated to Ra; i.e., to the sun-god, the Egyptian to whom the Ishmaelites sold Joseph ([[@1039001|Gen. 39:1]]). He was “captain of the guard”, i.e., chief, probably, of the state police, who, while they formed part of the Egyptian army, were also largely employed in civil duties (37:36; marg., “chief of the executioners”). Joseph, though a foreigner, gradually gained his confidence, and became overseer over all his possessions. Believing the false accusation which his profligate wife brought against Joseph, Potiphar cast him into prison, where he remained for some years.

column5: Egyptian priest, father-in-law of Joseph
column7: Potiphera, the priest of On (Heliopolis), whose daughter Asenath was given to Joseph as a wife by Pharaoh.

column5: A gate in Jerusalem mentioned by Jeremiah
column7: The Potsherd Gate was a gate in Jerusalem near the Valley of Ben Hinnom, where Jeremiah was instructed to proclaim a message of judgment against Judah.

The Greek word (praitorion) thus rendered in [[@41015016|Mark 15:16]] is rendered “common hall” ([[@40027027|Matt. 27:27]], marg., “governor’s house”), “judgment hall,” ([[@43018028|John 18:28]], [[@43018033|John 18:33]], marg., “Pilate’s house”, 19:9; [[@44023035|Acts 23:35]]), “palace” ([[@50001013|Phil. 1:13]]). This is properly a military word.

The Heb. kohen, Gr. hierus, Lat. sacerdos, always denote one who offers sacrifices. At first every man was his own priest, and presented his own sacrifices before God. Afterwards that office devolved on the head of the family, as in the cases of Noah ([[@1008020|Gen. 8:20]]), Abraham (12:7; 13:4), Isaac (26:25), Jacob (31:54), and Job ([[@18001005|Job 1:5]]). The name first occurs as applied to Melchizedek ([[@1014018|Gen. 14:18]]).

column5: Early Christian teacher; wife of Aquila
column7: The wife of Aquila ([[@44018002|Acts 18:2]]), who is never mentioned without her. Her name sometimes takes the precedence of his ([[@45016003|Rom. 16:3]]; [[@55004019|2 Tim. 4:19]]).

column5: One of the seven deacons in Jerusalem
column6: he that presides over the choirs
column7: Prochorus, one of the seven men chosen by the early church in Jerusalem to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows.
The prophets of the northern kingdom (Israel), viz., Hosea, Amos, Joel, Jonah.

Is used in the LXX. for “stranger” ([[@13022002|1 Chr. 22:2]]), i.e., a comer to Palestine; a sojourner in the land ([[@2012048|Ex. 12:48]]; [[@2020010|Ex 20:10]]; [[@2022021|Ex 22:21]]), and in the New Testament for a convert to Judaism. There were such converts from early times ([[@23056003|Isa. 56:3]]; [[@16010028|Neh. 10:28]]; [[@17008017|Esther 8:17]]).

column5: Son of Issachar, grandson of Jacob
column7: Puah, also known as Puvah, was a son of Issachar and grandson of Jacob, and his descendants were called the Punites.

column5: Hebrew midwife in Egypt
column7: One of the two midwives who feared God, and refused to kill the Hebrew male children at their birth ([[@2001015-2001021|Ex. 1:15-21]]).

column5: Father of judge Tola
column7: Puah, the son of Dodo from the tribe of Issachar, who's son Tola judged Israel after Abimelech.

column5: Chief official of Malta who hosted Paul
column7: “the chief man of the island” of Malta ([[@44028007|Acts 28:7]]), who courteously entertained Paul and his shipwrecked companions for three days, till they found a more permanent place of residence; for they remained on the island for three months, till the stormy season had passed.

column5: Christian in Rome who greeted Timothy
column7: Bashful, a Christian at Rome, who sent his greetings to Timothy ([[@55004021|2 Tim. 4:21]]).

column5: A stopping place for the Israelites in the wilderness
column7: Punon was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness wanderings, located between Zalmonah and Oboth.

column5: Gideon's servant who accompanied him to the Midianite camp
column7: Purah was Gideon's servant who went with him to spy on the Midianite camp.

column5: Son of Ham, grandson of Noah
column7: Phut is placed between Egypt and Canaan in [[@1010006|Gen. 10:6]], and elsewhere we find the people of Phut described as mercenaries in the armies of Egypt and Tyre ([[@24046009|Jer. 46:9]]; [[@26030005|Ezek. 30:5]]; [[@26027010|Ezek 27:10]]).

column5: A port city in Italy visited by Paul
column7: A city on the coast of Campania, on the north shore of a bay running north from the Bay of Naples, at which Paul landed on his way to Rome, from which it was distant 170 miles. Here he tarried for seven days ([[@44028013|Acts 28:13]], [[@44028014|Acts 28:14]]). This was the great emporium for the Alexandrian corn ships. Here Paul and his companions began their journey, by the “Appian Way,” to Rome.

column5: A clan from the tribe of Judah
column7: The Puthites were a clan from the tribe of Judah.

column5: Father-in-law of Eleazar, son of Aaron
column7: Putiel was the father-in-law of Eleazar, son of Aaron.

column5: A Berean who accompanied Paul to Asia
column7: Pyrrhus was a Berean who accompanied Paul on his journey to Asia.

column5: A Christian brother in Corinth who sent greetings to Rome
column7: Fourth, a Corinthian Christian who sent by Paul his salutations to friends at Rome ([[@45016023|Rom. 16:23]]).

column5: A queen who visited Solomon and praised his wisdom
column7: The Queen of Sheba visited King Solomon, tested him with questions, and praised his wisdom and prosperity.

column5: Governor of Syria during a census mentioned in Luke
column7: The Grecized form of Quirinus. His full name was Publius Sulpicius Quirinus. Recent historical investigation has proved that Quirinus was governor of Cilicia, which was annexed to Syria at the time of our Lord’s birth. Cilicia, which he ruled, being a province of Syria, he is called the governor, which he was de jure, of Syria.

column5: A trading partner of Tyre, possibly in Arabia
column6: greatness; thunder; some sort of evil
column7: A country which traded with Tyre ([[@26027022|Ezek. 27:22]]).

column5: A store city built by the Israelites in Egypt
column7: Raamses was one of the store cities built by the Israelites during their enslavement in Egypt, along with Pithom.

column5: A Babylonian official present at the fall of Jerusalem
column7: Rab-mag, a Babylonian official, was present at the capture of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar's army.

column5: A Babylonian official sent by King Sennacherib to Jerusalem
column7: Chief of the Heads, one of the three officers whom Sennacherib sent from Lachish with a threatening message to Jerusalem ([[@12018017|2 Kings 18:17]]; [[@24039003|Jer. 39:3]], [[@24039013|Jer. 39:13]]).

column5: A Babylonian official present at the fall of Jerusalem
column7: Rab-saris, a Babylonian official, was present at the capture of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar's army.

column5: A town allotted to the tribe of Issachar
column7: Rabbith was a town in the territory of Issachar, mentioned in the list of cities and towns allocated to the tribe during the division of the Promised Land.

column5: A Babylonian official who taunted Hezekiah and Jerusalem's people
column7: Chief of the princes, the name given to the chief cup-bearer or the vizier of the Assyrian court; one of Sennacherib’s messengers to Hezekiah. See the speech he delivered, in the Hebrew language, in the hearing of all the people, as he stood near the wall on the north side of the city ([[@12018017-12018037|2 Kings 18:17-37]]).
Vain, empty, worthless, only found in [[@40005022|Matt. 5:22]]. The Jews used it as a word of contempt.

column5: Wife of Jacob; mother of Joseph and Benjamin
column7: Ewe, “the daughter”, “the somewhat petulant, peevish, and self-willed though beautiful younger daughter” of Laban, and one of Jacob’s wives ([[@1029006|Gen. 29:6]], [[@1029028|Gen. 29:28]]). He served Laban fourteen years for her, so deep was Jacob’s affection for her. She was the mother of Joseph ([[@1030022-1030024|Gen. 30:22-24]]). Afterwards, on Jacob’s departure from Mesopotamia, she took with her her father’s teraphim (31:34, 35). As they journeyed on from Bethel, Rachel died in giving birth to Benjamin (35:18, 19), and was buried “in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.

column5: One of David's brothers, son of Jesse
column7: Raddai was one of David's brothers, a son of Jesse.

column5: A Canaanite woman who helped the Israelite spies in Jericho
column7: Insolence; pride, a poetical name applied to Egypt in [[@19087004|Ps. 87:4]]; [[@19089010|Ps 89:10]]; [[@23051009|Isa. 51:9]], as “the proud one.” Rahab, (Heb. Rahab; i.e., “broad,” “large”). When the Hebrews were encamped at Shittim, in the “Arabah” or Jordan valley opposite Jericho, ready to cross the river, Joshua, as a final preparation, sent out two spies to “spy the land.” After five days they returned, having swum across the river, which at this season, the month Abib, overflowed its banks from the melting of the snow on Lebanon.

column5: Son of Shema and founder of Jorkeam, of Judah
column7: Merciful, one of the descendants of Caleb, the son of Hezron ([[@13002044|1 Chr. 2:44]]).

column5: Son of Sheresh, of the tribe of Manasseh
column7: Rakem was a son of Sheresh, from the tribe of Manasseh.

column5: City on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee
column7: Shore-town, a “fenced city” of the tribe of Naphtali ([[@6019035|Josh. 19:35]]).

column5: A town allotted to the tribe of Dan
column7: A place upon the shore, a town belonging to Dan ([[@6019046|Josh. 19:46]]). It is now Tell er-Rakkeit, 6 miles north of Joppa, on the sea-shore, near the mouth of the river ‘Aujeh, i.e., “yellow water.”

column5: Son of Hezron, ancestor of David and Jesus
column7: The son of Hezron, and one of the ancestors of the royal line ([[@8004019|Ruth 4:19]]).

column5: Firstborn son of Jerahmeel, of the tribe of Judah
column7: Ram was the firstborn son of Jerahmeel, from the tribe of Judah.

column5: Ancestor of Elihu, who spoke to Job
column7: A person mentioned in [[@18032002|Job 32:2]] as founder of a clan to which Elihu belonged.

column5: A town in Benjamin, near Gibeah and Jerusalem
column7: A city first mentioned in [[@6018025|Josh. 18:25]], near Gibeah of Benjamin. It was fortified by Baasha, king of Israel ([[@11015017-11015022|1 Kings 15:17-22]]; [[@14016001-14016006|2 Chr. 16:1-6]]). Asa, king of Judah, employed Benhadad the Syrian king to drive Baasha from this city ([[@11015018|1 Kings 15:18]], [[@11015020|1 Kings 15:20]]). Isaiah (10:29) refers to it, and also Jeremiah, who was once a prisoner there among the other captives of Jerusalem when it was taken by Nebuchadnezzar ([[@24039008-24039012|Jer. 39:8-12]]; [[@24040001|Jer 40:1]]).

column5: A town on the border of Asher and Tyre
column7: Ramah was a town located on the border between the territory of Asher and the city-state of Tyre.

column5: A fortified city in the territory of Naphtali
column7: Ramah was a fortified city located in the territory of Naphtali, mentioned in the list of cities allocated to the tribe during the division of the Promised Land.

column5: The place where Samson killed a thousand Philistines
column7: Elevation of Lehi, or the jawbone height; i.e., the Ramah of Lehi ([[@7015015-7015017|Judg. 15:15-17]]). The phrase “in the jaw,” ver. 19, Authorized Version, is in the margin, also in the Revised Version, “in Lehi.”

column5: People from Ramah who tended King David's vineyards
column7: The designation given to Shimei, the manager of David’s vineyard ([[@13027027|1 Chr. 27:27]]).

column5: Egyptian city where Israelites lived before the Exodus
column7: “the land of” ([[@1047011|Gen. 47:11]]), was probably “the land of Goshen” (q.v.) 45:10. After the Hebrews had built Rameses, one of the “treasure cities,” it came to be known as the “land” in which that city was built. The city bearing this name ([[@2012037|Ex. 12:37]]) was probably identical with Zoan, which Rameses II. (“son of the sun”) rebuilt.

column5: One of the men who married foreign women
column7: Ramiah was one of the men who had married foreign women during the time of Ezra.

column5: City of refuge east of the Jordan
column7: Ramoth, also called Ramoth-gilead, was a city of refuge in Gad and a Levitical city (<ref="Deu. 4:43; Jos. 20:8; 21:38">Deu. 4:43; Jos. 20:8; 21:38</ref>).

column5: Ancestor of Philistine giants; his descendants fought against David's warriors.
column7: Margin of [[@13020004|1 Chr. 20:4]], [[@13020006|1 Chr. 20:6]], where “giant” is given in the text.

column5: Son of Binea, a descendant of King Saul
column7: A Benjamite, the son of Binea ([[@13008002|1 Chr. 8:2]], [[@13008037|1 Chr. 8:37]]), a descendant of Saul.

column5: Father of Palti, a spy sent by Moses
column7: Healed, a Benjamite, whose son Palti was one of the twelve spies ([[@4013009|Num. 13:9]]).

column5: A Reubenite, son of Micah
column7: Reaiah was a Reubenite, the son of Micah, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Reuben.

column5: Ancestor of temple servants who returned from Babylonian exile
column7: Reaiah was an ancestor of temple servants who returned to Jerusalem from Babylonian exile.

column5: A Midianite king killed by the Israelites
column6: the fourth; a square; that lies or stoops down
column7: Fourth, one of the Midianite chiefs slain by the Israelites in the wilderness ([[@4031008|Num. 31:8]]; [[@6013021|Josh. 13:21]]).

column5: Wife of Isaac; mother of Jacob and Esau
column7: A noose, the daughter of Bethuel, and the wife of Isaac ([[@1022023|Gen. 22:23]]; [[@1024067|Gen 24:67]]). The circumstances under which Abraham’s “steward” found her at the “city of Nahor,” in Padan-aram, are narrated in Gen. 24-27. “She can hardly be regarded as an amiable woman.

column5: Descendant of Judah
column7: Recah was a descendant of Judah through Caleb (<ref="1Ch. 4:12">1Ch. 4:12</ref>).

column5: A captain of Ishbosheth's army, with his brother Baanah
column6: square; chariot with team of four horses
column7: One of Ishbosheth’s “captains of bands” or leaders of predatory troops ([[@10004002|2 Sam. 4:2]]).

column5: Ancestor of the Rechabites, who were faithful to God
column6: square; chariot with team of four horses
column7: The father of Jehonadab, who was the father of the Rechabites ([[@12010015|2 Kings 10:15]], [[@12010023|2 Kings 10:23]]; [[@24035006-24035019|Jer. 35:6-19]]).

column5: Father of Malchijah, who repaired the Dung Gate
column6: square; chariot with team of four horses
column7: Rechab was the father of Malchijah, who repaired the Dung Gate during the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.

column5: Sea crossed by Israelites in the Exodus
column7: The Red Sea was the body of water miraculously crossed by the Israelites in their escape from Egypt (<ref="Exo. 13:18; 15:4">Exo. 13:18; 15:4</ref>).

The purchase back of something that had been lost, by the payment of a ransom. The Greek word so rendered is apolutrosis , a word occurring nine times in Scripture, and always with the idea of a ransom or price paid, i.e., redemption by a lutron (see [[@40020028|Matt. 20:28]]; [[@41010045|Mark 10:45]]). There are instances in the LXX.

column5: One of the leaders who returned with Zerubbabel
column6: shepherd or companion to the Lord
column7: Thunder of the Lord, one of the princes who returned from the Exile ([[@16007007|Neh. 7:7]]); called also Reelaiah ([[@15002002|Ezra 2:2]]).

column5: Son of Jahdai, of the tribe of Judah
column6: that stones or is stoned; purple
column7: Regem was a son of Jahdai, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah.

column5: A messenger sent to inquire of the Lord
column7: Friend of the king, one of the two messengers sent by the exiled Jews to Jerusalem in the time of Darius ([[@38007002|Zech. 7:2]]) to make inquiries at the temple.

column5: Son of Eliezer, grandson of Moses, a Levite
column6: breadth, or extent, of the Lord
column7: Enlargement of the Lord, the son of Eliezer, and grandson of Moses ([[@13023017|1 Chr. 23:17]]; [[@13024021|1 Chr. 24:21]]).

column5: City on the border of Asher
column7: A town of Asher ([[@6019028|Josh. 19:28]]), to the east of Zidon.

column5: Levitical city in Asher
column7: Another town of Asher ([[@6019030|Josh. 19:30]]), kept possession of by the Canaanites ([[@7001031|Judg. 1:31]]).

column5: Father of Hadadezer, king of Zobah
column7: The father of Hadadezer, king of Tobah ([[@10008003|2 Sam. 8:3]], [[@10008012|2 Sam. 8:12]]).

column5: One of the leaders who sealed the covenant
column7: Rehob was one of the leaders who sealed the covenant during the time of Nehemiah.

column5: Son of Solomon, first king of Judah
column6: who sets the people at liberty
column7: He enlarges the people, the successor of Solomon on the throne, and apparently his only son. He was the son of Naamah “the Ammonitess,” some well-known Ammonitish princess ([[@11014021|1 Kings 14:21]]; [[@14012013|2 Chr. 12:13]]). He was forty-one years old when he ascended the throne, and he reigned seventeen years (B.C. 975-958). Although he was acknowledged at once as the rightful heir to the throne, yet there was a strongly-felt desire to modify the character of the government.

column5: Well dug by Isaac
column7: A well in Gerar dug by Isaac ([[@1026022|Gen. 26:22]]), supposed to be in Wady er-Ruheibeh, about 20 miles south of Beersheba.

column5: City associated with an Edomite king
column7: An ancient city on the Euphrates ([[@1036037|Gen. 36:37]]; [[@13001048|1 Chr. 1:48]]), “Rehoboth by the river.”

column5: One of the leaders who returned with Zerubbabel
column7: One of “the children of the province” who returned from the Captivity ([[@15002002|Ezra 2:2]]); the same as “Nehum” ([[@16007007|Neh. 7:7]]).

column5: A Persian official who wrote to King Artaxerxes
column7: The “chancellor” of Artaxerxes, who sought to stir him up against the Jews ([[@15004008-15004024|Ezra 4:8-24]]) and prevent the rebuilding of the walls and the temple of Jerusalem.

column5: A Levite who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem
column7: Rehum was a Levite who helped repair a section of the wall of Jerusalem during Nehemiah's time.

column5: One who sealed the covenant during Nehemiah's time
column7: Rehum was one of the individuals who sealed the covenant during the time of Nehemiah.

column5: A supporter of Solomon during Adonijah's rebellion
column6: my shepherd; my companion; my friend
column7: Friendly, one who maintained true allegiance to king David ([[@11001008|1 Kings 1:8]]) when Adonijah rebelled.

column5: A Midianite king killed by the Israelites
column7: One of the five Midianite kings whom the Israelites destroyed ([[@4031008|Num. 31:8]]).

column5: City in Benjamin
column7: Rekem was a city allotted to the tribe of Benjamin (<ref="Jos. 18:27">Jos. 18:27</ref>).

column5: Son of Hebron, of the tribe of Judah
column7: Rekem was a son of Hebron, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah.

column5: Father of Pekah, king of Israel
Levitical city in Issachar
column7: Another form of Ramah (q.v.) or Ramoth ([[@13006073|1 Chr. 6:73]]; [[@6019021|Josh. 19:21]]), and probably also of Jarmuth ([[@6021029|Josh. 21:29]]).

Metanoeo, meaning to change one’s mind and purpose, as the result of after knowledge. This verb, with (3) the cognate noun metanoia , is used of true repentance, a change of mind and purpose and life, to which remission of sin is promised.

column5: A gatekeeper of the temple during David's reign
column6: the physic or medicine of God
column7: Healed of God, one of Shemaiah’s sons.

column5: Son of Beriah, of the tribe of Asher
column7: Rephah was a son of Beriah, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher.

column5: A descendant of King David
column6: medicine or refreshment of the Lord
column7: Rephaiah was a descendant of King David, mentioned in the genealogy of David's descendants.

column5: A Simeonite leader who attacked the Amalekites
column6: medicine or refreshment of the Lord
column7: Rephaiah was a Simeonite leader who led an attack against the Amalekites during the time of Hezekiah.

column5: Son of Tola, of the tribe of Issachar
column6: medicine or refreshment of the Lord
column7: Rephaiah was a son of Tola, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Issachar.

column5: Son of Hur, who helped repair Jerusalem's wall
column6: medicine or refreshment of the Lord
column7: Rephaiah was the son of Hur and ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, who helped repair a section of the city wall.

column5: A race of giants who inhabited Canaan
column7: Lofty men; giants, ([[@1014005|Gen. 14:5]]; [[@10021016|2 Sam. 21:16]], [[@10021018|2 Sam. 21:18]], marg. A.V., Rapha, marg. R.V., Raphah; [[@5003013|Deut. 3:13]], R.V.; A.V., “giants”). The aborigines of Palestine, afterwards conquered and dispossessed by the Canaanite tribes, are classed under this general title. They were known to the Moabites as Emim, i.e., “fearful”, ([[@5002011|Deut. 2:11]]), and to the Ammonites as Zamzummim. Some of them found refuge among the Philistines, and were still existing in the days of David.

column5: Valley near Jerusalem, site of battles
column7: The Valley of Rephaim was a valley near Jerusalem where David fought the Philistines (<ref="2Sa. 5:18, 22; 23:13; 1Ch. 11:15; 14:9">2Sa. 5:18, 22; 23:13; 1Ch. 11:15; 14:9</ref>).

column5: Israelite encampment during the Exodus
column7: Supports, one of the stations of the Israelites, situated in the Wady Feiran, near its junction with the Wady esh-Sheikh. Here no water could be found for the people to drink, and in their impatience they were ready to stone Moses, as if he were the cause of their distress. At the command of God Moses smote “the rock in Horeb,” and a copious stream flowed forth, enough for all the people. After this the Amalekites attacked the Israelites while they were here encamped, but they were utterly defeated ([[@2017001|Ex. 17:1]], [[@2017008|Ex. 17:8]]-16).

column5: Ancient Assyrian city built by Nimrod
column7: Head of the stream; bridle, one of Nimrod’s cities ([[@1010012|Gen. 10:12]]), “between Nineveh and Calah.” It has been supposed that the four cities named in this verse were afterwards combined into one under the name of Nineveh (q.v.). Resen was on the east side of the Tigris.

column5: Son of Beriah, of the tribe of Asher
column7: Resheph was a son of Beriah, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher.

column5: Son of Peleg, ancestor of Abraham
column7: Reu was the son of Peleg and an ancestor of Abraham, living to the age of 239 years.

column5: Firstborn son of Jacob and Leah
column6: who sees the son; the vision of the son
column7: Behold a son!, the eldest son of Jacob and Leah ([[@1029032|Gen. 29:32]]). His sinful conduct, referred to in [[@1035022|Gen. 35:22]], brought down upon him his dying father’s malediction (48:4). He showed kindness to Joseph, and was the means of saving his life when his other brothers would have put him to death (37:21, 22). It was he also who pledged his life and the life of his sons when Jacob was unwilling to let Benjamin go down into Egypt.

column5: Son of Esau and Basemath, a chief of Edom
column6: the shepherd or friend of God
column7: Reuel was a son of Esau and Basemath, and he became a chief in the land of Edom.

column5: A Benjamite, son of Ibnijah
column6: the shepherd or friend of God
column7: Reuel was a Benjamite mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin.

column5: Concubine of Nahor, Abraham's brother
column7: Reumah was the concubine of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and she bore him four sons.

column5: City conquered by the Assyrians
column7: Solid; a stone, ([[@12019012|2 Kings 19:12]]; [[@23037012|Isa. 37:12]]), a fortress near Haran, probably on the west of the Euphrates, conquered by Sennacherib.

column5: King of Aram (Syria) during the reign of Ahaz
column7: Firm; a prince, a king of Syria, who joined Pekah (q.v.) in an invasion of the kingdom of Judah ([[@12015037|2 Kings 15:37]]; [[@12016005-12016009|2 Kings 16:5-9]]; [[@23007001-23007008|Isa. 7:1-8]]). Ahaz induced Tiglath-pileser III. to attack Damascus, and this caused Rezin to withdraw for the purpose of defending his own kingdom.

column5: Ancestor of a family of temple servants (Nethinim)
column7: Firm; a prince, a king of Syria, who joined Pekah (q.v.) in an invasion of the kingdom of Judah ([[@12015037|2 Kings 15:37]]; [[@12016005-12016009|2 Kings 16:5-9]]; [[@23007001-23007008|Isa. 7:1-8]]). Ahaz induced Tiglath-pileser III. to attack Damascus, and this caused Rezin to withdraw for the purpose of defending his own kingdom.

column5: Son of Eliada, adversary of Solomon
column7: Prince, son of Eliadah. Abandoning the service of Hadadezer, the king of Zobah, on the occasion of his being defeated by David, he became the “captain over a band” of marauders, and took Damascus, and became king of Syria ([[@11011023-11011025|1 Kings 11:23-25]]; [[@10008003-10008008|2 Sam. 8:3-8]]). For centuries after this the Syrians were the foes of Israel.

column5: Italian city visited by Paul
column7: Breach, a town in the south of Italy, on the Strait of Messina, at which Paul touched on his way to Rome ([[@44028013|Acts 28:13]]).

column5: Son of Zerubbabel, ancestor of Jesus
column7: Affection, son of Zorobabel, mentioned in the genealogy of our Lord ([[@42003027|Luke 3:27]]).

column5: Servant girl in the house of Mary
column7: A rose, the damsel in the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark.

column5: Island visited by Paul on his journey
column7: A rose, an island to the south of the western extremity of Asia Minor, between Coos and Patara, about 46 miles long and 18 miles broad.

column5: Father of Ittai, one of David's mighty men
column7: Ribai was the father of Ittai the Gibeathite, one of David's mighty men.

column5: Place on the eastern border of the Promised Land
column7: Fruitful, an ancient town on the northern frontier of Palestine, 35 miles north-east of Baalbec, and 10 or 12 south of Lake Homs, on the eastern bank of the Orontes, in a wide and fertile plain. Here Nebuchadnezzar had his head-quarters in his campaign against Jerusalem, and here also Necho fixed his camp after he had routed Josiah’s army at Megiddo ([[@12023029-12023035|2 Kings 23:29-35]]; [[@12025006|2 Kings 25:6]], [[@12025020|2 Kings 25:20]], [[@12025021|2 Kings 25:21]]; [[@24039005|Jer. 39:5]]; [[@24052010|Jer 52:10]]).

column5: Babylonian headquarters during the conquest of Judah
column7: Fruitful, an ancient town on the northern frontier of Palestine, 35 miles north-east of Baalbec, and 10 or 12 south of Lake Homs, on the eastern bank of the Orontes, in a wide and fertile plain. Here Nebuchadnezzar had his head-quarters in his campaign against Jerusalem, and here also Necho fixed his camp after he had routed Josiah’s army at Megiddo ([[@12023029-12023035|2 Kings 23:29-35]]; [[@12025006|2 Kings 25:6]], [[@12025020|2 Kings 25:20]], [[@12025021|2 Kings 25:21]]; [[@24039005|Jer. 39:5]]; [[@24052010|Jer 52:10]]).
See JUSTIFICATION.

column5: A town in Judah and Simeon
column7: One of the “uttermost cities” of Judah, afterwards given to Simeon ([[@6015021|Josh. 15:21]], [[@6015032|Josh. 15:32]]; 19:7; [[@13004032|1 Chr. 4:32]]). In [[@6015032|Josh. 15:32]] Ain and Rimmon are mentioned separately, but in 19:7 and [[@13004032|1 Chr. 4:32]] (comp. [[@16011029|Neh. 11:29]]) the two words are probably to be combined, as forming together the name of one place, Ain-Rimmon=the spring of the pomegranate.

column5: Rock where Benjamites fled after battle
column7: “Rock of,” to which the Benjamites fled ([[@7020045|Judg. 20:45]], [[@7020047|Judg. 20:47]]; 21:13), and where they maintained themselves for four months after the fearful battle at Gibeah, in which they were almost exterminated, 600 only surviving out of about 27,000.

column5: Father of Baanah and Rechab, murderers of Ish-bosheth
column7: A man of Beeroth ([[@10004002|2 Sam. 4:2]]), one of the four Gibeonite cities.

column5: Israelite encampment during the Exodus
column7: A pomegranate breach, or Rimmon of the breach, one of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness ([[@4033019|Num. 33:19]], [[@4033020|Num. 33:20]]).

column5: Son of Shimon, of the tribe of Judah
column7: Rinnah was a son of Shimon, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah.

column5: Son of Gomer, grandson of Japheth
column7: A crusher, Gomer’s second son ([[@1010003|Gen. 10:3]]), supposed to have been the ancestor of the Paphlagonians.

column5: Israelite encampment during the Exodus
column7: Heap of ruins; dew, a station of the Israelites in the wilderness ([[@4033021|Num. 33:21]], [[@4033022|Num. 33:22]]).

column5: Israelite encampment during the Exodus
column7: Wild broom, a station in the wilderness ([[@4033018|Num. 33:18]], [[@4033019|Num. 33:19]]), the “broom valley,” or “valley of broombushes,” the place apparently of the original encampment of Israel, near Kadesh.

column5: Son of Ulla, of the tribe of Asher
column7: Rizia was a son of Ulla, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher.

column5: Concubine of Saul; mother of Armoni and Mephibosheth
column7: Coal; hot stone, the daughter of Aiah, and one of Saul’s concubines. She was the mother of Armoni and Mephibosheth ([[@10003007|2 Sam. 3:7]]; [[@10021008|2 Sam. 21:8]], [[@10021010|2 Sam. 21:10]], [[@10021011|2 Sam. 21:11]]). It happened that a grievous famine, which lasted for three years, fell upon the land during the earlier half of David’s reign at Jerusalem. This calamity was sent “for Saul and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites.”

column5: Place where Saul stopped pursuing David
column7: Cliff of divisions the name of the great gorge which lies between Hachilah and Maon, south-east of Hebron. This gorge is now called the Wady Malaky. This was the scene of the interview between David and Saul mentioned in [[@9026013|1 Sam. 26:13]].

column5: Hometown of Barzillai the Gileadite
column7: Fullers, a town of Gilead, the residence of Barzillai the Gileadite ([[@10017027|2 Sam. 17:27]]; [[@10019031|2 Sam. 19:31]]), probably near to Mahanaim.

column5: Son of Shomer, of the tribe of Asher
column7: Rohgah was a son of Shomer (or 'Shamer'), mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher.

column5: Son of Heman, a Levitical singer
column7: Elevation of help, one of the sons of Heman, “the king’s seer in the words of God, to lift up the horn.”

column5: Capital city of the Roman Empire
column7: The most celebrated city in the world at the time of Christ. It is said to have been founded B.C. 753. When the New Testament was written, Rome was enriched and adorned with the spoils of the world, and contained a population estimated at 1,200,000, of which the half were slaves, and including representatives of nearly every nation then known. It was distinguished for its wealth and luxury and profligacy.

column5: Son of Benjamin, grandson of Jacob
column7: ([[@26038002|Ezek. 38:2]], [[@26038003|Ezek. 38:3]]; 39:1) is rendered “chief” in the Authorized Version. It is left untranslated as a proper name in the Revised Version. Some have supposed that the Russians are here meant, as one of the three Scythian tribes of whom Magog was the prince. They invaded the land of Judah in the days of Josiah.

column5: Son of Simon of Cyrene, who carried Jesus' cross
column7: Red, the son of Simon the Cyrenian ([[@41015021|Mark 15:21]]), whom the Roman soldiers compelled to carry the cross on which our Lord was crucified. Probably it is the same person who is again mentioned in [[@45016013|Rom. 16:13]] as a disciple at Rome, whose mother also was a Christian held in esteem by the apostle.

column5: Believer in Rome, son of Paul's "mother"
column7: Red, the son of Simon the Cyrenian ([[@41015021|Mark 15:21]]), whom the Roman soldiers compelled to carry the cross on which our Lord was crucified. Probably it is the same person who is again mentioned in [[@45016013|Rom. 16:13]] as a disciple at Rome, whose mother also was a Christian held in esteem by the apostle.

column5: Moabite woman, ancestor of David and Jesus
column7: A friend, a Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, whose father, Elimelech, had settled in the land of Moab. On the death of Elimelech and Mahlon, Naomi came with Ruth, her daughter-in-law, who refused to leave her, to Bethlehem, the old home from which Elimelech had migrated. There she had a rich relative, Boaz, to whom Ruth was eventually married. She became the mother of Obed, the grandfather of David.

(Heb. verb shabbath, meaning “to rest from labour”), the day of rest. It is first mentioned as having been instituted in Paradise, when man was in innocence ([[@1002002|Gen. 2:2]]). “The sabbath was made for man,” as a day of rest and refreshment for the body and of blessing to the soul. It is next referred to in connection with the gift of manna to the children of Israel in the wilderness ([[@2016023|Ex. 16:23]]); and afterwards, when the law was given from Sinai (20:11), the people were solemnly charged to “remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.”

column5: Son of Cush, grandson of Ham
column6: a going about or circuiting; old age
column7: Sabtah (or Sabta) was a son of Cush and a grandson of Ham, mentioned in the Table of Nations.

column5: Son of Cush, grandson of Ham
column7: Sabteca was a son of Cush and a grandson of Ham, mentioned in the Table of Nations.

column5: Son of Obed-edom, a Levitical gatekeeper
column7: A son of Obed-edom the Gittite, and a temple porter ([[@13026004|1 Chr. 26:4]]).

column5: Son of Shaharaim, a Benjamite
column7: Sachia was a son of Shaharaim, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin.

Cloth made of black goats’ hair, coarse, rough, and thick, used for sacks, and also worn by mourners ([[@1037034|Gen. 37:34]]; [[@1042025|Gen 42:25]]; [[@10003031|2 Sam. 3:31]]; [[@17004001|Esther 4:1]], [[@17004002|Esther 4:2]]; [[@19030011|Ps. 30:11]], etc.), and as a sign of repentance ([[@40011021|Matt. 11:21]]).

The origin of this Jewish sect cannot definitely be traced. It was probably the outcome of the influence of Grecian customs and philosophy during the period of Greek domination. The first time they are met with is in connection with John the Baptist’s ministry. They came out to him when on the banks of the Jordan, and he said to them, “O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?”

column5: Unknown location mentioned in Ezekiel's prophecy
column7: Sahar is a place mentioned in Ezekiel's prophecy, but its exact location is unknown (<ref="Ezk. 27:18">Ezk. 27:18</ref>).

column5: City on Cyprus visited by Paul and Barnabas
column7: A city on the south-east coast of Cyprus ([[@44013005|Acts 13:5]]), where Saul and Barnabas, on their first missionary journey, preached the word in one of the Jewish synagogues, of which there seem to have been several in that place.

column5: City in Bashan, east of the Jordan River
column7: Wandering, a city of Bashan assigned to the half tribe of Manasseh ([[@5003010|Deut. 3:10]]; [[@6012005|Josh. 12:5]]; [[@6013011|Josh 13:11]]), identified with Salkhad, about 56 miles east of Jordan.

column5: Place near Aenon where John the Baptist baptized
column7: Peaceful, a place near AEnon (q.v.), on the west of Jordan, where John baptized ([[@43003023|John 3:23]]).

column5: Benjamite who settled in Jerusalem after the exile
column7: Sallai was a Benjamite who settled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, as recorded in Nehemiah 11.

column5: Benjamite who lived in Jerusalem
column7: Sallu was a Benjamite who lived in Jerusalem, as recorded in the genealogy of 1Chronicles 9.

column5: Benjamite who settled in Jerusalem after the exile
column7: Sallu was a Benjamite leader who settled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, as recorded in Nehemiah 11.

column5: Priest who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel
column7: Sallu (or Sallai) was a priest who returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel and later signed the covenant under Nehemiah.

column5: Son of Hur, founder of Bethlehem
column7: Salma was the son of Hur and the  father (ie founder) of Bethlehem, as mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.

column5: Son of Nahshon; husband of Rahab; ancestor of David
column7: Garment, the son of Nashon ([[@8004020|Ruth 4:20]]; [[@40001004|Matt. 1:4]], [[@40001005|Matt. 1:5]]), possibly the same as Salma in [[@13002051|1 Chr. 2:51]].

column5: Promontory on the island of Crete
column7: A promontory on the east of Crete, under which Paul sailed on his voyage to Rome ([[@44027007|Acts 27:7]]); the modern Cape Sidero.

column5: Danced for Herod, requested John the Baptist's execution
column7: Salome, the daughter of Herodias, danced before Herod and requested the execution of John the Baptist.

column5: Witness of Jesus' crucifixion and resurrection
column7: The wife of Zebedee and mother of James and John ([[@40027056|Mat. 27:56]]), and probably the sister of Mary, the mother of our Lord ([[@43019025|John 19:25]]). She sought for her sons places of honour in Christ’s kingdom ([[@40020020|Matt. 20:20]], [[@40020021|Matt. 20:21]]; comp. 19:28).

Used to season food ([[@18006006|Job 6:6]]), and mixed with the fodder of cattle ([[@23030024|Isa. 30:24]], “clean;” in marg. of R.V. “salted”). All meat-offerings were seasoned with salt ([[@3002013|Lev. 2:13]]). To eat salt with one is to partake of his hospitality, to derive subsistence from him; and hence he who did so was bound to look after his host’s interests ([[@15004014|Ezra 4:14]], “We have maintenance from the king’s palace;” A.V. marg., “We are salted with the salt of the palace;” R.V., “We eat the salt of the palace”).

column5: Another name for the Dead Sea
column7: The name given by Greek writers of the second century to that inland sea called in Scripture the “salt sea” ([[@1014003|Gen. 14:3]]; [[@4034012|Num. 34:12]]), the “sea of the plain” ([[@5003017|Deut. 3:17]]), the “east sea” ([[@26047018|Ezek. 47:18]]; [[@29002020|Joel 2:20]]), and simply “the sea” ([[@26047008|Ezek. 47:8]]). The Arabs call it Bahr Lut, i.e., the Sea of Lot. It lies about 16 miles in a straight line to the east of Jerusalem. Its surface is 1,292 feet below the surface of the Mediterranean Sea.

column5: Valley where David and his commanders defeated enemies
column7: The Salt Valley was a location where David and his commanders defeated the Edomites and Arameans (<ref="2Sa. 8:13; 2Ki. 14:7; 1Chr. 18:12; 2Chr. 25:11; Psa. 60:1">2Sa. 8:13; 2Ki. 14:7; 1Chr. 18:12; 2Chr. 25:11; Psa. 60:1</ref>).

column5: Father of Zimri, a Simeonite prince
column7: Salu was the father of Zimri, a Simeonite prince who was killed by Phinehas for his involvement with a Midianite woman.
