column5: Capital city of the northern kingdom of Israel; Samaritan inhabitants
column7: A watch-mountain or a watch-tower. In the heart of the mountains of Israel, a few miles north-west of Shechem, stands the “hill of Shomeron,” a solitary mountain, a great “mamelon.” It is an oblong hill, with steep but not inaccessible sides, and a long flat top. Omri, the king of Israel, purchased this hill from Shemer its owner for two talents of silver, and built on its broad summit the city to which he gave the name of “Shomeron”, i.e., Samaria, as the new capital of his kingdom instead of Tirzah ([[@11016024|1 Kings 16:24]]). As such it possessed many advantages.

The name given to the new and mixed inhabitants whom Esarhaddon (B.C. 677), the king of Assyria, brought from Babylon and other places and settled in the cities of Samaria, instead of the original inhabitants whom Sargon (B.C. 721) had removed into captivity ([[@12017024|2 Kings 17:24]]; comp. [[@15004002|Ezra 4:2]], [[@15004009|Ezra 4:9]], [[@15004010|Ezra 4:10]]). These strangers (comp. [[@42017018|Luke 17:18]]) amalgamated with the Jews still remaining in the land, and gradually abandoned their old idolatry and adopted partly the Jewish religion.

column5: Babylonian official present at the fall of Jerusalem
column7: Be gracious, O Nebo! or a cup-bearer of Nebo, probably the title of Nergal-sharezer, one of the princes of Babylon ([[@24039003|Jer. 39:3]]).

column5: King of Edom before Israel had kings
column6: his raiment; his left hand; his astonishment
column7: Samlah was a king of Edom who reigned before Israel had kings, as mentioned in the genealogies of Esau.

column5: Island visited by Paul during his travels
column7: An island in the AEgean Sea, which Paul passed on his voyage from Assos to Miletus ([[@44020015|Acts 20:15]]), on his third missionary journey.

column5: Island visited by Paul during his second missionary journey
column6: an island possessed by the Samians and Thracians
column7: An island in the AEgean Sea, off the coast of Thracia, about 32 miles distant. This Thracian Samos was passed by Paul on his voyage from Troas to Neapolis ([[@44016011|Acts 16:11]]) on his first missionary journey. It is about 8 miles long and 6 miles broad.

column5: Israelite judge with great strength from God
column6: his sun; his service; there the second time
column7: Of the sun, the son of Manoah, born at Zorah. The narrative of his life is given in Judg. 13-16. He was a “Nazarite unto God” from his birth, the first Nazarite mentioned in Scripture ([[@7013003-7013005|Judg. 13:3-5]]; comp. [[@4006001-4006021|Num. 6:1-21]]). The first recorded event of his life was his marriage with a Philistine woman of Timnath ([[@7014001-7014005|Judg. 14:1-5]]).

column5: Prophet and last judge of Israel before the kings
column6: heard of God; asked of God
column7: Heard of God. The peculiar circumstances connected with his birth are recorded in [[@9001020|1 Sam. 1:20]]. Hannah, one of the two wives of Elkanah, who came up to Shiloh to worship before the Lord, earnestly prayed to God that she might become the mother of a son. Her prayer was graciously granted; and after the child was weaned she brought him to Shiloh nd consecrated him to the Lord as a perpetual Nazarite (1:23-2:11). Here his bodily wants and training were attended to by the women who served in the tabernacle, while Eli cared for his religious culture.

column5: Governor of Samaria, opposed Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem
column7: Held some place of authority in Samaria when Nehemiah went up to Jerusalem to rebuild its ruined walls. He vainly attempted to hinder this work ([[@16002010|Neh. 2:10]], [[@16002019|Neh. 2:19]]; 4:1-12; 6).

Involves more than a mere moral reformation of character, brought about by the power of the truth: it is the work of the Holy Spirit bringing the whole nature more and more under the influences of the new gracious principles implanted in the soul in regeneration. In other words, sanctification is the carrying on to perfection the work begun in regeneration, and it extends to the whole man ([[@45006013|Rom. 6:13]]; [[@47004006|2 Cor. 4:6]]; [[@51003010|Col. 3:10]]; [[@62004007|1 John 4:7]]; [[@46006019|1 Cor. 6:19]]).

Mentioned only in [[@41006009|Mark 6:9]] and [[@44012008|Acts 12:8]]. The sandal was simply a sole, made of wood or palm-bark, fastened to the foot by leathern straps. Sandals were also made of seal-skin ([[@26016010|Ezek. 16:10]]; lit. tahash, “leather;” A.V., “badger’s skin;” R.V., “sealskin,” or marg., “porpoise-skin”).

More correctly Sanhedrin (Gr. synedrion), meaning “a sitting together,” or a “council.” This word (rendered “council,” A.V.) is frequently used in the New Testament ([[@40005022|Matt. 5:22]]; [[@40026059|Matt 26:59]]; [[@41015001|Mark 15:1]], etc.) to denote the supreme judicial and administrative council of the Jews, which, it is said, was first instituted by Moses, and was composed of seventy men ([[@4011016|Num. 11:16]], [[@4011017|Num. 11:17]]). But that seems to have been only a temporary arrangement which Moses made.

column5: Town in the Negev region of Judah
column6: bough or bramble of the enemy
column7: A palm branch, or a thorn bush, a town in the south (the negeb) of Judah ([[@6015031|Josh. 15:31]]); called also Hazarsusah (19:5), or Hazar-susim ([[@13004031|1 Chr. 4:31]]).

column5: Philistine giant killed by Sibbechai the Hushathite
column7: Extension, the son of the giant whom Sibbechai slew ([[@10021018|2 Sam. 21:18]]); called also Sippai ([[@13020004|1 Chr. 20:4]]).

column5: Wife of Ananias, lied to the apostles, died
column7: Beautiful, the wife of Ananias (q.v.).

column5: Wife of Abraham; mother of Isaac
column6: lady; princess; princess of the multitude
column7: Princess, the wife and at the same time the half-sister of Abraham ([[@1011029|Gen. 11:29]]; [[@1020012|Gen 20:12]]). This name was given to her at the time that it was announced to Abraham that she should be the mother of the promised child. Her story is from her marriage identified with that of the patriarch till the time of her death. Her death, at the age of one hundred and twenty-seven years (the only instance in Scripture where the age of a woman is recorded), was the occasion of Abraham’s purchasing the cave of Machpelah as a family burying-place.

column5: Son of Shelah, descendant of Judah
column7: Saraph was a son of Shelah and a descendant of Judah, mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.

column5: Border town of Zebulun's territory
column7: Sarid was a border town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Zebulun (<ref="Josh. 19:10, 12">Josh. 19:10, 12</ref>).

Adversary; accuser. When used as a proper name, the Hebrew word so rendered has the article “the adversary” ([[@18001006-18001012|Job 1:6-12]]; [[@18002001-18002007|Job 2:1-7]]). In the New Testament it is used as interchangeable with Diabolos, or the devil, and is so used more than thirty times.

column5: First king of Israel, anointed by Samuel
column7: The son of Kish (probably his only son, and a child of prayer, “asked for”), of the tribe of Benjamin, the first king of the Jewish nation. The singular providential circumstances connected with his election as king are recorded in 1 Sam. 8-10. His father’s she-asses had strayed, and Saul was sent with a servant to seek for them.

column5: Jewish chief priest whose seven sons attempted to exorcise demons
column7: An implement, a Jew, chief of the priests at Ephesus ([[@44019013-44019016|Acts 19:13-16]]); i.e., the head of one of the twenty-four courses of the house of Levi. He had seven sons, who “took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus,” in imitation of Paul. They tried their method of exorcism on a fierce demoniac, and failed.

Anciently held various important offices in the public affairs of the nation. The Hebrew word so rendered (sopher) is first used to designate the holder of some military office ([[@7005014|Judg. 5:14]]; A.V., “pen of the writer;” R.V., “the marshal’s staff;” marg., “the staff of the scribe”).

The common form of ancient books. The Hebrew word rendered “roll” or “volume” is meghillah , found in [[@15006002|Ezra 6:2]]; [[@19040007|Ps. 40:7]]; [[@24036002|Jer. 36:2]], [[@24036006|Jer. 36:6]], [[@24036023|Jer. 36:23]], [[@24036028|Jer. 36:28]], [[@24036029|Jer. 36:29]]; [[@26002009|Ezek. 2:9]]; [[@26003001-26003003|Ezek 3:1-3]]; [[@38005001|Zech. 5:1]], [[@38005002|Zech 5:2]]. “Rolls” (Chald. pl. of sephar, corresponding to Heb. sepher) in [[@15006001|Ezra 6:1]] is rendered in the Revised Version “archives.”

column5: Nomadic people group mentioned by Paul
column7: The Scythians consisted of “all the pastoral tribes who dwelt to the north of the Black Sea and the Caspian, and were scattered far away toward the east. Of this vast country but little was anciently known. Its modern representative is Russia, which, to a great extent, includes the same territories.” They were the descendants of Japheth ([[@1009027|Gen. 9:27]]).

Commonly a ring engraved with some device ([[@1038018|Gen. 38:18]], [[@1038025|Gen. 38:25]]). Jezebel “wrote letters in Ahab’s name, and sealed them with his seal” ([[@11021008|1 Kings 21:8]]). Seals are frequently mentioned in Jewish history ([[@5032034|Deut. 32:34]]; [[@16009038|Neh. 9:38]]; [[@16010001|Neh 10:1]]; [[@17003012|Esther 3:12]]; [[@22008006|Cant. 8:6]]; [[@23008016|Isa. 8:16]]; [[@24022024|Jer. 22:24]]; [[@24032044|Jer 32:44]], etc.). Sealing a document was equivalent to the signature of the owner of the seal.

column5: Son of Cush, brother of Raamah
column7: Seba was a son of Cush and brother of Raamah.

column5: Kingdom mentioned in prophetic and poetic texts
column7: The name of a country and nation ([[@23043003|Isa. 43:3]]; [[@23045014|Isa 45:14]]) mentioned along with Egypt and Ethiopia, and therefore probably in north-eastern Africa. The ancient name of Meroe.

column5: Town in the territory of Reuben
column7: Sebam was one of the towns in the territory of Reuben, east of the Jordan River (<ref="Num. 32:3">Num. 32:3</ref>).

column5: Town in the wilderness of Judah
column7: Enclosure, one of the six cities in the wilderness of Judah, noted for its “great cistern” ([[@6015061|Josh. 15:61]]).

column5: District in Jerusalem mentioned by Huldah and Zephaniah
column7: The Second Quarter was a district in Jerusalem mentioned in connection with the prophetess Huldah (<ref="2Ki. 22:14; 2Chr. 34:22">2Ki. 22:14; 2Chr. 34:22</ref>) and in Zephaniah's prophecy (<ref="Zeph. 1:10">Zeph. 1:10</ref>).

column5: Place near Ramah visited by Saul
column7: A hill or watch-tower, a place between Gibeah and Ramah noted for its “great well” ([[@9019022|1 Sam. 19:22]]); probably the modern Suweikeh, south of Beeroth.

column5: Thessalonian believer who accompanied Paul
column7: Second, a Christian of Thessalonica who accompanied Paul into Asia ([[@44020004|Acts 20:4]]).

column5: Son of Hiel the Bethelite
column7: The youngest son of Hiel the Bethelite.

column5: Son of Hezron; father of Jair
column7: Segub, son of Hezron, was the father of Jair, who had twenty-three cities in Gilead.

column5: Region inhabited by Edomites, descendants of Esau
column7: The name of a mountainous region occupied by the Edomites, extending along the eastern side of the Arabah from the south-eastern extremity of the Dead Sea to near the Akabah, or the eastern branch of the Red Sea. It was originally occupied by the Horites ([[@1014006|Gen. 14:6]]), who were afterwards driven out by the Edomites ([[@1032003|Gen. 32:3]]; [[@1033014|Gen 33:14]], [[@1033016|Gen 33:16]]).

column5: Horite chief, ancestor of the Horites of Seir
column7: A Horite; one of the “dukes” of Edom ([[@1036020-1036030|Gen. 36:20-30]]).

column5: Mountainous region in Seir, associated with Edom
column7: Mount Seir refers to the mountainous region within Seir, often associated with the Edomites (<ref="Deut. 1:2; 2:1, 5; 1Chr. 4:42; Ezek. 35:2, 3, 7, 15">Deut. 1:2; 2:1, 5; 1Chr. 4:42; Ezek. 35:2, 3, 7, 15</ref>).

column5: Landmark on the boundary of Judah
column7: Mount Seir was a landmark on the boundary of Judah, near Kiriath-jearim and Chesalon (<ref="Josh. 15:10">Josh. 15:10</ref>).

column5: Place where Ehud escaped after killing Eglon
column7: Woody district; shaggy, a place among the mountains of Ephraim, bordering on Benjamin, to which Ehud fled after he had assassinated Eglon at Jericho ([[@7003026|Judg. 3:26]], [[@7003027|Judg. 3:27]]).

column5: Edomite stronghold captured by King Amaziah of Judah
column7: =Se’lah, rock, the capital of Edom, situated in the great valley extending from the Dead Sea to the Red Sea ([[@12014007|2 Kings 14:7]]). It was near Mount Hor, close by the desert of Zin. It is called “the rock” ([[@7001036|Judg. 1:36]]). When Amaziah took it he called it Joktheel (q.v.) It is mentioned by the prophets ([[@23016001|Isa. 16:1]]; Obad. 1:3) as doomed to destruction.
A word frequently found in the Book of Psalms, and also in [[@35003009|Hab. 3:9]], [[@35003013|Hab 3:13]], about seventy-four times in all in Scripture. Its meaning is doubtful.

column5: Port city from which Paul and Barnabas sailed
column6: shaken or beaten by the waves
column7: The sea-port of Antioch, near the mouth of the Orontes. Paul and his companions sailed from this port on their first missionary journey ([[@44013004|Acts 13:4]]). This city was built by Seleucus Nicator, the “king of Syria.” It is said of him that “few princes have ever lived with so great a passion for the building of cities.

column5: Son of Shemaiah, gatekeeper of the temple
column7: Semachiah, a son of Shemaiah, served as a gatekeeper in the temple during the time of David.

column5: Ancestor of Jesus Christ
column7: Mentioned in the genealogy of our Lord ([[@42003026|Luke 3:26]]).

column5: A leader from the tribe of Benjamin
column7: Thorny, a place many of the inhabitants of which returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel ([[@15002035|Ezra 2:35]]; [[@16007038|Neh. 7:38]]).

column5: Rocky crag near Michmash
column7: The acacia; rock-thorn, the southern cliff in the Wady es-Suweinit, a valley south of Michmash, which Jonathan climbed with his armour-bearer ([[@9014004|1 Sam. 14:4]], [[@9014005|1 Sam. 14:5]]).

column5: Assyrian Emperor who invaded Judah
column7: Sin (the god) sends many brothers, son of Sargon, whom he succeeded on the throne of Assyria (B.C. 705), in the 23rd year of Hezekiah. “Like the Persian Xerxes, he was weak and vainglorious, cowardly under reverse, and cruel and boastful in success.” He first set himself to break up the powerful combination of princes who were in league against him. Among these was Hezekiah, who had entered into an alliance with Egypt against Assyria.

column5: Priest during David's reign, head of the fourth division
column7: Barley, the chief of the forth priestly course ([[@13024008|1 Chr. 24:8]]).

column5: Boundary of the territory settled by Joktan's descendants
column7: Numbering, ([[@1010030|Gen. 10:30]]), supposed by some to be the ancient Himyaritic capital, “Shaphar,” Zaphar, on the Indian Ocean, between the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea.

column5: City in Asia Minor; destination of exiled Jews
column7: (Obad. 1:20), some locality unknown. The modern Jews think that Spain is meant, and hence they designate the Spanish Jews “Sephardim,” as they do the German Jews by the name “Ashkenazim,” because the rabbis call Germany Ashkenaz. Others identify it with Sardis, the capital of Lydia. The Latin father Jerome regarded it as an Assyrian word, meaning “boundary,” and interpreted the sentence, “which is in Sepharad,” by “who are scattered abroad in all the boundaries and regions of the earth.”

column5: City of origin for people resettled in Samaria
column6: the two books; the two scribes
column7: Taken by Sargon, king of Assyria ([[@12017024|2 Kings 17:24]]; [[@12018034|2 Kings 18:34]]; [[@12019013|2 Kings 19:13]]; [[@23037013|Isa. 37:13]]). It was a double city, and received the common name Sepharvaim, i.e., “the two Sipparas,” or “the two booktowns.” The Sippara on the east bank of the Euphrates is now called Abu-Habba; that on the other bank was Accad, the old capital of Sargon I., where he established a great library.

column5: Daughter of Asher, sister of Asher's sons
column6: lady of scent; song; the morning star
column7: Abundance; princess, the daughter of Asher and grand-daughter of Jacob ([[@1046017|Gen. 46:17]]); called also Sarah ([[@4026046|Num. 26:46]]; R.V., “Serah”).

column5: David's scribe, also known as Shavsha, Sheva, Sheya, or Shisha
column7: One of David’s scribes or secretaries ([[@10008017|2 Sam. 8:17]]).

column5: High priest during the reign of Zedekiah
column7: A Netophathite ([[@24040008|Jer. 40:8]]), a chief priest of the time of Zedekiah.

column5: Officer under Gedaliah, son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite
column7: A Netophathite ([[@24040008|Jer. 40:8]]), a chief priest of the time of Zedekiah.

column5: Son of Kenaz; father of Joab
column7: Seraiah, the son of Kenaz, was the father of Joab, who was the father of the Valley of Craftsmen.

column5: Son of Asiel, descendant of Simeon
column7: Seraiah, the son of Asiel, was a descendant of Simeon mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Simeon.

column5: Priest who returned from Babylonian exile
column7: A priest of the days of Jehoiakim ([[@16012001|Neh. 12:1]], [[@16012012|Neh. 12:12]]).

column5: Son of Azriel, sent to capture Jeremiah and Baruch
column7: Seraiah, the son of Azriel, was one of the men sent by King Jehoiakim to capture Jeremiah and Baruch.

column5: Neriah's son, Baruch's brother, accompanied Zedekiah to Babylon
column7: Seraiah, the son of Neriah and brother of Baruch, accompanied King Zedekiah to Babylon and carried a message from Jeremiah.

Mentioned in [[@23006002|Isa. 6:2]], [[@23006003|Isa. 6:3]], [[@23006006|Isa. 6:6]], [[@23006007|Isa. 6:7]]. This word means fiery ones, in allusion, as is supposed, to their burning love. They are represented as “standing” above the King as he sat upon his throne, ready at once to minister unto him. Their form appears to have been human, with the addition of wings.

column5: Son of Zebulun, ancestor of the Seredites
column7: Fear, one of the sons of Zebulun ([[@1046014|Gen. 46:14]]).

column5: Proconsul of Cyprus, converted under Paul's ministry
column7: Sergius Paulus, the proconsul of Cyprus, was an intelligent man who sought to hear the word of God and believed after witnessing Paul's confrontation with Elymas the sorcerer.

column5: Son of Reu; father of Nahor, ancestor of Abraham
column7: Branch, the father of Nahor ([[@1011020-1011023|Gen. 11:20-23]]); called Saruch in [[@42003035|Luke 3:35]].

column5: Third son of Adam and Eve, ancestor of righteous line
column7: Appointed; a substitute, the third son of Adam and Eve ([[@1004025|Gen. 4:25]]; [[@1005003|Gen 5:3]]).

column5: Son of Michael, spy from the tribe of Asher
column7: Hidden, one of the spies sent to search the Promised Land.

column5: Town in Dan, home of David's mighty men
column7: Or Shaal’bim, a place of foxes, a town of the tribe of Dan ([[@6019042|Josh. 19:42]]; [[@7001035|Judg. 1:35]]). It was one of the chief towns from which Solomon drew his supplies ([[@11004009|1 Kings 4:9]]).

column5: Region traversed by Saul in search of donkeys
column7: Shaalim was a region through which Saul passed while searching for his father's lost donkeys (<ref="1Sam. 9:4">1Sam. 9:4</ref>).

column5: Son of Jahdai, a Calebite
column7: Shaaph, a son of Jahdai, was a descendant of Caleb.

column5: Son of Maacah, Caleb's concubine
column7: Shaaph, a son of Caleb's concubine Maacah, was the father of Madmannah.

column5: Town in Judah; site of Philistine retreat
column7: A city in the plain of Judah ([[@9017052|1 Sam. 17:52]]); called also Sharaim ([[@6015036|Josh. 15:36]]).

column5: Eunuch in charge of King Ahasuerus' concubines
column6: he that presses the fleece; that shears the sheep
column7: Servant of the beautiful, a chief eunuch in the second house of the harem of king Ahasuerus ([[@17002014|Esther 2:14]]).

column5: Levite who opposed Ezra's marriage reforms
column7: Sabbath-born, a Levite who assisted in expounding the law and investigating into the illegal marriages of the Jews ([[@15010015|Ezra 10:15]]; [[@16008007|Neh. 8:7]]; [[@16011016|Neh 11:16]]).

column5: Levite who helped explain the Law to the people
column7: Sabbath-born, a Levite who assisted in expounding the law and investigating into the illegal marriages of the Jews ([[@15010015|Ezra 10:15]]; [[@16008007|Neh. 8:7]]; [[@16011016|Neh 11:16]]).

column5: Levite in charge of external affairs in Jerusalem
column7: Sabbath-born, a Levite who assisted in expounding the law and investigating into the illegal marriages of the Jews ([[@15010015|Ezra 10:15]]; [[@16008007|Neh. 8:7]]; [[@16011016|Neh 11:16]]).

column5: Benjamite who had wives Hushim and Baara
column7: Shaharaim, a Benjamite, had two wives, Hushim and Baara, and he sent them away.

column5: Border town of Issachar
column7: Shahazumah was a town on the border of Issachar's territory (<ref="Josh. 19:22">Josh. 19:22</ref>).

column5: Region Saul passed through seeking donkeys
column7: Shalishah was a region Saul and his servant passed through while searching for his father's lost donkeys (<ref="1Sam. 9:4">1Sam. 9:4</ref>).

column5: Gate in Jerusalem assigned to Shuppim and Hosah
column7: Shallecheth was a gate in Jerusalem assigned to the Levites Shuppim and Hosah for guard duty (<ref="1Chr. 26:16">1Chr. 26:16</ref>).

column5: King of Israel who conspired against Zechariah
column7: The son of Jabesh, otherwise unknown. He “conspired against Zachariah, and smote him before the people, and slew him, and reigned in his stead” ([[@12015010|2 Kings 15:10]]). He reigned only “a month of days in Samaria” (15:13, marg.).

column5: Husband of Huldah the prophetess
column7: Keeper of the temple vestments in the reign of Josiah ([[@12022014|2 Kings 22:14]]).

column5: Son of Sismai, descendant of Judah
column7: Shallum, the son of Sismai, was a descendant of Judah through the line of Jerahmeel.

column5: Son of Josiah, king of Judah
column7: A son of king Josiah ([[@13003015|1 Chr. 3:15]]; [[@24022011|Jer. 22:11]]), who was elected to succeed his father on the throne, although he was two years younger than his brother Eliakim. He assumed the crown under the name of Jehoahaz (q.v.). He did not imitate the example of his father ([[@12023032|2 Kings 23:32]]), but was “a young lion, and it learned to catch the prey; it devoured men” ([[@26019003|Ezek. 19:3]]). His policy was anti-Egyptian therefore.

column5: Son of Shaul, descendant of Simeon
column7: Shallum was the son of Shaul and a descendant of Simeon.

column5: High priest, son of Zadok and father of Hilkiah
column7: One of the line of the high priests ([[@13006013|1 Chr. 6:13]]).

column5: Gatekeeper of the tabernacle during David's reign
column7: Shallum was a gatekeeper of the tabernacle during the reign of David, and his descendants continued to serve as gatekeepers in the temple.

column5: Ephraimite leader who opposed taking captives from Judah
column7: Shallum, along with other leaders from Ephraim, opposed the army of Israel taking captives from Judah during the reign of King Ahaz.

column5: Singer who married a foreign woman during Ezra's time
column7: Shallum was one of the singers who had married a foreign woman and agreed to put her away during Ezra's reforms.

column5: Israelite who married a foreign woman during Ezra's time
column7: Shallum was one of the Israelites who had married a foreign woman and pledged to put her away during Ezra's reforms.

column5: Son of Hallohesh, repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall
column7: Shallum, the son of Hallohesh and ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, repaired a section of the city wall along with his daughters.

column5: Son of Col-hozeh, repaired the Fountain Gate
column7: Shallum, the son of Col-hozeh and ruler of the district of Mizpah, repaired the Fountain Gate and the wall of the Pool of Shelah during Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.

column5: Uncle of Jeremiah the prophet
column7: The uncle of the prophet Jeremiah ([[@24032007|Jer. 32:7]]).

column5: Father of Maaseiah, keeper of the threshold
column7: Shallum was the father of Maaseiah, who was a keeper of the threshold during the time of Jeremiah the prophet.

column5: Nethinim ancestor whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile
column7: Shalmai (or Shamlai) was an ancestor of the Nethinim, and his descendants were among those who returned to Jerusalem from the Babylonian exile.

column5: Assyrian king who conquered Samaria and exiled Israelites
column7: An Assyrian king ([[@28010014|Hos. 10:14]]), identified with Shalmaneser II. (Sayce) or IV. (Lenormant), the successor of Pul on the throne of Assyria (B.C. 728). He made war against Hoshea, the king of Israel, whom he subdued and compelled to pay an annual tribute.

column5: Mighty man in David's army, a Harodite
column7: Shama, the son of Hotham the Aroerite, was one of the mighty men in David's army.

column5: Judge of Israel who killed 600 Philistines
column6: named a stranger; he is here a stranger
column7: The Philistines from the maritime plain had made incursions into the Hebrew upland for the purposes of plunder, when one of this name, the son of Anath, otherwise unknown, headed a rising for the purpose of freeing the land from this oppression. He repelled the invasion, slaying 600 men with an “ox goad” (q.v.). The goad was a formidable sharpointed instrument, sometimes ten feet long.

column5: Fifth division commander in David's army
column7: Shamhuth the Izrahite was the commander of the fifth division in David's army, serving during the fifth month.

column5: A man who carried Jesus' cross on the way to crucifixion.
column7: A Jew of Cyrene, in North Africa, then a province of Libya. A hundred thousand Jews from Palestine had been settled in this province by Ptolemy Soter (B.C. 323-285), where by this time they had greatly increased in number. They had a synagogue in Jerusalem for such of their number as went thither to the annual feasts. Simon was seized by the soldiers as the procession wended its way to the place of crucifixion as he was passing by, and the heavy cross which Christ from failing strength could no longer bear was laid on his shoulders.

column5: Father of Judas Iscariot, the disciple who betrayed Jesus.
column7: Simon was the father of Judas Iscariot, the disciple who betrayed Jesus.

column5: Sorcerer in Samaria who tried to buy the Holy Spirit's power.
column7: A sorcerer of great repute for his magical arts among the Samaritans ([[@44008009-44008011|Acts 8:9-11]]). He afterwards became a professed convert to the faith under the preaching of Philip the deacon and evangelist (12, 13). His profession was, however, soon found to be hollow. His conduct called forth from Peter a stern rebuke (8:18-23).

column5: A tanner in Joppa who hosted Peter.
column7: A Christian at Joppa, a tanner by trade, with whom Peter on one occasion lodged ([[@44009043|Acts 9:43]]).

column5: Wilderness area between Elim and Sinai
column7: Sin was a wilderness area between Elim and Sinai where the Israelites camped during their journey from Egypt to the Promised Land (<ref="Exod. 16:1; 17:1; Num. 33:11-12">Exod. 16:1; 17:1; Num. 33:11-12</ref>).

(Heb. hattath), the law of, is given in detail in Lev. 4-6:13; 9:7-11, 22-24; 12:6-8; 15:2, 14, 25-30; 14:19, 31; [[@4006010-4006014|Num. 6:10-14]]. On the day of Atonement it was made with special solemnity ([[@3016005|Lev. 16:5]], [[@3016011|Lev 16:11]], [[@3016015|Lev 16:15]]). The blood was then carried into the holy of holies and sprinkled on the mercy-seat. Sin-offerings were also presented at the five annual festivals (Num. 28, 29), and on the occasion of the consecration of the priests ([[@2029010-2029014|Ex. 29:10-14]], [[@2029036|Ex 29:36]]).

column5: Mountain where Moses received the Ten Commandments
column7: Of Sin (the moon god), called also Horeb, the name of the mountain district which was reached by the Hebrews in the third month after the Exodus. Here they remained encamped for about a whole year. Their journey from the Red Sea to this encampment, including all the windings of the route, was about 150 miles. The last twenty-two chapters of Exodus, together with the whole of Leviticus and Num. ch. 1-11, contain a record of all the transactions which occurred while they were here.

column5: Wilderness where Israel camped after leaving Egypt
column7: The Sinai Wilderness was the region where the Israelites camped after the Exodus and received the Law.

column5: Canaanite people group descended from Canaan.
column7: An inhabitant of Sin, near Arka ([[@1010017|Gen. 10:17]]; [[@13001015|1 Chr. 1:15]]).

column5: Town in southern Judah that received spoils from David
column7: Fruitful places, some unknown place in the south, where David found friends when he fled from Saul ([[@9030028|1 Sam. 30:28]]).

column5: Place near Hebron where Abner was killed by Joab
column7: Retiring, a well from which Joab’s messenger brought back Abner ([[@10003026|2 Sam. 3:26]]).

column5: Canaanite commander defeated by Deborah and Barak.
column6: that sees a horse or a swallow
column7: The captain of Jabin’s army ([[@7004002|Judg. 4:2]]), which was routed and destroyed by the army of Barak on the plain of Esdraelon. After all was lost he fled to the settlement of Heber the Kenite in the plain of Zaanaim. Jael, Heber’s wife, received him into her tent with apparent hospitality, and “gave him butter” (i.e., lebben, or curdled milk) “in a lordly dish.” Having drunk the refreshing beverage, he lay down, and soon sank into the sleep of the weary.

column5: Ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned from exile.
column6: that sees a horse or a swallow
column7: The ancestor of some of the Nethinim who returned with Zerubbabel ([[@15002053|Ezra 2:53]]; [[@16007055|Neh. 7:55]]).

column5: Egyptian queen, given in marriage to Hadad
column7: The sister of Tahpenes, an Egyptian queen, was given in marriage to Hadad the Edomite by Pharaoh.

column5: Son of Uzziel, a Levite of the Kohathite clan.
column7: The Lord protects, a Levite, son of Uzziel ([[@2006022|Ex. 6:22]]).

column5: Well dug by Isaac, disputed by Philistines
column7: Strife, the second of the two wells dug by Isaac, whose servants here contended with the Philistines ([[@1026021|Gen. 26:21]]).

With a sling and a stone David smote the Philistine giant ([[@9017040|1 Sam. 17:40]], [[@9017049|1 Sam. 17:49]]). There were 700 Benjamites who were so skilled in its use that with the left hand they “could sling stones at a hair breadth, and not miss” ([[@7020016|Judg. 20:16]]; [[@13012002|1 Chr. 12:2]]). It was used by the Israelites in war ([[@12003025|2 Kings 3:25]]).

column5: One of the seven churches of Asia Minor
column7: Myrrh, an ancient city of Ionia, on the western coast of Asia Minor, about 40 miles to the north of Ephesus. It is now the chief city of Anatolia, having a mixed population of about 200,000, of whom about one-third are professed Christians. The church founded here was one of the seven addressed by our Lord ([[@66002008-66002011|Rev. 2:8-11]]). The celebrated Polycarp, a pupil of the apostle John, was in the second century a prominent leader in the church of Smyrna.

column5: Egyptian pharaoh to whom King Hoshea sent messengers.
column7: (Nubian, Sabako), an Ethiopian king who brought Egypt under his sway. He was bribed by Hoshea to help him against the Assyrian monarch Shalmaneser ([[@12017004|2 Kings 17:4]]).

column5: Son of Heber, from the tribe of Judah.
column7: A fence; hedge, ([[@13004018|1 Chr. 4:18]]; R.V., Soco)=So’choh ([[@11004010|1 Kings 4:10]]; R.V., Socoh), Sho’choh ([[@9017001|1 Sam. 17:1]]; R.V., Socoh), Sho’co ([[@14011007|2 Chr. 11:7]]; R.V., Soco), Sho’cho ([[@14028018|2 Chr. 28:18]]; R.V., Soco), a city in the plain or lowland of Judah, where the Philistines encamped when they invaded Judah after their defeat at Michmash. It lay on the northern side of the valley of Elah (Wady es-Sunt). It has been identified with the modern Khurbet Shuweikeh, about 14 miles south-west of Jerusalem.

column5: Town in Judah; site of David's battle with Goliath
column7: Socoh was a town in the Shephelah region of Judah (<ref="Josh. 15:35">Josh. 15:35</ref>), known for being near the site of David's battle with Goliath (<ref="1Sam. 17:1">1Sam. 17:1</ref>) and later fortified by Rehoboam (<ref="2Chr. 11:7">2Chr. 11:7</ref>).

column5: A town in the hill country of Judah
column7: Socoh, a town allotted to the tribe of Judah in the hill country (<ref="Jos. 15:48">Jos. 15:48</ref>).

column5: Father of the Zebulunite spy Gaddiel.
column7: Sodi was the father of Gaddiel, the man chosen from the tribe of Zebulun to spy out the land of Canaan.

column5: Wicked city destroyed by God for its sins
column7: Burning; the walled, a city in the vale of Siddim ([[@1013010|Gen. 13:10]]; [[@1014001-1014016|Gen 14:1-16]]). The wickedness of its inhabitants brought down upon it fire from heaven, by which it was destroyed (18:16-33; 19:1-29; [[@5023017|Deut. 23:17]]).

column5: Son of David, king of Israel, known for his wisdom.
column7: Peaceful, (Heb. Shelomoh), David’s second son by Bathsheba, i.e., the first after their legal marriage (2 Sam. 12). He was probably born about B.C. 1035 ([[@13022005|1 Chr. 22:5]]; [[@13029001|1 Chr. 29:1]]). He succeeded his father on the throne in early manhood, probably about sixteen or eighteen years of age. Nathan, to whom his education was intrusted, called him Jedidiah, i.e., “beloved of the Lord” ([[@10012024|2 Sam. 12:24]], [[@10012025|2 Sam. 12:25]]). He was the first king of Israel “born in the purple.”

column5: Colonnade in Jerusalem's temple where apostles taught
column7: Solomon's Portico, a colonnade in the Jerusalem temple where the apostles gathered to teach (<ref="Act.3.11; 5:12">Act.3.11; 5:12</ref>).

column5: Son of Jashen - One of David's mighty men
column7: The son of Jashen, unnamed in the Bible, was one of David's mighty men.

column5: Grandson of Eliashib, married Sanballat's daughter
column7: The son of Joiada, a grandson of the high priest Eliashib, married the daughter of Sanballat the Horonite.

column5: Companion of Paul from Berea, greeted the Roman church.
column7: The father who saves, probably the same as Sosipater, a kinsman of Paul ([[@45016021|Rom. 16:21]]), a Christian of the city of Berea who accompanied Paul into Asia ([[@44020004-44020006|Acts 20:4-6]]).

column5: Ancestor of a family of Solomon's servants who returned from exile.
column7: Sophereth (or Hassophereth) was the ancestor of a family of Solomon's servants who were among the exiles that returned to Jerusalem from Babylon.

column5: Valley where Delilah lived, Samson's downfall occurred
column7: Sorek Valley, the place where Delilah lived and where Samson's downfall began (<ref="Judg. 16:4">Judg. 16:4</ref>).

column5: Synagogue ruler in Corinth, co-sender of 1 Corinthians.
column7: Safe in strength, the chief ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, who was seized and beaten by the mob in the presence of Gallio, the Roman governor, when he refused to proceed against Paul at the instigation of the Jews ([[@44018012-44018017|Acts 18:12-17]]). The motives of this assault against Sosthenes are not recorded, nor is it mentioned whether it was made by Greeks or Romans.

column5: Ancestor of a family of Solomon's servants who returned from exile.
column7: Sotai was the ancestor of a family of Solomon's servants who were among the exiles that returned to Jerusalem from Babylon.

column5: Country Paul intended to visit to preach gospel
column7: Paul expresses his intention ([[@45015024|Rom. 15:24]], [[@45015028|Rom. 15:28]]) to visit Spain. There is, however, no evidence that he ever carried it into effect, although some think that he probably did so between his first and second imprisonment.

column5: Believer in Rome, greeted by Paul as a beloved friend.
column7: Spike; an ear of corn, a convert at Rome whom Paul salutes ([[@45016009|Rom. 16:9]]).

column5: Corinthian believer, baptized by Paul, sent to visit him.
column7: Crown, a member of the church at Corinth, whose family were among those the apostle had baptized ([[@46001016|1 Cor. 1:16]]; [[@46016015|1 Cor. 16:15]], [[@46016017|1 Cor. 16:17]]). He has been supposed by some to have been the “jailer of Philippi” (comp. [[@44016033|Acts 16:33]]).

column5: One of seven deacons, full of faith, performed miracles, martyred.
column7: One of the seven deacons, who became a preacher of the gospel. He was the first Christian martyr. His personal character and history are recorded in Acts 6. “He fell asleep” with a prayer for his persecutors on his lips (7:60).

column5: Street in Damascus where Saul stayed after conversion
column7: Straight, a street in Damascus where Saul stayed in the house of Judas after his conversion (<ref="Act.9.11">Act.9.11</ref>).

column5: Son of Zophah, from the tribe of Asher
column7: Suah, a descendant of Asher mentioned in a genealogy.

column5: First Israelite campsite after leaving Egypt during Exodus
column7: The first encampment of the Israelites after leaving Ramesses ([[@2012037|Ex. 12:37]]); the civil name of Pithom (q.v.).

column5: City in Canaan, location of Solomon's bronze works
column7: A city on the east of Jordan, identified with Tell Dar’ala, a high mound, a mass of debris, in the plain north of Jabbok and about one mile from it ([[@6013027|Josh. 13:27]]). Here Jacob ([[@1032017|Gen. 32:17]], [[@1032030|Gen. 32:30]]; 33:17), on his return from Padan-aram after his interview with Esau, built a house for himself and made booths for his cattle. The princes of this city churlishly refused to afford help to Gideon and his 300 men when “faint yet pursuing” they followed one of the bands of the fugitive Midianites after the great victory at Gilboa.

column5: African people who invaded Judah under Shishak
column7: The Sukkiim were an African people who joined Shishak's invasion of Judah.

column5: Place near where Moses spoke to Israel
column7: ([[@5001001|Deut. 1:1]], R.V.; marg., “some ancient versions have the Red Sea,” as in the A.V.). Some identify it with Suphah ([[@4021014|Num. 21:14]], marg., A.V.) as probably the name of a place. Others identify it with es-Sufah = Maaleh-acrabbim ([[@6015003|Josh. 15:3]]), and others again with Zuph ([[@9009005|1 Sam. 9:5]]).

column5: Place mentioned in the Book of the Wars of the Lord
column7: ([[@4021014|Num. 21:14]], marg.; also R.V.), a place at the south-eastern corner of the Dead Sea, the Ghor es-Safieh.

column5: Gate of the temple in Jerusalem
column7: Sur, a gate of the temple in Jerusalem, possibly referring to the Foundation Gate (<ref="2Kgs. 11:6">2Kgs. 11:6</ref>).

column5: Capital city of the Persian Empire
column7: A lily, the Susa of Greek and Roman writers, once the capital of Elam. It lay in the uplands of Susiana, on the east of the Tigris, about 150 miles to the north of the head of the Persian Gulf. It is the modern Shush, on the northwest of Shuster. Once a magnificent city, it is now an immense mass of ruins.

column5: Woman who helped support Jesus and his disciples
column7: Lily, with other pious women, ministered to Jesus ([[@42008003|Luke 8:3]]).

column5: Father of the Manassite spy Gaddi
column7: The father of Gaddi, who was one of the twelve spies ([[@4013011|Num. 13:11]]).

column5: Samaritan city near Jacob's well
column7: Liar or drunkard (see [[@23028001|Isa. 28:1]], [[@23028007|Isa. 28:7]]), has been from the time of the Crusaders usually identified with Sychem or Shechem ([[@43004005|John 4:5]]).

column5: Southern border of Egypt, modern-day Aswan
column7: Opening ([[@26029010|Ezek. 29:10]]; [[@26030006|Ezek 30:6]]), a town of Egypt, on the borders of Ethiopia, now called Assouan, on the right bank of the Nile, notable for its quarries of beautiful red granite called “syenite.”

(Gr. sunagoge, i.e., “an assembly”), found only once in the Authorized Version of [[@19074008|Ps. 74:8]], where the margin of Revised Version has “places of assembly,” which is probably correct; for while the origin of synagogues is unknown, it may well be supposed that buildings or tents for the accommodation of worshippers may have existed in the land from an early time, and thus the system of synagogues would be gradually developed.

column5: Woman in the Philippian church whom Paul exhorted
column7: Fortunate; affable, a female member of the church at Philippi, whom Paul beseeches to be of one mind with Euodias ([[@50004002|Phil. 4:2]], [[@50004003|Phil 4:3]]).

column5: City in Sicily where Paul's ship stopped
column7: A city on the south-east coast of Sicily, where Paul landed and remained three days when on his way to Rome ([[@44028012|Acts 28:12]]). It was distinguished for its magnitude and splendour.

column5: Ancient region north of Israel, often in conflict
column6: highness, magnificence, one that deceives; curse
column7: (Heb. Aram), the name in the Old Testament given to the whole country which lay to the north-east of Phoenicia, extending to beyond the Euphrates and the Tigris. Mesopotamia is called ([[@1024010|Gen. 24:10]]; [[@5023004|Deut. 23:4]]) Aram-naharain (=Syria of the two rivers), also Padan-aram ([[@1025020|Gen. 25:20]]). Other portions of Syria were also known by separate names, as Aram-maahah ([[@13019006|1 Chr. 19:6]]), Aram-beth-rehob ([[@10010006|2 Sam. 10:6]]), Aram-zobah ([[@10010006|2 Sam. 10:6]], [[@10010008|2 Sam. 10:8]]).

column5: Dangerous shallow waters off the coast of Libya
column7: Syrtis, a dangerous area of shallow waters off the coast of Libya, feared by sailors (<ref="Act.27.17">Act.27.17</ref>).

column5: Canaanite city allotted to Manasseh, later a Levitical city
column6: who humbles thee; who answers thee
column7: A sandy place, an ancient royal city of the Canaanites, on the south-western border of the plain of Esdraelon, 4 miles south of Megiddo. Its king was conquered by Joshua (12:21). It was assigned to the Levites of the family of Kohath (17:11-18; 21:25). It is mentioned in the song of Deborah ([[@7005019|Judg. 5:19]]).

column5: Landmark on the border of Ephraim's territory
column7: Approach to Shiloh, a place on the border of Ephraim ([[@6016006|Josh. 16:6]]), probably the modern T’ana, a ruin 7 miles south-east of Shechem, on the ridge east of the Mukhnah plain.

column5: Family of temple servants who returned from exile
column7: Impressions; rings, “the children of,” returned from the Captivity ([[@15002043|Ezra 2:43]]).

column5: Place near where Midianites fled from Gideon
column7: Famous, a town in the tribe of Ephraim ([[@7007022|Judg. 7:22]]), to the south of Bethshean, near the Jordan.

column5: Man whom Syria and Ephraim wanted to make king of Judah
column7: Goodness of God, the father of one whom the kings of Syria and Samaria in vain attempted to place on the throne of Ahaz ([[@23007006|Isa. 7:6]]).

column5: Persian official involved in accusing the Jews to Artaxerxes
column7: A Persian governor of Samaria, who joined others in the attempt to prevent the rebuilding of Jerusalem ([[@15004007|Ezra 4:7]]).

column5: Israelite camp where God sent fire as judgment
column7: Burning, a place in the wilderness of Paran, where the “fire of the Lord” consumed the murmuring Israelites ([[@4011003|Num. 11:3]]; [[@5009022|Deut. 9:22]]).

The sacred tent (Heb. mishkan, “the dwelling-place”); the movable tent-temple which Moses erected for the service of God, according to the “pattern” which God himself showed to him on the mount ([[@2025009|Ex. 25:9]]; [[@58008005|Heb. 8:5]]).

column5: Charitable woman in Joppa whom Peter raised from the dead
column7: (in Greek called Dorcas), gazelle, a disciple at Joppa. She was distinguished for her alms-deeds and good works. Peter, who was sent for from Lydda on the occasion of her death, prayed over the dead body, and said, “Tabitha, arise.”

column5: Oak tree near Bethel, mentioned in Samuel's prophecy
column7: The “plain of Tabor” ([[@9010003|1 Sam. 10:3]]) should be, as in the Revised Version, “the oak of Tabor.”

column5: Mountain in Israel, site of Deborah and Barak's victory
column7: Mount Tabor, a mountain in Israel, known for the gathering of Deborah and Barak's forces and their victory over Sisera (<ref="Judg. 4:6, 12, 14">Judg. 4:6, 12, 14</ref>).

column5: Father of Ben-hadad I, king of Syria
column6: good pomegranate; the navel; the middle
column7: Good is Rimmon, the father of Benhadad, king of Syria ([[@11015018|1 Kings 15:18]]).

column5: City built by Solomon in the wilderness
column7: Palm, a city built by Solomon “in the wilderness” ([[@14008004|2 Chr. 8:4]]). In [[@11009018|1 Kings 9:18]], where the word occurs in the Authorized Version, the Hebrew text and the Revised Version read “Tamar,” which is properly a city on the southern border of Palestine and toward the wilderness (comp. [[@26047019|Ezek. 47:19]]; [[@26048028|Ezek 48:28]]). In [[@14008014|2 Chr. 8:14]] Tadmor is mentioned in connection with Hamath-zobah. It is called Palmyra by the Greeks and Romans.

column5: Son of Ephraim, ancestor of the Tahanites clan
column7: Tahan was a son of Ephraim and the ancestor of the Tahanites clan.

column5: Son of Telah, from the tribe of Ephraim
column7: Tahan was a descendant of Ephraim, the son of Telah and father of Ladan.

column5: Son of Nahor and Reumah
column6: that makes haste; that keeps silence
column7: A badger, a son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother ([[@1022024|Gen. 22:24]]).

column5: Israelite campsite during the wilderness journey
column7: Tahath, a place where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey (<ref="Num. 33:26-27">Num. 33:26-27</ref>).

column5: Levite of the Kohathite clan, son of Assir
column7: Tahath was a Levite of the Kohathite clan, the son of Assir and father of Uriel.

column5: Egyptian city where Jewish refugees fled after Jerusalem's destruction
column7: =Tahpanhes=Tehaphnehes, (called “Daphne” by the Greeks, now Tell Defenneh), an ancient Egyptian city, on the Tanitic branch of the Nile, about 16 miles from Pelusium. The Jews from Jerusalem fled to this place after the death of Gedaliah (q.v.), and settled there for a time ([[@24002016|Jer. 2:16]]; [[@24043007|Jer 43:7]]; [[@24044001|Jer 44:1]]; [[@24046014|Jer 46:14]]). A platform of brick-work, which there is every reason to believe was the pavement at the entry of Pharaoh’s palace, has been discovered at this place. “Here,” says the discoverer, Mr.

column5: Egyptian queen who raised Hadad the Edomite
column7: The wife of Pharaoh, who gave her sister in marriage to Hadad the Edomite ([[@11011019|1 Kings 11:19]], [[@11011020|1 Kings 11:20]]).

column5: A place visited during David's census of Israel
column6: one who is broken; who fears
column7: The land of the newly inhabited, ([[@10024006|2 Sam. 24:6]]). It is conjectured that, instead of this word, the reading should be, “the Hittites of Kadesh,” the Hittite capital, on the Orontes.

Of silver contained 3,000 shekels ([[@2038025|Ex. 38:25]], [[@2038026|Ex. 38:26]]), and was equal to 94 3/7 lbs. avoirdupois. The Greek talent, however, as in the LXX., was only 82 1/4 lbs. It was in the form of a circular mass, as the Hebrew name kikkar denotes. A talent of gold was double the weight of a talent of silver ([[@10012030|2 Sam. 12:30]]).

column5: Anakim king of Hebron, defeated by Judah
column6: my furrow; that suspends the waters; heap of waters
column7: One of the Anakim of Hebron, who were slain by the men of Judah under Caleb ([[@4013022|Num. 13:22]]; [[@6015014|Josh. 15:14]]; [[@7001010|Judg. 1:10]]).

column5: King of Geshur; father of David's wife Maacah
column6: my furrow; that suspends the waters; heap of waters
column7: A king of Geshur, to whom Absalom fled after he had put Amnon to death ([[@10003003|2 Sam. 3:3]]; [[@10013037|2 Sam. 13:37]]).

column5: Levite gatekeeper who returned from Babylonian exile
column7: Talmon was a Levite gatekeeper who returned from Babylon and served at the temple.

column5: Judah's daughter-in-law who bore Perez and Zerah
column7: The daughter-in-law of Judah, to whose eldest son, Er, she was married ([[@1038006|Gen. 38:6]]). After her husband’s death, she was married to Onan, his brother (8), and on his death, Judah promised to her that his third son, Shelah, would become her husband.

column5: David's daughter, raped by her half-brother Amnon
column7: A daughter of David ([[@10013001-10013032|2 Sam. 13:1-32]]; [[@13003009|1 Chr. 3:9]]), whom Amnon shamefully outraged and afterwards “hated exceedingly,” thereby illustrating the law of human nature noticed even by the heathen, “Proprium humani ingenii est odisse quem laeseris”, i.e., “It is the property of human nature to hate one whom you have injured.”

column5: Absalom's beautiful daughter
column7: Tamar was the beautiful daughter of Absalom, named after his tragic sister.

column5: Landmark on the southeastern border of Israel
column7: Tamar, a place mentioned as a landmark on the southeastern border of the Promised Land (<ref="Ezek. 47:18-19; 48:28">Ezek. 47:18-19; 48:28</ref>).

column5: Supporter of Gedaliah after Jerusalem's fall
column7: Consolation, a Netophathite; one of the captains who supported Gedaliah ([[@12025023|2 Kings 25:23]]; [[@24040008|Jer. 40:8]]).

column5: Daughter of Solomon; wife of Ben-abinadab
column7: Taphath was a daughter of Solomon who married Ben-abinadab, one of Solomon's district governors.

column5: Canaanite city allotted to Ephraim and Manasseh
column7: A town in the valley or lowland of Judah; formerly a royal city of the Canaanites ([[@6012017|Josh. 12:17]]; [[@6015034|Josh 15:34]]).

column5: Town in the Judean Shephelah
column7: A town in the valley or lowland of Judah; formerly a royal city of the Canaanites ([[@6012017|Josh. 12:17]]; [[@6015034|Josh 15:34]]).

column5: Son of Hebron from the tribe of Judah
column7: Tappuah was a son of Hebron, a descendant of Judah.

column5: Town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin
column7: Taralah, a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin (<ref="Josh. 18:27">Josh. 18:27</ref>).

column5: Son of Micah and grandson of Mephibosheth
column7: Tarea, also called Tahrea, was a son of Micah and grandson of Mephibosheth.

column5: Son of Javan, great-grandson of Noah
column7: Tarshish was a son of Javan and great-grandson of Noah, associated with the ancient city of Tarshish.

column5: Distant maritime city known for its wealth and trade
column7: The name of a place which first comes into notice in the days of Solomon. The question as to the locality of Tarshish has given rise to not a little discussion. Some think there was a Tarshish in the East, on the Indian coast, seeing that “ships of Tarshish” sailed from Eziongeber, on the Red Sea ([[@11009026|1 Kings 9:26]]; [[@11022048|1 Kings 22:48]]; [[@14009021|2 Chr. 9:21]]). Some, again, argue that Carthage was the place so named.

column5: Son of Bilhan from the tribe of Benjamin
column7: Tarshish was a son of Bilhan, a descendant of Benjamin.

column5: One of the seven princes of Persia and Media
column7: Tarshish was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media who had access to King Ahasuerus's presence and held the highest positions in the kingdom.

column5: City in Cilicia, birthplace of the apostle Paul
column7: The chief city of Cilicia. It was distinguished for its wealth and for its schools of learning, in which it rivalled, nay, excelled even Athens and Alexandria, and hence was spoken of as “no mean city.” It was the native place of the Apostle Paul ([[@44021039|Acts 21:39]]). It stood on the banks of the river Cydnus, about 12 miles north of the Mediterranean.

column5: Title of an Assyrian military commander
column7: One of Sennacherib’s messengers to Hezekiah ([[@12018017|2 Kings 18:17]]).

column5: Persian governor who questioned the Jews' authority to rebuild
column6: that gives; the overseer of the gifts and tributes
column7: Gift, a Persian governor (Heb. pehah, i.e., “satrap;” modern “pasha”) “on this side the river”, i.e., of the whole tract on the west of the Euphrates. This Hebrew title pehah is given to governors of provinces generally. It is given to Nehemiah (5:14) and to Zerubbabel ([[@37001001|Hag. 1:1]]). It is sometimes translated “captain” ([[@11020024|1 Kings 20:24]]; [[@27003002|Dan. 3:2]], [[@27003003|Dan. 3:3]]), sometimes also “deputy” ([[@17008009|Esther 8:9]]; [[@17009003|Esther 9:3]]).

One who farmed the taxes (e.g., Zacchaeus, [[@42019002|Luke 19:2]]) to be levied from a town or district, and thus undertook to pay to the supreme government a certain amount. In order to collect the taxes, the publicans employed subordinates (5:27; 15:1; 18:10), who, for their own ends, were often guilty of extortion and peculation. In New Testament times these taxes were paid to the Romans, and hence were regarded by the Jews as a very heavy burden, and hence also the collectors of taxes, who were frequently Jews, were hated, and were usually spoken of in very opprobrious terms.

column5: Son of Nahor and Reumah
column6: murder; butchery; guarding of the body; a cook
column7: Tebah was a son of Abraham's brother Nahor and his concubine Reumah.

column5: Levite gatekeeper, son of Hosah
column6: baptism, or goodness, of the Lord
column7: Tebaliah was a Levite gatekeeper, the third son of Hosah.

column5: Father of Ir-nahash from the tribe of Judah
column7: Tehinnah was the father of Ir-nahash and a descendant of Chelub from the tribe of Judah.

column5: Town in Judah, home of the prophet Amos
column7: Tekoa, a town in Judah, known as the birthplace of the prophet Amos and the home of one of David's mighty men (<ref="2Sam. 14:2; 1Chr. 11:28; Amo.1.1">2Sam. 14:2; 1Chr. 11:28; Amo.1.1</ref>).

column5: Settlement of exiled Jews in Babylonia
column7: Hill of corn, a place on the river Chebar, the residence of Ezekiel ([[@26003015|Ezek. 3:15]]).

column5: Babylonian city from which exiles returned
column7: Hill of the wood, a place in Babylon from which some captive Jews returned to Jerusalem ([[@15002059|Ezra 2:59]]; [[@16007061|Neh. 7:61]]).

column5: Babylonian city from which exiles returned
column7: Hill of salt, a place in Babylon from which the Jews returned (id.).

column5: Son of Resheph from the tribe of Ephraim
column7: Telah was a descendant of Ephraim, the son of Resheph and father of Tahan.

column5: Place where Saul gathered his army
column7: Young lambs, a place at which Saul gathered his army to fight against Amalek ([[@9015004|1 Sam. 15:4]]); probably the same as Telem (2).

column5: Mesopotamian city conquered by the Assyrians
column7: Or Thelasar, ([[@23037012|Isa. 37:12]]; [[@12019012|2 Kings 19:12]]), a province in the south-east of Assyria, probably in Babylonia.

column5: Town in the Negev region of Judah
column7: A town in the southern border of Judah ([[@6015024|Josh. 15:24]]); probably the same as Telaim.

column5: Temple servant who married a foreign wife
column7: Telem was a temple servant who married a foreign wife during the Exile and later divorced her.

column5: Son of Ishmael, associated with an Arabian city
column7: South; desert, one of the sons of Ishmael, and father of a tribe so called ([[@1025015|Gen. 25:15]]; [[@13001030|1 Chr. 1:30]]; [[@18006019|Job 6:19]]; [[@23021014|Isa. 21:14]]; [[@24025023|Jer. 25:23]]) which settled at a place to which he gave his name, some 250 miles south-east of Edom, on the route between Damascus and Mecca, in the northern part of the Arabian peninsula, toward the Syrian desert; the modern Teyma’.

column5: Arabian city and tribe known for trade
column7: South; desert, one of the sons of Ishmael, and father of a tribe so called ([[@1025015|Gen. 25:15]]; [[@13001030|1 Chr. 1:30]]; [[@18006019|Job 6:19]]; [[@23021014|Isa. 21:14]]; [[@24025023|Jer. 25:23]]) which settled at a place to which he gave his name, some 250 miles south-east of Edom, on the route between Damascus and Mecca, in the northern part of the Arabian peninsula, toward the Syrian desert; the modern Teyma’.

column5: Ancestor of a family of temple servants
column7: Temah was the ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned from the Babylonian exile.

column5: Grandson of Esau, associated with an Edomite clan
column7: A grandson of Esau, one of the “dukes of Edom” ([[@1036011|Gen. 36:11]], [[@1036015|Gen 36:15]], [[@1036042|Gen 36:42]]).

column5: Region and town in Edom, known for wisdom
column7: A place in Southern Idumea, the land of “the sons of the east,” frequently mentioned in the Old Testament. It was noted for the wisdom of its inhabitants ([[@30001012|Amos 1:12]]; Obad. 1:8; [[@24049007|Jer. 49:7]]; [[@26025013|Ezek. 25:13]]).

column5: Son of Ashhur (or 'Ashur') from the tribe of Judah
column7: One of the sons of Ashur, the father of Tekoa ([[@13004006|1 Chr. 4:6]]).

Heb. succah ([[@10011011|2 Sam. 11:11]]), a tent or booth made of green boughs or branches (see [[@1033017|Gen. 33:17]]; [[@3023034|Lev. 23:34]], [[@3023042|Lev. 23:42]]; [[@19018011|Ps. 18:11]]; [[@32004005|Jonah 4:5]]; [[@23004006|Isa. 4:6]]; [[@16008015-16008017|Neh. 8:15-17]], where the word is variously rendered). Jubal was “the father of such as dwell in tents” ([[@1004020|Gen. 4:20]]).

column5: Abraham's father who settled in Haran
column7: The wanderer; loiterer, for some unknown reason emigrated with his family from his native mountains in the north to the plains of Mesopotamia. He had three sons, Haran, Nahor, and Abraham, and one daughter, Sarah. He settled in “Ur of the Chaldees,” where his son Haran died, leaving behind him his son Lot. Nahor settled at Haran, a place on the way to Ur.

column5: Israelite campsite during the wilderness journey
column7: The wanderer; loiterer, for some unknown reason emigrated with his family from his native mountains in the north to the plains of Mesopotamia. He had three sons, Haran, Nahor, and Abraham, and one daughter, Sarah. He settled in “Ur of the Chaldees,” where his son Haran died, leaving behind him his son Lot. Nahor settled at Haran, a place on the way to Ur.

column5: Persian official who plotted against King Ahasuerus
column7: Severe, a eunuch or chamberlain in the palace of Ahasuerus, who conspired with another to murder him. The plot was detected by Mordecai, and the conspirators were put to death ([[@17002021|Esther 2:21]]; [[@17006002|Esther 6:2]]).

column5: Paul's scribe who wrote the Epistle to the Romans
column7: The third, a Roman Christian whom Paul employed as his amanuensis in writing his epistle to the Romans (16:22).

column5: Lawyer who accused Paul before Governor Felix
column7: A modification of “Tertius;” a Roman advocate, whom the Jews employed to state their case against Paul in the presence of Felix ([[@44024001-44024009|Acts 24:1-9]]). The charges he adduced against the apostle were, “First, that he created disturbances among the Romans throughout the empire, an offence against the Roman government (crimen majestatis). Secondly, that he was a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes; disturbed the Jews in the exercise of their religion, guaranteed by the state; introduced new gods, a thing prohibited by the Romans.

Strictly the ruler over the fourth part of a province; but the word denotes a ruler of a province generally ([[@40014001|Matt. 14:1]]; [[@42003001|Luke 3:1]], [[@42003019|Luke 3:19]]; [[@42009007|Luke 9:7]]; [[@44013001|Acts 13:1]]). Herod and Phasael, the sons of Antipater, were the first tetrarchs in Palestine.

column5: Ancient Egyptian city, known for its wealth and power
column7: Or No-A’mon, the home of Amon, the name of Thebes, the ancient capital of what is called the Middle Empire, in Upper or Southern Egypt. “The multitude of No” ([[@24046025|Jer. 46:25]]) is more correctly rendered, as in the Revised Version, “Amon of No”, i.e., No, where Jupiter Amon had his temple. In [[@26030014|Ezek. 30:14]], [[@26030016|Ezek. 30:16]] it is simply called “No;” but in ver. 15 the name has the Hebrew Hamon prefixed to it, “Hamon No.” This prefix is probably the name simply of the god usually styled Amon or Ammon.

column5: Canaanite city where Abimelech was killed
column6: muddy; eggs; fine linen or silk
column7: Brightness, a place some 11 miles north-east of Shechem, on the road to Scythopolis, the modern Tabas.

column5: Recipient of Luke's Gospel and Acts
column7: Lover of God, a Christian, probably a Roman, to whom Luke dedicated both his Gospel ([[@42001003|Luke 1:3]]) and the Acts of the Apostles (1:1).

column5: Macedonian city, site of an early Christian church
column7: A large and populous city on the Thermaic bay. It was the capital of one of the four Roman districts of Macedonia, and was ruled by a praetor. It was named after Thessalonica, the wife of Cassander, who built the city. She was so called by her father, Philip, because he first heard of her birth on the day of his gaining a victory over the Thessalians. On his second missionary journey, Paul preached in the synagogue here, the chief synagogue of the Jews in that part of Macedonia, and laid the foundations of a church ([[@44017001-44017004|Acts 17:1-4]]; [[@52001009|1 Thes. 1:9]]).

column5: Jewish rebel leader killed by Roman authorities
column7: Thanksgiving, referred to by Gamaliel in his speech before the council at Jerusalem ([[@44005036|Acts 5:36]]). He headed an insurrection against the Roman authority.

column5: One of Jesus' twelve disciples, known for doubting
column7: Twin, one of the twelve ([[@40010003|Matt. 10:3]]; [[@41003018|Mark 3:18]], etc.). He was also called Didymus ([[@43011016|John 11:16]]; [[@43020024|John 20:24]]), which is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew name. All we know regarding him is recorded in the fourth Gospel ([[@43011015|John 11:15]], [[@43011016|John 11:16]]; 14:4, 5; 20:24, 25, 26-29).

column5: Staging post on the Appian Way near Rome
column7: Three Taverns, a staging post on the Appian Way, about 33 miles from Rome, where Paul was met by Roman Christians (<ref="Act.28.15">Act.28.15</ref>).
See AGRICULTURE.

column5: City in Asia Minor, home of the prophet Lydia
column7: A city of Asia Minor, on the borders of Lydia and Mysia. Its modern name is Ak-hissar, i.e., “white castle.” Here was one of the seven churches ([[@66001011|Rev. 1:11]]; [[@66002018-66002028|Rev 2:18-28]]). Lydia, the seller of purple, or rather of cloth dyed with this colour, was from this city ([[@44016014|Acts 16:14]]).

column5: Roman emperor during Jesus' ministry and death
column7: The title assumed by the Roman emperors after Julius Caesar. In the New Testament this title is given to various emperors as sovereigns of Judaea without their accompanying distinctive proper names ([[@43019015|John 19:15]]; [[@44017007|Acts 17:7]]). The Jews paid tribute to Caesar ([[@40022017|Matt. 22:17]]), and all Roman citizens had the right of appeal to him ([[@44025011|Acts 25:11]]).

column5: City from which David took bronze for the Temple
column6: murder; butchery; guarding of the body; a cook
column7: Tibhath, a city from which David took a large amount of bronze, used in the construction of the Temple (<ref="1Chr. 18:8">1Chr. 18:8</ref>).

column5: Rival to Omri for the throne of Israel
column7: Building of Jehovah, the son of Ginath, a man of some position, whom a considerable number of the people chose as monarch.

column5: King of Goiim, ally of Chedorlaomer
column6: that breaks the yoke; knowledge of elevation
column7: (in the LXX. called “Thorgal”), styled the “king of nations” ([[@1014001-1014009|Gen. 14:1-9]]). Mentioned as Tudkhula on Arioch’s brick (see facing page 139).

column5: Assyrian king who conquered parts of Israel
column6: that binds or takes away captivity
column7: An Assyrian king. It has been a question whether he was identical with Tiglath-pileser III. (q.v.), or was his predecessor. The weight of evidence is certainly in favour of their identity.

column5: River flowing from Eden, mentioned in Daniel's vision
column7: Called by the Accadians id Idikla; i.e., “the river of Idikla”, the third of the four rivers of Paradise ([[@1002014|Gen. 2:14]]). Gesenius interprets the word as meaning “the rapid Tigris.” The Tigris rises in the mountains of Armenia, 15 miles south of the source of the Euphrates, which, after pursuing a south-east course, it joins at Kurnah, about 50 miles above Bassorah.

column5: Father of Shallum, husband of Huldah the prophetess
column7: Tikvah, also known as Tokhath, was the father of Shallum and the father-in-law of Huldah the prophetess.

column5: Opposed Ezra's reforms regarding foreign wives
column7: Tikvah was one of two men who opposed Ezra's reforms requiring Jewish men to divorce their foreign wives.

column5: Son of Shimon from the tribe of Judah
column7: Tilon was a son of Shimon, a descendant of Judah.

column5: Father of Bartimaeus, a blind man healed by Jesus
column7: Defiled, the father of blind Bartimaeus ([[@41010046|Mark 10:46]]).

column5: Concubine of Eliphaz; mother of Amalek
column7: Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz, son of Esau, and the mother of Amalek.

column5: Canaanite city associated with Judah and Dan
column7: A town of Judah ([[@6015010|Josh. 15:10]]). The Philistines took possession of it in the days of Ahaz ([[@14028018|2 Chr. 28:18]]). It was about 20 miles west of Jerusalem.

column5: Town in the hill country of Judah
column7: A city in the mountains of Judah ([[@6015057|Josh. 15:57]])= Tibna near Jeba’.

column5: Town allotted to Joshua, where he was buried
column6: or Timnath-serah, image of the sun; numbering of the rest
column7: Portion of the sun, where Joshua was buried ([[@7002009|Judg. 2:9]]). It was “in the mount of Ephraim, in the north side of the hill Gaash,” 10 miles south-west of Shechem.

column5: One of the seven chosen to serve the church
column7: Honouring, one of the seven deacons at Jerusalem ([[@44006005|Acts 6:5]]).

column5: Paul's young disciple and co-worker
column6: honor of God; valued of God
column7: Honouring God, a young disciple who was Paul’s companion in many of his journeyings. His mother, Eunice, and his grandmother, Lois, are mentioned as eminent for their piety ([[@55001005|2 Tim. 1:5]]). We know nothing of his father but that he was a Greek ([[@44016001|Acts 16:1]]). He is first brought into notice at the time of Paul’s second visit to Lystra (16:2), where he probably resided, and where it seems he was converted during Paul’s first visit to that place ([[@54001002|1 Tim. 1:2]]; [[@55003011|2 Tim. 3:11]]).

column5: City on the Euphrates, extent of Solomon's kingdom
column7: Passing over; ford, one of the boundaries of Solomon’s dominions ([[@11004024|1 Kings 4:24]]), probably “Thapsacus, a great and wealthy town on the western bank of the Euphrates,” about 100 miles north-east of Tadmor. All the land traffic between the east and the west passed through it. Menahem undertook an expedition against this city, and “smote Tiphsah and all that were therein” ([[@12015016|2 Kings 15:16]]).

column5: City attacked by King Menahem of Israel
column7: Passing over; ford, one of the boundaries of Solomon’s dominions ([[@11004024|1 Kings 4:24]]), probably “Thapsacus, a great and wealthy town on the western bank of the Euphrates,” about 100 miles north-east of Tadmor. All the land traffic between the east and the west passed through it. Menahem undertook an expedition against this city, and “smote Tiphsah and all that were therein” ([[@12015016|2 Kings 15:16]]).

column5: Son of Japheth, grandson of Noah
column7: The youngest of the sons of Japheth ([[@1010002|Gen. 10:2]]; [[@13001005|1 Chr. 1:5]]).

column5: King of Cush (Ethiopia) who opposed Sennacherib
column7: The last king of Egypt of the Ethiopian (the fifteenth) dynasty. He was the brother-in-law of So (q.v.). He probably ascended the throne about B.C. 692, having been previously king of Ethiopia ([[@12019009|2 Kings 19:9]]; [[@23037009|Isa. 37:9]]), which with Egypt now formed one nation.

column5: Son of Caleb by his concubine Maacah
column7: Tirhanah was a son of Caleb by his concubine Maacah, mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.

column5: Son of Jehallelel from the tribe of Judah
column7: Tiria was a son of Jehallelel, a descendant of Judah, mentioned in the genealogy of Judah.

column5: Daughter of Zelophehad, granted inheritance rights
column7: Tirzah was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad who were granted inheritance rights in the absence of male heirs.

column5: Canaanite city that became the capital of Israel
column7: Tirzah, a Canaanite city captured by Joshua, later served as the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel before Samaria (<ref="Josh. 12:24; 1Kgs. 14:17; 15:21, 33; 16:6-23">Josh. 12:24; 1Kgs. 14:17; 15:21, 33; 16:6-23</ref>).

column5: Hometown of the prophet Elijah
column7: Elijah the prophet was thus named ([[@11017001|1 Kings 17:1]]; [[@11021017|1 Kings 21:17]], [[@11021028|1 Kings 21:28]], etc.). In [[@11017001|1 Kings 17:1]] the word rendered “inhabitants” is in the original the same as that rendered “Tishbite,” hence that verse may be read as in the LXX., “Elijah the Tishbite of Tishbi in Gilead.” Some interpret this word as meaning “stranger,” and read the verse, “Elijah the stranger from among the strangers in Gilead.”

A tenth of the produce of the earth consecrated and set apart for special purposes. The dedication of a tenth to God was recognized as a duty before the time of Moses. Abraham paid tithes to Melchizedek ([[@1014020|Gen. 14:20]]; [[@58007006|Heb. 7:6]]); and Jacob vowed unto the Lord and said, “Of all that thou shalt give me I will surely give the tenth unto thee.” The first Mosaic law on this subject is recorded in [[@3027030-3027032|Lev. 27:30-32]].

column5: Gentile convert and companion of Paul
column7: Honourable, was with Paul and Barnabas at Antioch, and accompanied them to the council at Jerusalem ([[@48002001-48002003|Gal. 2:1-3]]; [[@44015002|Acts 15:2]]), although his name nowhere occurs in the Acts of the Apostles. He appears to have been a Gentile, and to have been chiefly engaged in ministering to Gentiles; for Paul sternly refused to have him circumcised, inasmuch as in his case the cause of gospel liberty was at stake.

column5: Clan from the tribe of Manasseh
column7: The Tizites were a clan from the tribe of Manasseh, mentioned among the mighty warriors who joined David at Ziklag.

column5: Region where Jephthah fled and recruited mercenaries
column7: Tob (or Ish-tob), a region east of the Jordan River where Jephthah fled and later recruited mercenaries to fight the Ammonites (<ref="Judg. 11:3, 5; 2Sam. 10:6, 8">Judg. 11:3, 5; 2Sam. 10:6, 8</ref>).

column5: Levite sent by Jehoshaphat to teach the Law
column6: my good God; the goodness of the foundation of the Lord
column7: Good is Jehovah, my Lord, a Levite sent out by Jehoshaphat to instruct the people of Judah in the law ([[@14017008|2 Chr. 17:8]]).

column5: Ancestor of returned exiles unable to prove lineage
column7: Pleasing to Jehovah, the “servant,” the “Ammonite,” who joined with those who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the Exile ([[@16002010|Neh. 2:10]]). He was a man of great influence, which he exerted in opposition to the Jews, and “sent letters” to Nehemiah “to put him in fear” ([[@16006017-16006019|Neh. 6:17-19]]).

column5: Ammonite official who opposed Nehemiah's rebuilding efforts
column7: Pleasing to Jehovah, the “servant,” the “Ammonite,” who joined with those who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the Exile ([[@16002010|Neh. 2:10]]). He was a man of great influence, which he exerted in opposition to the Jews, and “sent letters” to Nehemiah “to put him in fear” ([[@16006017-16006019|Neh. 6:17-19]]).

column5: Levite sent by Jehoshaphat to teach the Law
column7: Id., a Levite sent out through Judah by Jehoshaphat to teach the people ([[@14017008|2 Chr. 17:8]]).

column5: Postexilic Jew who provided silver and gold for crowns
column7: Id., a Levite sent out through Judah by Jehoshaphat to teach the people ([[@14017008|2 Chr. 17:8]]).

column5: Town in the territory of Simeon
column7: Tochen, a town allotted to the tribe of Simeon (<ref="1Chr. 4:32">1Chr. 4:32</ref>).

column5: Son of Gomer, grandson of Japheth
column7: A son of Gomer, and grandson of Japheth ([[@1010003|Gen. 10:3]]).

column5: Ancestor of the prophet Samuel
column7: Tohu, also known as Nahath or Toah, was an ancestor of the prophet Samuel, mentioned in his genealogy.

column5: King of Hamath who sent his son to David
column7: A king of Hamath, who sent “Joram his son unto King David to salute him,” when he “heard that David had smitten all the host of Hadadezer” ([[@10008009|2 Sam. 8:9]], [[@10008010|2 Sam. 8:10]]).

column5: Son of Issachar, ancestor of the Tolaites
column7: Tola was a son of Issachar and the ancestor of the Tolaite clan.

column5: Judge of Israel who succeeded Abimelech
column7: A judge of the tribe of Issachar who “judged” Israel twenty-three years ([[@7010001|Judg. 10:1]], [[@7010002|Judg 10:2]]), when he died, and was buried in Shamir.

column5: Town in the territory of Simeon
column7: Productive, a town of Simeon, in the south of Judah ([[@13004029|1 Chr. 4:29]]).

column5: A place near where Moses addressed the Israelites
column7: Lime, a place in the wilderness of Sinai ([[@5001001|Deut. 1:1]]), now identified with Tafyleh or Tufileh, on the west side of the Edomitish mountains.

column5: Site of pagan child sacrifice, south of Jerusalem
column7: =Topheth, from Heb. toph “a drum,” because the cries of children here sacrificed by the priests of Moloch were drowned by the noise of such an instrument; or from taph or toph, meaning “to burn,” and hence a place of burning, the name of a particular part in the valley of Hinnom. “Fire being the most destructive of all elements, is chosen by the sacred writers to symbolize the agency by which God punishes or destroys the wicked. We are not to assume from prophetical figures that material fire is the precise agent to be used.

column5: A tower near Bethlehem, associated with the Messiah
column7: The Tower of Eder, a watchtower near Bethlehem, where Jacob pitched his tent and later associated with the coming of the Messiah (<ref="Gen. 35:21; Mic. 4:8">Gen. 35:21; Mic. 4:8</ref>).

column5: A tower in Jerusalem's wall, rebuilt by Nehemiah
column7: The Tower of Hananel, a tower in Jerusalem's wall, rebuilt by Nehemiah and mentioned in prophetic visions of the city's restoration (<ref="Neh. 3:1; 12:39; Jer. 31:38; Zech. 14:10">Neh. 3:1; 12:39; Jer. 31:38; Zech. 14:10</ref>).

column5: A tower in Jerusalem's wall, rebuilt by Nehemiah
column7: The Tower of the Ovens, a tower in Jerusalem's wall, rebuilt during Nehemiah's restoration of the city (<ref="Neh. 3:11; 12:38">Neh. 3:11; 12:38</ref>).

column5: A rugged region northeast of the Jordan River
column7: A rugged region, corresponds to the Heb. Argob (q.v.), the Greek name of a region on the east of Jordan ([[@42003001|Luke 3:1]]); one of the five Roman provinces into which that district was divided.

(Heb. ‘asham, “debt”), the law concerning, given in [[@3005014-3006007|Lev. 5:14-6:7]]; also in [[@4005005-4005008|Num. 5:5-8]]. The idea of sin as a “debt” pervades this legislation. The asham , which was always a ram, was offered in cases where sins were more private.

column5: A city in Asia Minor, visited by Paul
column7: A city on the coast of Mysia, in the north-west of Asia Minor, named after ancient Troy, which was at some little distance from it (about 4 miles) to the north. Here Paul, on his second missionary journey, saw the vision of a “man of Macedonia,” who appeared to him, saying, “Come over, and help us” ([[@44016008-44016011|Acts 16:8-11]]). He visited this place also on other occasions, and on one of these visits he left his cloak and some books there ([[@47002012|2 Cor. 2:12]]; [[@55004013|2 Tim. 4:13]]).

column5: A city near Ephesus, visited by Paul
column7: A town on the western coast of Asia Minor, where Paul “tarried” when on his way from Assos to Miletus, on his third missionary journey ([[@44020015|Acts 20:15]]).

column5: Gentile Christian from Ephesus, companion of Paul
column7: A foster-child, an Ephesian who accompanied Paul during a part of his third missionary journey ([[@44020004|Acts 20:4]]; [[@44021029|Acts 21:29]]). He was with Paul in Jerusalem, and the Jews, supposing that the apostle had brought him with him into the temple, raised a tumult which resulted in Paul’s imprisonment. (See TEMPLE, HEROD’S.) In writing to Timothy, the apostle says, “Trophimus have I left at Miletum sick” ([[@55004020|2 Tim. 4:20]]).

Were of a great variety of forms, and were made of divers materials. Some were made of silver ([[@4010002|Num. 10:2]]), and were used only by the priests in announcing the approach of festivals and in giving signals of war. Some were also made of rams’ horns ([[@6006008|Josh. 6:8]]). They were blown at special festivals, and to herald the arrival of special seasons ([[@3023024|Lev. 23:24]]; [[@3025009|Lev 25:9]]; [[@13015024|1 Chr. 15:24]]; [[@14029027|2 Chr. 29:27]]; [[@19081003|Ps. 81:3]]; [[@19098006|Ps 98:6]]).

column5: Christian woman in Rome greeted by Paul
column7: Tryphaena was a Christian woman in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings in his letter to the Romans.

column5: Christian woman in Rome greeted by Paul
column7: Tryphosa was a Christian woman in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings in his letter to the Romans.

column5: Son of Japheth, grandson of Noah
column7: Tubal was a son of Japheth and grandson of Noah, mentioned in the Table of Nations.

column5: A nation, descendant of Japheth, known for trading
column7: A nation, probably descended from the son of Japheth. It is mentioned by Isaiah (66:19), along with Javan, and by Ezekiel (27:13), along with Meshech, among the traders with Tyre, also among the confederates of Gog ([[@26038002|Ezek. 38:2]], [[@26038003|Ezek. 38:3]]; 39:1), and with Meshech among the nations which were to be destroyed (32:26).

column5: Faithful companion and messenger of Paul
column7: Chance, an Asiatic Christian, a “faithful minister in the Lord” ([[@49006021|Eph. 6:21]], [[@49006022|Eph. 6:22]]), who, with Trophimus, accompanied Paul on a part of his journey from Macedonia to Jerusalem ([[@44020004|Acts 20:4]]).

column5: Ephesian teacher who hosted Paul's discussions
column7: Prince, a Greek rhetorician, in whose “school” at Ephesus Paul disputed daily for the space of two years with those who came to him ([[@44019009|Acts 19:9]]).
